BESIDE THE SEA.

rp on the hill where t he odorous heather Mingles is sweets with the breath of the sea, Merrily singing and laughing together, Weaving with flower-ban is love's thrice-welcome tether, In bright summer sunshine, my true love and me. what did we say in the bright summer weather, With the bloom on the flower and thelight on the sea? What were the words that we murmured tegether, That made her cheeks glow like the flowers in the tether That bound us together, my true love and me?. ;--" Cassell's Magazine" for February.
TILE VOCATII

Noble be mail, Friendly and good, For goodness alone Stamps him diverse From all the creatures That walk the earth. Hail to the unknown Mightier beings Whom we anticipate What in the human lyped we behold _cads to a faith In the primal divine. For Nature knows No feeling for man. The sun doth shine On the bad and the good; On fair and on foul With indifferent eye Look moon and stars. Wind and water, Thunder and hail, Bush on their path, And with hasty clutch They seize as they pass This one and that.
Even so Fortune Blindly seizes Now the light locks Of innocent boyhood, Now the bald crown Of the hcary offender. Bound by eternal All-embracing, Iron decrees,
ON OF MAN.

We must accomplish Each man his fated Circle of being. But in the human Range of his action Man, like a god, May achieve the impossible; He distinguishes, Chooses, and judges, And gives to the moment The stamp of endurance. He alone Rewardeth the good, Chastiseth the bad. And all extravagant Random endeavours Binds with the bond Of a common design. And we wisely Adore the immortals, Deeming them brothered With what is most human, In the great cosmos, Willing and working What in their small lives Men may achieve. The noble man Be friendly and good, Shaping unwearied, The useful, the right, Planting before us A sensible type Of those beings unseen Whom by faith we divine! —Goethe.

The esthetes now speak of hash as "a mosaic." • Theatrical managers are known by the company they keep. A coal fire is a grate comfort, but a nutmeg often suggests a grater. 'The tobacco crop of Virginia yields b•at half a crop this year. Fortunately there are cabbages in this country to sup- ply the deficiency. IT'S a WEIENESS.—Good Samaritan: "Kb, Tam! Yonner'e the Meenister !"—Tam (glorious) : "Never heed man! A'll tell 'urn ye're—(hic)—no west !"—Fun. A farmer in Hampshire recently forwarded a letter to a • neighbouring town, requesting the postmaster to deliver i "to any respectable attorney." After a few days it wa returned with the significant endorsement, "None here." INNOCENT ESJOIMENT.—Citizen : "Did a good stbroke o' bithneth yethterday, l`do'! rho I treated the mithitb to the Moothic Hall last night—'ethood her a bottle o' Thee- dcne, and she thought it was thamgagne !—took it down beautiful !"—Punch. GOOD BUSINESS.—(Scene : Outside a hospital.)—First Patient (to second, who has fallen and broken his leg whilst! running to catch the train) : Sa you never caught the train after all, Jim ?—Second Patient (triaeophantly) : No, but I saved the railway fare !—,Tudy. "THE QUEEN'S ENGLIStei (OE SC'OTCH).—Minister : Weel, John, an hoo did ye like ma son's discoorse ? John: Wed, meenister„ ah mann admeet he's vera soond, but, oh men! he's no deep! His pronoenciation's no vera gweed ; I but ala've nae doobt impruy'!—Punch. 1 A Philadelphia lady was about engaging a servant—a : waitress. " What wages do you ask ?" she inquired. "Well," responded the girl, meditatively, "three dollars ! and a half a week if I'm expected to pass round the dishes, and three dollars if the family 'stretch' for themselves. A sacred burden is the life ye bear ; Look on it ; lift it ; bear it solemnly ; Stand up and walk beneath it steadfastly; Fail not for sorrow ; falter not for sin, But onward, and upward, till the coal you win. . Frances A. Kernb!e. A gentleman, calling on a farmer, observed :—" Mr. Jones, your clock is not right, is it ?" " Weil, you see, sir," said Mr. Jones, "nobody don't understand much about that clock 'out me. When the hands of that clock stand at tweive then it strikes two, and then I know it's 20 minutes to seven." Things which never could have made a man happy de- velop a power to make him strong. Strength and not hap- piness, or rather only that happiness which comes by strength, is the end of human living. And with that test and standard the best order and beauty reappear.—Phillips Mr. Spurgeon recently made this remark :—" Doubts aboat the fundamentals of the Gospel exist in certain churches, lam told, to a large extent. My dear friends, where there is a warm-hearted church you do not hear of ' them. /They do not come neat; it is too hot. I never saw • a fly alight on a red-hot plate." " 13. en to see Mrs. Tittletattle," said Mrs. Telltale, "and the way she ran on about you was perfectly scaedal- ous." "Sa she's been talkin,g about me, has she?" asked Mrs. Brown, quietly. . " Yee, indeed she has," replied Mrs. Telltale, with emphasis. " What a good time you two must have had," said Mrs. Brown, with a sweet smile. A man was one day wheeling a barrow across a church- yard, not 20 miles from Manchester, when he was threatened • , by a clergyman with condign punshment for his daring - outrage in polluting the consecrated ground by his wheel- barrow. The man, scratching his head, said, "I did not know bat the wheelbarrow waS consecrated, too, for I bor- rowed it of the sexton." Judge Jeremiah Black has long worn a black wig. Having , lately donned a new one, which looks still darker, and meet- ' ing Secator Blvarsl, of Delaware, the latter accosted him with, u Why, Black, how long you look ; von are not as gray as I am, and you mast be twenty years older." " Humph," said the Judge, "good reason; your hair comes by descent, ; and I get mine by purchase.' A Ca.aue TO ROBERT.—Facetious Youth: "Been busy lately, Bobby? Raneing anybody in? , No? What a ! pity ! Well, if you're hard up for a job, perhaps you'd like to take us."—Bobby : " Well, gents, Ido think, a-look in' ; careful like at the shape of your 'oath!, and aperient want of intellex, as you-oid ought to he charged with belts' with- ; out 'avin' any visible means of gettin' a livin'."—Fun. Dr. Hinchcliffe, who died Bishop of Peterborough, had much ready wit, and was extremely apt at checking those , who were fond of cavilling at the meaning of different texts • of Scripture. On being asked one day what was to be 1 under'etood by the expression, "He clothed himself with I curses as with a garment," "The clearest thing in the world," replied the doctor; "the man had a habit of swear- ing." A STRANGS Case or A Fre:E.—The story goes that in ancient days Archimedes, the famous mechanician of Syra-1 case, succeeded in destroying the ships of an enemy by ' directing the rays of the sun upon them through burning. glasses. A house in Massachusetts was nearly burnt down last summer in much the same way. On a very hot day smoke was observed to come from the sunny side of the house, and it was found that a hole had been burnt through the boarding of the dwelling, which would have been de- stroyed but for the timely discovery. A supply of water socn put an end to all danger, and on searching fcr the cause of the fire it was found a few feet distant in a pile of bright tin railkpans, some of which were placed so as to concen- trate the rays of a fierce sun upon a small part of the sur- face of the boards.—Little Folks Magazine. THE COESET.—What does the Ladies' Rational Dress Association, with Lady Hahertton at its head, say about the advertisements in the Queen anent corsets ?—" They reduce the size of the figure without causing any injurious pres- sure, while their graceful shape adds a new charm to the form." Whether the audacity or the mendacity of this statement is the greater nelv be a matter on which opinions can differ, the magnitude of each being so great. A liver compressed till the marks of the ribs are visible after death; that is not injurious pressure !" Neither is displacement of some of the less fixed organs "injurious pressure," I sup- pose. To have the viscera driven downwards until dis- placement follows is quite a trifle from the modiste's point of view, perhaps; but to the physician it is a grave matter, often entailing ill-health for the rest of a lifetime. And as to the "graceful shape" of a wasp-waisted lady, that, too, only exists from the modiste's mint of view.—Good Words A good, but we know not how true a story, is related of a venerable doctor of the exoerimental and electric school of medicine. It was one of his rules never to have anything wasted; and therefore when any prescription remained after the patient had died or recovered, he would empty it into a bottle kept for the -purpose, that became the recep- tacle of a heterogenous compound that science could not analyse. A younger member of the faculty noted this as a very singular fact, and asked of him the reason for it. The doctor hesitated a little, and then replied that, though in ordinary cases he knew well what to do, there were instances when all his medical skill failed. At such time it was his custom to resort to the big bottle, and leave nature and acci- dent to accomplish the cure. "And will you believe it ?" said he, " some of my most brilliant successes have resulted from it !" An American Democratic sneaker was addressing a large audience, and descanting with great vehemence upon the prospective tenets of Know-Nothingism with regard to foreigners, when his eye fell upon a little German Jew, a pedlar of ready-made clothing, who seemed to be very much impressed with the argument of the orator, and greedily swallowing everything he uttered. This was too good an opportunity not to be made the most of. Looking the little pedlar in the eye, he exclaimed—"Furriner, didn't you come to this country to escape from tyrannical, down. trodden, and oppressed Europe? Didn't you flee to these happy shores to live in a land of freedom, where the great right of suffrage is guaranteed to all? Didn't you, furri- ner?" He paused for a reply, when the little pedlar squeaked oat, "No, sur ; I comes to us country to sell- sheap ready-made clothes." The astonishment of the ora- tor, the shouts and roars of the multitude, cannot be de- , scribed. The speech was finished, and the orator quitted the rostrum, cursing all foreigners generally, and clothes- pedlars in particular. A circalar issued by the Society e French Agriculturists, with tle signatures of BBL De Dampier and Leconteaux, the president and secretary, a:,tact-eil to it, calls upon each member of the society to recruit each year one new mem- ber, so that the society may become "the grand army of agriculture." LOOK TO Yours MANGEL- HEAPS.—The exceptionally mild winter is developing a somewhat novel feature in mangel and other heaps of roots. Usually we can hardly put too much earth on our mangel, and for the last two or three winters the thickest of coats has proved insufficient to keep out the frost on the exposed side. It is well known that about the month of March it is a wise precaution to strip off the topmost parts of the covering to let out the beat naturally generated when roots are sprouting. It is not, however, often that this precautionary measure need be takes in January, which is our coldest month. The excep- tionally warm weather *bas, however, stimulated the dor- m Int life into action, heat has been generated, and, not find- ing a vent at the apex of the heap, rotting has ensued. We speak froth personal knowledge as well as from hearsay. A heap of parsnips showed signs of sinking in at the top, and, on opening, it was found to be rather seriously damaged. A friend informs us of a case in which the top layers of a mangel heap have been similarly affected, involving a loss of many tons. We therefore sound a warning note, that our friends may give-an eye to the stores, whether of ma.ngel, parsnips, carrots, or potatoes, on the principal that "a stitch in time saves nine."

MANAGEMENT.—' A InTierszen."—Ort a visit lately, I got a "wrinkle," by which my friend is saving close upon £2 a week in his dairy management, so I send it to yeti. If it should prove of value to others, I hope they will show it to those of their friends who do not sub- scribe to the Agricultural Gazette. The cattle in question are large-framed dairy pedigreed shorthorns. During the palmy days of shorthorn prices the calves were reared for sale, the new milk being consumed by them, with the ex. ception of sufficient to churn for butter for family use. Recently the drop in prices induced my friend to cast about for some scheme to lessen expenses, whilst not deteriorating his young stock. He is the owner of a good many horses. mostly Clydesdales; and for these it is his custom to steam the food, using cut hay, turnips, malt culms, crushed malt, Oats, irec. He likes to vary the food, using alternately such of the latter as are available. As barley is scarcely looked at this year by musters, and brings a very low price, he has hid some malted, and uses both malt and barley alternately in feeding. He had frequently heard of the virtues of hay tea for calves; bat, like many others of us, treated it as an "old wife's tile," having every faith in the efficacy of new. milk. The "broth" from the steaming of the horses' food was mostly wasted, and the hay tea recipe was recalled. He determined to give it a trial. At the time of my visit it had been in use three mouths, so that we had a fair oppor- tunite ot comparing results. For a trial only the calves over three months had been selected, the younger ones still receiving new milk. Those from three months up to six months were having twice a day one quart of new milk, two quarts of the broth or tea, two quarts of oatmeal water por- ridge, a handful of long hay, and about 11b. of oilcake per day. Calves from six months to twelve months were get- ting four quarts of tea at each end of the day, with an allowance of chopped food, compcsed of swedes, brewers' graies, barley chaff, and crushed corn or malt—the latter only once a day; also an allowance of long hay. The yoang bulls got four quarts of the tea, with two quarts of blue milk, long hay, and chop each end of the day. The railch cows are getting a cow tub of chop, such as described above, long hay, and whole swedes, twice a day; no oilcake or other artificial. They are thriving, and milking well. By this substitution of "broth" for new milk my host had been enabled to churn some 251 b. of butter additional weekly, a saving of close upon £2 per week.—R. Mater. GROWING IN INDIA.—The Indian Daily IVews (Calcutta), December 7th, gives a report of a meeting of the Agricultural and Horticultural Society of India, held the previous day, irom which we take the following infor- mation:—A letter was read from Captain Pogson on the sub- ject of maize cultivation in the Panjaub. It appears that some very successful experiments in the cultivation of a few of the best speciee of American maize have been conducted in 1881, in the Kulu district, by the Rev. Mr. Carleton, who for some years past has been living there. Some splendid specimens of stalks and cobs of the different descriptions of maize, and a large quantiiy of seed, have been ritit to the Punjab Government and district officers, and the Lieutenant- Governor, as a mark of his appreciation of the services of the Rev. Mr. Carleton, and to encourage him in his efforts to improve and increase the food' supply of the province, has given him a grant of 500 rs. The following particulars regarding the experiments will prove of interest :—Mam- moth Dent Corn: A new variety, said to yield in America, under high cultivation, up to 139 bushels per acre. In Kulu, under fairly good cultivation, a crop of nearly 100 bushels per acre has been grown, and the Rev. Mr. Carleton coneidsrs that this description surpasses all that he has ever introduced. Blount's Field Corn: This variety was intro- duced last year; it bears f four to six cobs per stalk, and promises well. Western White Corn: The Rev. Mr. Carleton introduced this variety four years ago, and it has I done remarkably well, seemingly in:proving in this country. Loagfellow's Field Corn: This variety comes from the ex- 1 trerne Northern States, especially New England, and is re- garded as one of the most prolific cf all the northern varie- ties. It ripens .very early, taking only about 70 days to grow. The crop of thi3 class was unfortunately almost entirely destroyed by monkeys. . MANCHESTER CORPORATION MANHRE. -- Writing in answer to a correspondent in the lark Lane Express, Mr. James Sutton, of Cheadle Huhne, says :—I visited the works of the company some time since, and was so convinced from the way the manure was made that it would do well that I tried it on several crops, against its value in other manures, and it has for three reasons done remarkably well. I used it last year at the ra.ee of 8 cwt. per acre for clover and rather more for swedes and potatoes, and have had capital results. It is a cheap manure, £3 per ton, and in portable 1 cwt. bane, delivered. The phosphates are low, about 5 per cent. The ammonia, however, is about 2'75 according to their last circular, but my opinion is that manure from ex- creta is of greater value than is simply shown from its analysis. Compared with some other, manures against which I have tried it, it is infinitely the best and cheapest. Your correspondent should write to the Corporation for a circular or price list, and be might then write to some per- son who has sent them testimonials for his experience on similar soil to that of his farm. I may add the Corporation will sell it by analysis should it be desired. TRAPPING RABBITS.—Mr. Joseph Saw, of Clifton Villa, Plymouth, writes to the .Maidstone an Kentish. Journal as follows :—What is it to trap a rabbit? How few people know. To trap a rabbit is to procure a powerful spring t:ap, four inehes square, with a row of teeth on each side made to fit in each, and to cut and crush with the greatest severity. This trap is plead at sunset in the hole or run of the rabbit, and in a short space of time the poor creature is secured either by both or one 9f its fore legs. In this painful condition the rabbit, with partially crushed bones, lingers on hour after hour in the most fearful agony ; the eyeballs often distended far beyond the socket, and its piti- ful cries may be heard far away, until the leg is broken off, which is frequently the case, and the pcor rabbit is found ' wandering in the woods on the three remaining legs, or on the arrival of the keeper or trapper its misery is terminated. We shall be told that this fearful cruelty is legalised—we know it to our shame. But surely the continuation of such cruelty can never be tolerated? That gentlemen such as at present compose the House of Commons can desire to per- petuate such brutality ! Men possessing the finest feeling of humanity, men of the highest possible culture, and dis- tinguished for the practice of the highest moral and domes- tic feeling, can never willingly and knowingly wish to torture any living creature; we cannot think it. The law for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, as it now stands, applies only to domestic animals ; we pray that it may be made to apply to wild animals also (and why not ?). May I ask your kind and merciful interference in this matter— to suppress a cruelty compared with which vivisection is mercy, which act of cruelty in thousands of instances is occurring daily? THE GOVERNMENT or NEW ZEALAND appears to bt in earnest about its sanitary cattle-disease legislation. From a recent Act we take the following schedule of penalties in the case of sheep-scab :—Obstructing inspection, not exceed- ing £lOO ; refusing to give evidence, £2O ; if sheep not clean nine months after inspector gives notice, not less than 3d. nor exceeding is. per sheep ; if sheep not clean six months after first conviction, not less than 4d. nor exceed- ing 25., and soon for every succeeding period of six months each ; not giving notice to neighbours, not less than £lO, and not exceeding £o0; not branding scabby sheep with 5.,l not less than 3d., and not exceeding 3s. per sheep ; not herding when directed by inspector, not less than £5, and not exceeding £2O ; removing infected sheep to another run, £5O; abandoning infected sheep on highway, £5O and imprisonment for six months; removing'. skins taken from scabby sheep, not less than £5, and not exceeding £5O; neglecting to assist inspector, £29 a day ; removing sheep from one district to another without giving seven days' -notice to inspector, not less than £lO and not exceeding £100; driving sheep through infected run, £10; driving sheep across another run without notice, not less than 3d. and not exceeding is. per sheep; when dip and material are not ready for use, not less than £25 and not exceeding £100; throwing carcase of infected sheep into ponds, not less than £5 and not exceeding £2O; not burning or burying ,dead sheep infected, per carcase, not less than 10s. and not exceeding £5; driving sheep from run not in his own occupation, £5O ; wilfully communicating scab or catarrh, guilty of misdemeanour. EARTHWORMS AND AGRICULTURE.—The subject of earth- worms has been shown by Darwin to be both interesting and important. Dr. Gilbert, of Rothamsted, has recently made some experiments in order to ascertain the proportion of nitrogen in their castings. These worm casts, according to Mr. Darwin, .amount to about 17 or 18 tons per annum per acre of two inches in depth. Dr. Gilbert collected the s nests of two or three weeks' formation, and found by analy- tie that they contained 35'0 per cent, of nitrogen, which is

much higher than that cotiGined in ordinary mould. It is - two or three times as high as that of arable land, is higher than that of pasture land, which has been found to contain 25.3 per cent. in the first nine inches of soil, but is not so rich as highly-manured kitchen-garden mould. Ten tons of these castings per annum would yield 80 lbs. of nitrogen per acre, or more than double that of ordinary meadows without manure. Dr. Gilbert's conclusions, however, were that no gain accrued to the soil, except what the worme brought up from below as by trenching. CONDENSED MILL—In the report on condensed milk by Dr: Yoelckee, pUblished ia the Journal of the Dairy Farmers' Association, it is stated that the majority of the samples re- presented partially skimmed milk evaporated at a low tem- perature, and with the addition of white refined sugar, A few exhibits were unsweetened milk, or milk evaporated to a certain consistency without the addition of sugar. Two of these samples contained about 57 per cent. of water. In the preparation of these, and the sweetened samples of con- densed milk, neither boracic acid, ,borax, nor preparations containing boracic acid (glacialine), nor salicylic acid, nor other preservative agents had been used. Really good con- densed milk, as a matter of fact, is always made from skim milk, or from milk unusually poor in cream. In the form of the well-known thick, honey-like preparations, condensed sweet milk is a useful article of food on board ship, or under all circumstances when fresh milk cannot be procured. It is preferable to milk powders, obtained by evaporating skim milk completely to dryness, and, with the addition of some sugar, reducing the residue to powder. It is not a perfect substitute for new milk, either chemically or physically. At the best, most kinds of good condensed milk are milk-syrups consisting of concentrated skim milk and white sugar.

XSTRETICISM.—The fashion perversely called "Esthe- ticism" is said, on the authority of M. Jules Claretie, to have crossed the Channel, and to have penetrated as far as Paris. There, as here (and as in New York), the women have began to indulge in that chromatic misery—the "green and yellow melancholy"—which is supposed to distinguish the eEsthetic habit of attire. It remains to be seen if the craze will spread. It is not too much to say that everything depends on the caricaturists. If M. Grevin and his fellows will only let the mania alone, and refrain from encouraging and fostering it by thinking it worth nctice, it should vanish instantly: as, but for the violent attentions of Messrs. Gil- bert and Du Maurier and Barnard, it would probably have vanished from among ourselves.—The 3fagazine of Art. LISTON BIDDING AT MATREWS' AIICTION.—Daring one of Mr. Mathew's performances at Brighton, while he was singing that part of his "Auction Song" where he solicits biddings for a particular "lot," after looking round the house, and making several appeals, exclaiming, " Only three pounds offered !—only three !" a voice from one of the pub- lic boxes, which it was impossible to mistake, cried out, "Four !" He turned to the spot to which every other eye alsa was directed. Though taken by surprise, he was not, however, thrown off his guard, but bowing smartly, a la Robins, exclaimed," Much obliged '--yours, sir." This bid- ding was made by Mr. Liston, who was seized, as he after- wards declared, to put up for a lot, in order to surprise his brother-actor; and was confounded after he had done it, and heard the roar of laughter he had caused, and the notice he had drawn upon himself.—Memoirs of Charles Mathews. ONE WAY FOR A GENFLEAIAN TO " PROPOSE."—A gentle, man had long been paying attention to a young lady whom he was anxious to marry, but to whom he had never ventured to declare his 'erasion. When opportunity offered, his cour- age deserted him, and when he was resolved to speak the fair one never could be found alone or disengaged. Driven to desperation he one day succeeding in accomplishing his purpose in a somewhat remarkable manner at a dinner party. To most people a dinner party would hardly seem the most suitable occasion for overtures of this description, especially when, as in this instance, the lady is seated at the opposite aide of the table from her admirer. The latter, however, was equal to the occasion. Tearing a leaf from his pocket-book he wrote on it, under cover of the table: "Will you be my wife? Write 4 Yes' or No' at the foot of this." Calling a servant, he asked him in a whisper to take the slip—which, of course, was carefully folded and directed—to "the lady in blue opposite." The servant did as requested; and the gentleman, in an agony of suspense, watched him give it to the lady, and fixed his eyes, with badly disguised eagerness to try and judge from her expression how the quaintly made offer was received. He had forgotten one thing—namely, ' that ladies seldom carry pencils about them at a dinner party. The beloved one was, however, not to be biffled by so trifling an obstacle. After reading the note calmly, she turned to servant and said, "Tell the gentleman, Yes." They were married in due course.—Chennbers's Journal.

HYPOCRISY OF THE PHARISEES.—On the evening* before the Sabbath they deposited some food at a distance of 2,000 yards from their own house, thus creating a fictitious home; from this fictitious home they could then go 2,000 yards farther to the place of meeting, thus giving themselves doable the real distance! This piece of transparent hypo- crisy was euphemistically described as an ideal amalgama- tion of distances, or " connection of places," and was called eriihh (" mixture "), a name under which it exists to the present day. In order to get over the second difficulty a still more miserable subterfuge was adopted, by putting door-posts and lintels at the end of various streets so that all the space between them might be regarded as one large house! Could any words of burning denunciation be too strong to denounce such a playing at "fast and loose" with obligations which they professed to regard as infinitely and divinely sacred, and the violation of which they were ready to avenge by inflicting death on the transgressor? They must have thought that both their Deity and their con- science were easily cheated! The Saddacees got over the difficulty, too, in a manner more daring, but infinitely less despicable, by calmly asserting that their meals were a con- tinuation of the Temple service, and therefore claiming the benefit of the maxim, that there was "no sabbatism in the Temple." These instances might be indefinitely plied: e.g., if a Jew's ox is dying, he may kill it on a holy day, provided he eats a piece of the meat as big as an olive, to make believe that it was killed for a necessary meal. If a Jew wants to bay anything which is sold by weight or measure on a holy day, he may do so, provided that he pays the next day, and does not mention the name, weight. or measure. If a Jew wants to buy cattle,fowls,&c., on a holy day, he may do so, only be must not mention money or the number required. He may buy from a butcher on a holy day, only he must not say, "Give me meat for so much money," but only " Give me a portion, OP half a portion," and he pays for it next day. Can any stretch of charity, however tender, avoid calling this the legality of evasion designed to cheat God with the letter instead of the spirit ? Is the word " hypocrites " too strong for those who thus reduced shiftiness to a sacred system ?—Canon Farrar's "Life of Christ."

THE LAND QUESTION, xix.

Having seen the great advantages resulting from the re- I form of the land laws on the Continent, and in the Channel Islands, where small holdings are the rule and not the ex- ception as with us, we are naturally led to ask,—Why should not we extend the system here, and how could it be done honestly and fairly, without injustice to anyone? Certainly this country is very differently situated to the rest of Europe in the number of its small owners who cultivate their own land. According to the return of 1873, in all Eng- land and Wales there are only 217,049 small proprietors who own over one acre and under 100 acres, or a total of 3,931,806 acres, being an average of about 18 acres each. If, however, we could ascertain the number of small pro- prietors who own over one acre and under 20 acres, and farm their own land, it is probable the number would be very small indeed. Many of those in the return are not agricul- tural owners at all, but occupants of freehold villas in the vicinity of large towns, and "their land is bestowed in lawns, in gardens, in shrubberies, in paddocks, producing nothing but perhaps a portion of the fodder required for saddle and carriage horses." What is specially required is that the ownership of land should be gradually spread among those who will themselves cultivate it, spend the most capital and labour on it, and get the greatest possible amount of produce out of it. Now, although we have seen from the experience of Con- tinental Europe and the Channel Islands, that the multi- plicity of ownerships increases the capital and labour spent on the soil, and the quantity of focd produced, and conse- quently increases the wealth of the community collectively and individually, improves the home trade, and diminishes pauperism, no English statesman or writer of any eminence advocates or even suggests the adoption of a system of com- pulsory division such as prevails in France and elsewhere, whereby the owner of land has not the legal power to leave his land by his will in favour of any particular child or children. No, the reforms advocated hereare more moderate and just, and simply consist in abolishing the means by which landed property is now arbitrarily kept in large es- tatee, in fact liberating the land from its present trammels, the relics of the old feudal system. If Primogeniture in cases of intestacy were done away with, if Entails were either prohibited altogether, or limited to people living at the time of the execution of the deed of settlement, if the present owners, or rather holders of entailed estates were enabled to sell portions and apply the purchase money towards the payment off of existing mortgages and other incumbrances, or the much needed improvement of the rest of the estate, a great extent of land now hopelessly locked up, would come into the market, and in order to fetch higher prices would often be divided and sold in smaller lots as has been the case elsewhere. These reforms must be accompa- nied by some scheme for the Registration of Titles, whereby a purchaser can have property conveyed to him with an unimpeachable title, at a fraction of the expense now in- volved in such a transaction. The fact that land could be sold and transferred as easily, quickly, and cheaply .as con- sols, would alone give a great impetus to the investing in land by those who would make the most of it, and in pro- cess of time, the number of landowners would be immensely increased, and it is to be hoped would be augmented from the ranks of the agricultural labourers. If the best of this class by wise legislation could be gradually invested with land, as has been done on the Continent, we should realise here that, as wise Adam Smith said 100 years ago, "A small proprietor, who knows every part of his little territory, views it with all the affection which property, especially! small property, naturally inspires, and who upon that ac- count, takes pleasure, not only in cultivating, but in adoring it, is generally of all improvers the most industrious, the most intelligent, and the•most successful." These changes would not break up all large estates. They would only operate in those cases where circumstances re- quired a Change, and if great landowning families like the Stanleys and Cavendishes go on generation after generation, wealthy, and able to manage their estates as well as they have done in the past, there is no reason whatever why their estates should be split up. It is where properties are so heavily encumbered, and the nominal owners are in such straitened circumstances that they have not the means to improve, and those tenants who are able dare not, that the power to sell and split up should come into operation. ' It would certainly be some time before the above-men- tioned reforms would create a very large number of small holdings, bat in the meantime would it not be the in- terest of some of the great landowners, who have now so many farms thrown on their hands, or the duty of some philanthropic landowners to try the experiment of small holdings or cottage farms on their estates something like the late Duke of Rutland, for in 1877 he had subdivided some of his farms into small allotments among the labourers, and there were 700 such allotments at Belvoir alone. The result was a commercial success, the land being brought into a high state of cultivation, and the rent regularly paid. A similar experiment was made a number of years ago on an estate in Dumfriesshire. Leases of 21 years were offered at ordinary farm rents to deserving labourers, carefully se- lected for their character, who built their own cottages, at a cost to themselves varying from £2l to £4O, exclusive of labour, while the landlord supplied timber, stone, and so forth, at a cost of about £22. These houses were not grouped in villages, but chiefly situated ale:lg roads, with plots of from two to six acres attached to each, or the addition of grass for a cow. All the work on these little farms was done at by hours, and by members of the family, the cottager buying roots from the farmer, and producing in return milk, butter, and pork, besides rearing calves. Among' such peasant farmers pauperism soon ceased to exist, and many of them soon bettered themselves in life. The moral effects of the system in fostering industry, sobriety, and contentment were no less satisfactory than its economical success, and when a farm of £lOO a year fell vacant, out of eleven eligible offers for it, four came from promoted labourers! !

What we want, however, is a large number of farms of about 10 acres in extent, the property of the cultivators. Mr. John Stuart Mill once wrote—"lt is `the magic of property' which in the words of Arthur Young turns sand into gold' The idea of property does not, however, neces- sarily imply that there should be no rent, any more than that there should be no taxes. It merely implies that the rent should be a fired charge, not liable. to be raised against the possessor by his own improvements or by the will of a landlord. A tenant at a quit rent is, to all intents and pur- poses, a proprietor, a copyholder is not less so than a free- holder. What is wanted is permanent possession on fixed terms." _

A small property of 100 acres parcelled off into 10 acre farms, each with its homestead, will yield far more valuable crops by peasant proprietorship than if in one ordinary Eng- lish farm of 100 actes with one tenant. How can this be so, for the general idea in England is that such small farms cannot pay? Tne reason is largely owing to the fact that the small farmer owning his land, or paying a fixed moderate rent in perpetuity, would be encouraged to make the very most of his small holding. The Belgian peasant derives large returns from a soil much poorer than ours by-1. The perfection of both plough and spade work. 2. Good culti- vation and drainage. 3. The use of large quantities of suit- able manure. 4. Great variety of crops, choosing what will pay best. 5. Second crops. G. Raising abundance of food for cattle and rearing stock. 7. House feeding of cattle, which increases the quantity of both milk and manure. 8. Minute weeding. What would be the style of farming or produce of a 10 acre farm, to employ a family, and enable them to make a comfortable living upon it? In the first place, by judicious management the farmer will be able to keep a larger amount of stock than the size of his farm would at first sight appear to warrant, in fact, a 10 acre farm should keep four milking cows. By limiting the quantity of land under pasture, he will be able to devote more land to the raising of lucerne, rye grass, prickly comfrey, clover?, Sze., which when once planted and deep rooted will yield much heavier crops than grass. Prickly comfrey (which at present is not generally known in the north of England) is a permanent crop, and when once planted it will practically last for ever. A gentleman in the midland counties writes—" My own experience after culti- vating it for six years is this—take one season with another, and allow for an average soil and fair cultivation, it will cer- tainly yield, in four to five cuttings in the season, a total of 80 to 100 tons to the acre of a valuable green forage, much relished by all kinds of stock, and especially adapted for the feeding of horses and store stock. When we bear in mind that an acre of good pasture land will yield but seven to eight tons of grass cut green, lucerne 40, vetches 20, and rye grass 30, we can readily appreciate the value of a per- Manent fodder plant, which will yield 80 to 100 tons, and that without the yearly expense of cultivation, which is necessary with most soiling crops. It comes in earlier and lasts longer than any other crop, and has other great ad- vantages. Other portions of the farm grow meadow grass for winter fodder, and corn, the straw and grain of which the farmer requires for his cattle and fowl. Then there are root clops, mangolds, and turnips for winter feeding, as well as cow cabbages. Another field can be used as a market garden, and cabbages, beans, peas, carrots, parsnips, and potatoes (early and late) raised for his own use and for sale. Fruit such as strawberries, raspberries, gooseberries, and currants, have a respectable space allotted to them, while a considerable area is planted with choice fruit trees as an orchard. On 10 acre farms in Normandy it is not unusual for the farmer's wife to have a couple of hundred poultry in her corner of the farm, besides raising great numbers of ducks for the market, and there is no reason why on the same class of farm here similar attention should not be given to the same source of profit. But sup- pose only 89 hens are kept, and for eggs only—Black Ham- burghs for instance,—they will produce on an average 150 eggs each, or near 12,000 per annum, which sold winter and summer at an average of is. a dozen, would show £5O. They have the run of the grass land in summer, and the arable land in winter, a great portion of their food is pro- duced on the farm, and slugs, grubs, &c., kept down. Some of other breeds might be kept for the purpose of raising chickens for the market, which, having regard to the retail price, should have a good margin of profit. A breeding sow is a valuable adjunct to a small farm, and is said under proper management will yield a clear profit of £2O a year, but where four good milking cows are kept—Alderneys for instance—several breeding sows can also be kept. Even goats can be kept to a profit, and a society to advocate the claims and educate people as to the commercial value of this useful and often despised animal, has for its President no Iless a person than the Duke of Wellington. It is a well known fact that bees alone to those who really understand their management, have realised £3O a year. Again take tame rabbits. Some may smile at the idea of a small farmer paying any attention to rabbits. In November last, how- ever, one of the principal firms in Leadenhall Market issued a circular "to the small farmers, cottiers, and farm labourers of England," in which attention is called to the fact that 200 tons of rabbits are imported every week from Ostend during the season, and the circular wants to know why this

enormous quantity of meat could not be supplied by Eng- lishmen themselves. If the rearing of tame rabbits can be made a profitable source of industry in Belgium, there would appear to be no reason why a similar industry could not be made to pay here. So we might go on. But we would ask, is there not ample room for thousands of such small farms where the farmer (being free from the fear of an advance of rent on his own improvement?, or of being turned out, and having his improvements, his property, "confiscated ") would make the very most of a holding not too large for himself and family to cultivate with very occasional help. If such farms were as common as they are now uncommon, is it likely this country would have purchased from abroad in 1880 alone

and other articles in proportion. No if we had a different system, if it was oftener the case that a man was his own landlord, tenant, and labourer, if the "three profits" which Lord Beaconsfield spoke about all went into one pocket, this country would produce a much greater proportion of its own food, the money instead of going abroad would remain in this country and improve our home trade, and a great deal more labour and capital would be employed, and pauperism 1 to that extent diminished.

The late Mr. Joseph Kay, Q.C., wrote: "It is constantly urged in this country by opponents to reform of the land laws, and by men who ought to know better, if indeed they have ever given a serious thought to the subject, that the system of free trade in land would never succeed in our country on account of our changeable, cold, and uncertain climate and that therefore it is better to tie up the land in estates of one million and 400,000 acres, and to farm them by tenants who generally have not even the security of a lease. The objection has been urged over and over again, and even before a Committee of the House of Commons. But what are the facts? In the short summers and long severe winters of Norway; in Holland, with its fogs and long winters; in Northern France, with a climate very similar to our own; in Southern France, with its sunny and hot climate; in the plains of Switzerland, with their short but hot summers; in the mountain cantons, with their se- vere winters and short summers; in Italy, with its hot climate; in the cold climate of Northern Germany, with its severe winters; in the hot climate of Southern Germ:my ; on the banks of the Rhine, with its splendid vineyards and orchards; in the Channel Islands, with a climate scarcely warmer than Devonshire; in fact, everywhere where free trade in land or the French system is being tried over the whole face of Eerope, these laws are promoting the welfare, the happiness, and the morality of the people.' Politically the increase in the number of landowners would be of immense importance, and would largely aug- ment the power of true conservatism (which has no better supporters than thousands in the Liberal ranks), and pre- vent topsy-ttirvey legislation in the future; for, as an emi- nent foreign writer has said: "The distribution of a number of small properties among the peasantry forms a kind of rampart and safeguard for the holders of large estates, and peasant property may, without exaggeration, be called the lightning conductor, that averts from society dangers which might otherwise lead to violent catastrophes. The concen- tration of land in large estates among a small number of families is a sort of provocative of levelling legislative measures. The position of England, so enviable in many respects, seems to be in this matter full of danger for the future."

RUS9IAN PRISONS.—The worst -prisons which Mr. Lens- dell visited in the Russian Empire were in Finland, those of Abo and Wilborg being the most dismal. "The descent by steps with candles to prisoners in the lower rooms, the dim light entering by windows in walls ten feet thick, the clanking of chains," all these things made a very unfavour- able impression upon his mind, especially as the Finns still use sets of irons "nearly ten times the weight of any others" he has seen in Europe. One or two revolting cases of cruelty were reported to him. On one occasion, he says— "a friend of mine, coming one day to a swollen river in Siberia near Ormsk, where a gendarme was also waiting .with a young lady prisoner of seventeen, was allowed to speak to her, and she told him that since she left Peters- , burg, a distance of 1,700 miles, she had not once had a gen- darme out of her presence." Here is another instance of I official brutality. A number of Poles, who had taken part in the insurrection of 18C3, we sent to Nijni Udinsk. While they were in prison there, "some of the prisoners lhaving escaped at night, the governor of the gaol procured rods from the neighbouring woods and birched the rest of them, I suppose on the ground of aiding and abetting the escape of the others. The twenty-one Po7.es, however, were not in the ward from which the escape was made, and this they urged, but apparently to no purpose, for the governor seemed to have been enraged beyond bounds, and in some cases to have used, not only rods, but the plete and clubs. My informant declared that of the 300 Russians and twenty- one Poles thus treated, seventeen subsequently died." It is pleasant to learn that, a petition having been presented to the governor of Irkutsk, "the violent official was tele- graphed for, and himself incarcerated." One of the saddest sights which Mr. Lansdell witnessed was the "old weather - beaten, smoke-dried, low-pitched building" in which were confined a number of old men waiting for their release by death:—" I do not remember any sight in Siberia that so touched me as this. To see 'scores of able-bodied men pent up in wards with nothing to do was bad, to hear the clanking of their chains was worse, though many of them were burly fellows who nould carry them well. More touching still were the convoys of exiles with faithful and innocent women following their husbands; but to see these old men thus waiting for death was a most melancholy pic- ture. The doctor inspects the convicts once a month, and determines upon those who are past work, who, in the ab- sence of any specific disease, are then brought into these wards for the remainder of their lives. To release them,the colonel pointed out, would be no charity, because, being too old to work, and being out of the near range of poor-houses or similar institutions, they would simply starve. And thus they were left in confinement for a Higher Power to set them free. They lounged in the prison and in the yard, and some sat near a fire, though it was a sunny day in July. One old man was pointed out who had attained to fourscore years, and another had reached the age of ninety, and so on. The difficult breathing of one, however, the wheezing lungs o a second, and the hacking cough of a third, proclaimed in prophetic tones that their time was short; and one wished them a softer pillow for a dying head than a convict's shelf in a prison ward." As a general rule, the scenes which Mr. Lansdell witnessed were not more painful than all prison scenes must be, and he is of opinion that "if a Russian exile behaves himself decently well, he may in Siberia be more comfortable than in many, and as comfortable as in most, of the prisons of the world." —Through Siberia by H. No. VI.—HENRY GRATTAN. "May God in whose hand Is the lot of each land, Who rules over ocean and dry land, Inspire our good king From his presence to fling 11l advisers who'd ruin our Island. Don't we feel 'tis our dear native island? A fertile and fine little island; May Orange and Green No longer be seen Distained with the blood of our island.
Each voice should resound through our island You're my neighbor, but Bull this is my land Nature's favourite spot; And, I'd sooner be shot, Than surrender the right of our island." Lysaght.

The "rainbow-like epoch," as Lord Byron describe-el the period of Ireland's Independence, was destined to be, as he farther declared, a " bright and, brief era." The long- cherished prize had no sooner been won by the Irish Patriots than the English Government tried to wrest it from their grasp. Had the Irish leaders presented a united front to their opponents, and had they, forgetful of self, combined in their efforts to secure Parliamentary Reform, the Act of Union might have been indefinitely postponed. But they quarrelled among themselves, and thus enabled the Govern- ment to resist all attempts to purify Parliament, and worse than all to steadily and deliberately increase its corruption. In hie efforts to strangle the Independence of Ireland Pitt found a valuable assistant in one who has been termed "the Robespierre of Ireland." This man was Lord Castlereagh, perhaps the "most despotic in intention, and the weakest in intellect that ever tyrannised over a country." On the resignation of Pelham .as Irish Secretary, Pitt objected to make Lord Castlereagh his successor on account of his Irish extraction. But Lord Cornwallis, the then Viceroy, wrote in the strongest terms to Mr. Pitt and the Duke of Portland, recommending his appointment to that office : "I know," said he to the latter, "that with some few ex- ceptions it has been a rule that the Irish Secretary should be an Irishman; but still exceptions have been made, and in no case could they have been with more propriety ad- mitted than to bring forward at so important a crisis a man of Lord Castlereagh's talents, who possesses the general es- teem of his countrymen, and who knows too well the real interests of Ireland to suppose that they can be promoted by any measures that are not equally favourable to the wel- fare and prosperity of Great Britain." And when the ap- pointment was made, Lord Cornwallis assured the Duke of Portland that "Lord Castlereagh's appointment gave me great satisfaction, and although I admit the propriety of the general rule, yet, as he is so 'eery unlike an Irishman, I think he has a just claim to an exception in his favour." An exception was made in his favour, and he soon caused his superiors to rejoice that such an exception had been made. A thorough believer in the doctrine that "the end justifies the means," he did not hesitate to set in motion every engine cf fraud and corruption to accomplish his ob- ject, and so successfully did he intimidate and bribe that Theobold Wolf Tone's picture of the corruption of the Irish Legislation was too true I have seen now the Parlia- ment of Ireland, the Parliament of England, the Congress of the United States, the Corps Legislatif of France, and the Convention of Batavia. I have likewise seen our shabby Volunteer Convention in 1783, and the General Committee of the Catholics in 1793; so that I hail seen, in the way of deliberate bodies, as many, I believe, as most men, and of all those I have mentioned, beyond comparison the most shamelessly profligate and abandoned by all sense of virtue. principle, or even common decency, was the Legislation of my own unfortunate country—the scoundrels." But bad as was the condition into which the Legislation had been brought by this " Wertha in Politics," when the measure for uniting the two countries was introduced in 1799 it was defeated by 109 to 104. The combined exertions of almost all the men of talent, and of almost all the men of pure patriotism in the Parliament was for once successful, and immense was the excitement produced and the rejoicings held on what was considered a decisive victory. Dublin was thrice illuminated, and the blaze of bonfires was seen far and wide on the mountains in the country. But Mr. Pitt and Lord Castlereagh so far from desponding over their de- feat were only the more confirmed in their resolution to per- severe in bringing it forward till it ultimately proved suc- cessful. The conduct of Government did not belie their firm determination. Several who had opposed the Govern- ment measure were dismissed from office. Fresh and larger bribes were offered and accepted. Every method of intimi- dation was resorted to in order to check opposition on the part of the people. Meetings to protest against the Govern- ment measure were dispersed by military violence. Most of the provincial papers were in the pay of the Castle, and every attention was paid to the Press generally. The Patri- ots, as they witnessed all this, clearly saw that the Act of Union was only a question of time, and there was one Patriot who beheld with anguish the edifice which he had done so much to construct sinking into ineffable dissolution. At length the eventful day, big with the future destinies of the British Empire, and for vrich both parties had made the utmost efforts, arrived. Dublin was in the most violent state of agitation, and though it was known Government would have a majority, yet as it was in part made up of un- willing supporters, it was very doubtful whether, though at first carried, the measure might not be ultimately defeated, as it had been on the former occasion. It was on the 15th January, 1800, that the last Session of the Parliament began. No reference was made to the Union in the Viceroy's speech, but an amendment was moved by Sir Lawrence Parsons declaratory of the resolution of Parliament to maintain the Independence of Ireland. A fierce debate followed. Pon- sonby, Bushe, and Plunket spoke in favour of the amend- ment, and against the Union. The debate had continued for some time, and Mr. Egan was speaking warmly on the Patriotic side, when a whisper ran round the House. An expression of incredulity was visible on the faces of nearly all who were present, while the Ministerialists smiled de- risively. Presently Mr. George Ponsonby and Arthur Moor stood up and left the House. A tremendous shout was heard along College Green. An instant after it was taken up within the walls of Parliament House, and rang along the corridors. The doors of the Chamber were flung wide open, and within the House the inspired face of Henry Grattan was seen once more. As he totterea feebly tcwards the table, supported by his two friends, the whole House rose respect- fully, and cheer followed cheer. Even the Ministerialiets felt themselves compelled to do him honour. Castleree.gh himself rose at the head of the whole Treasury Bench, bowed with stately courtesy, and remained standing till Grattan had taken the oaths and his seat. Ever since his secession from Parliament Grattan had been an invalid, and most of the time had been away from Ireland trying to recruit his shattered health. He was again in Dublin, and his friends were anxious that his voice should be heard once more in the theatre of his former glory, and in the denunciation ef the conduct of the Government. He had been returned almost against his will for the close borough of Wicklow, which belonged to Mr. Fighe. When the vacancy occurred the Government withheld the writ as long as possible in order to keep Grattan out of Parliament till the discussion should be past. In fact it was only on the day of the open- ing of the Session that the writ reached the returning officer. Through the exertions of Grattan's friends the election was held at once. Their energy was such that voters enough were got together to return him before midnight. The re- turn reached Dublin by five o'clock in the morning. The friends of Gratten hastened to the house of the proper officer. He was forced out of bed and made to present the writ to Parliament before seven, while the debate on the Union was still going on. Meanwhile Mr. Fighe had ridden from Wick- low to Dnblin, and called at Grattan's house in Baggot- street. "Will they not let me die in peace ?" exclaimed the illustrious Irishman, as he heard of Mr. Fighe's arrival. But his brave-hearted wife told him that he must rise at once and go to the House. In his old Volunteer uniform, with a brace of loaded pistols in his pocket, lie was borne to the House in a Sedan chair. His wife looked anxiously after him. The bravoes of the Castle might try to pick a personal quarrel with him, and a duel might be the result. But when friends assured her that in such an event others would take the part of Grattan, the brave woman stoutly re- plied, "My husband cannot die better than in the defence of his country." One of the Patriots, Egan, as we have seen, was on his legs when Grattan entered the House. But he made no at- tempt to resume his harangue when the excitement conse- quent on Grattan's entry had subsided. All waited for that "noblest Roman of them all" to thunder forth again those iron words that thrilled like the clash of spears. At first .he found himself unable to stand, and begged permission to speak sitting. This permission was granted. Socn his eoul, rising supremely over the frailties of his body, bore him along into the lull tide and sweep of his oratory. For two hours his eloeuence blazed before the House with uninter- rupted fire and splendour. He concluded by saying He (the Minister) proposes to you to substitute the British Parliament in your place, to destroy the body that restored your liberties and ta restore that body which destroyed them. Against such a proposition, were I expiring on the floor, I should beg to utter my last breath and record my dying testimony." But all his eloquence was unavailing. After a debate of eighteen hours the result, though not so favourable as Lord Castlereagh had anticipated, gave a de- cided victory to the Government. The amendment was re- jected by a bribed majority of 42—the numbers being 138 to 96.

On the sth of February Grattan ably argued against the Union on Constitutional grounds giving copious quotations from the greatest writers in support of his opinion that Par- liament was incompetent.to pass such an Act. He concluded a powerful argumentative speech with the folio ing words : " The question is not now suck as occupied you of old—not old Poynings, not peculation, not plunder, not the embargo, not the Catholic Bill, not the Reform Bill, it is your being; it is more—it is your life to come, whether you will go with the Castle at your head to the tomb of Charlemont and the Volunteers, and erase his epitaph, or whether your children shall go to your grave saying—A venial military Court at- tacked the liberties of the Irish, and here lie the bones of the honourable'dead men who saved their country. Such an epitaph is a nobility which the King cannot give his slaves —it is a glory which the Crown cannot give the King." On the 14th of February Corry made a personal attack on Grattan. This was the second attack of the kind made since the Patriot's return to Parliament. Grattan replied in one of the finest and most scathing invectives in any language. After the close of this terrible phillipic Grattan and Corry both left the House. Next morning in a field by the Dodder Bank not far from Ball's Bridge, the two met to exchange shots. We need not be surprised at this. All public men —politicians and lawyers alike—had to fight on the shortest notice for any or no reason at all. Curran fought several duels. Flood killed his man. O'Connell killed his man. Grattan had an encounter of the kind before, and now he has another, fortunately without any serious result.

TRADLAUGH.— t,IIC g°TriPlejelli,"Y of swearing in these new members Bradlaueb, who had feen standing at Co 111' against the cross bench, advanced to the leojtrit or'nipanied by any introducer.—Having tendered tfey,l•Yeerr,.: ceCit „,-eatd to Sir Ersleine May, Sir STAFFORD --(r. Speaker, I rise—(loud cheers)—to tia, With tili?it Rouse a resolution identical, or nearly identi- n when IMI'lee"181° which Was passed on the 29th of April last, on ie e tesente the i d , . e hon. gentleman who s now at the 'de tnesoleti, nlmself for the purpose of taking the Oath. 44a oeNutionn,. I have to submit is "that having 'regard to i,.eel. the 26,1 of this House, on the 22nd of Jane, 1830, Qite R'gs of t;:`' or April, 1881, and of the reports and pro- tacit txvo 4ugh be"e Select Committees therein referred to, not permitted to go through the form of

repeating the words of the Oath prescribed by statute 29th, Vic. chap. 19 and 31, and 32 Vic. chap. 72.4 The circum- stances of the case, as I stated them last year, are doubtless in the recollection of the House. The lion. gentleman was returned in the first instance to the Parliament, and on the occasion of his proposing then to take his seat, he requested that he might be, or he claimed that he should be, allowed to affirm, instead of taking .the oath, and he rested that claim upon certain statutes which were only applicable to the case of the persons upon whom the oath was not„bind- ing. ("No, no," and Opposition cheers.) Such, at all events, was the contention of those who objected to the honourable gentleman taking the affirmation, and such was the opinion of the committees who sat upon- the case— (hear, hear)—and such also, I think, was the opinion of the courts of law upon the subject. At all events objection was taken, and the hon. gentleman was held by the House, on the recommendation of the committee, to be disqualified from taking the affirmation. Subsequently he lied permis- sion given him to take the affirmation subject to the deci- sions of the courts of law. We all know what the result of that was, that the decision of the courts of law was against his:being admissible to affirm, and that in consequence his seat was vacated by reason of his laving sat without having taken the proper oath or affirmation. He was re- elected, and upon his re-election the question arose as to his being permitted to take the oath. The House had been pre- viously advised by one of the committees who sat on this subject, that for a gentleman to claim to repeat the words of the oath with such qualifications as were necessarily implied in the proceedings which had taken place in Mr. Bradlaugh's instance was not to take the oath according to law, and accordingly I moved, and the House by a majority after discussion affirmed, a resolution which prevented his taking the oath last year. We are the same House as we were then. The hon. gentleman is in precisely the same position as he was then, and -I presume that the decision of the Mouse will be the same as the decision was last year. sCheers.)— Sir W. Hancounr said: The view that the government have always taken on this question is that this Ts a matter, whether it be of oath or affirmation, that is prescribed by and determined by statute; that the statute referred to by the right hon. gentleman orders a cerfain form of oath to be taken—the view that the Government have always taken on this matter is that the House of Commons ought not—and, indeed, speaking with all respect, has not the right—to vary the provisions of the statute—(hear, hear,)—that is to say, they have no right to interpose and say that a person duly elected by a constituency is not entitled to come to this table and take the oath which the 'statute affirms he is to take; and that is the short and simple view of the question. We regard a resolution of this character as, in fact, doing what a resolution of the House of Commons ought not to do, viz., to set aside the provisions of an Act of Parliament. We consider that a House of Commons has no business to inquire into the opinions of any individual ' • that if he presents him- self to take the oath prescribed by the Act of Parliament, he ought to take the oath as the statute prescribed. It is for us apparently, according to the suggestion of the right hon. gentleman, to determine whether a person uttering a certain form of words is or is not taking the oath. Now that in- troduces considerations which, I venture to submit, the House has nothing to do with. If it be the fact that there are certain circumstances which prevented a repetition of that form of words constituting the oath according to the true sense and meaning of the statute, that, in our opinion, is a question for the courts of law to determine. If it be contended that the repetition of the form of words is not an oath within the meaning of the statute, we say that that question ought to be referred to the courts of law. As the House decided that the form should be left to the courts of law, the course that we took, and as far as any ad- vice of ours is of value, we should advise the House of Ccimmons to take, is that as they permitted Mr. Bradlaugh to take the affirmation subject to the opinion of the courts of law, so he should be allowed—(loud Opposition cheers) —to take the oath in the form of words presented by the statute subject to the judgment of the courts of law as to whether that is a fulfilment of the conditions prescribed by statute. He then moved the previous question. (Cheers.) —Mr. NEWDEGATE declined to be a party to any subterfuge by which a man should be allowed to subscribe to an oath which he declared to be meaningless, and thus to take die name of God in vain.—Mr. BR.ADLAUGH declined to follow Mr. Newdegate into his reckless misrepresentations, and said since he stood there before every effort had been made to effect his ruin, even to the length of driving him into the Court of Bankruptcy. If the House was prepared to try him by his opinions, he :Isl.:edit to do it fairly, intelligibly, and without prejudice. The only way in which his opinion with regard to an oath was brought before the House was by distorting a statement contained in a private letter written by him outside Parliament. He asked the House to deal legally and fairly with him, even if they regarded his political and theological views as obnoxious and dangerous. He urged that it was in the highest deg,lke inexpedient to deal exceptionally and illegally with an individual. .He disputed the authority of Parliament to go back upon any resolution passed previously to the Bth of April, which was the date of his last election. The argument that to permit him to take the oath would be a profanation of it was worth- less, unless the House was prepared to dell with every in- dividual case, and he asked if the oath was profaned when Mr. Hill, steeped to the lips in bribery, stepped up to the table cheered to the echo to take the oath. Was the oath Profaned when Mr. Mill, who held views which he (Mr. Bradlaugh) entertained, was allowed to take it? He denied that he had ever asserted that if be took the oath the cere- mony would not be binding upon his conscience, and he was prepared to declare solemnly that he was prepared to take the oath according to the law, and that if he took it it would undoubtedly be binding on his conscience. He asked if the House was prepared to substitute force for law; if not, let them deal with him by an action or by petition. If he was not fit for his position, let his constituents dismiss him ; but the House should not dismiss him from it. (Hear, hear.)— Mr. LABOrCHERE said that something like 750 petitions, con- taining 170,000 signatures, were ready for presentation in favour of Mr. Bradlaugh being allowed to take his seat, and the Opposition had petitions containing about 100,000 signatures; but, according to the rules of the House, no petitions could be presented on the first day of the Session. —Sir S. NORTHCOTE said that among the petitions prepared for presentation was one signed by 10,300 persons resident in Northampton, but as it was not within the rules of the House to rece ive!them on that day, the petitions could not be presented.—Mr. GLADSTONE expressed his regret that a more liberal acknowledgement had not been drawn from Sir S. Northcote. The view of the Government was that as in the case of the affirmation it should be left to a court of law to decide whether, on taking the Oath, Mr. Bradlaugh in- fringed the statute. With all respect, he contended that the question of profanation was traversing the question, and that Parliament bad no right to look outside the legality of the Act. It must not be forgotten that the Oath had already been taken by a known Atheist, and the protrusion of the fact in this case that the Oath was not regarded as binding was entirely outside the question. If there was profanation in the one case there was profanation in the other. It was their duty to secure justice to every subject in the realm, to Mr. Bradlaugh as well as every other man, and he was of opinion that adequate justice would be secured by the deci- s'on of a court of law. The first and bounden duty of the Government was to adhere to the strict interpretation of the law, and any departure from that strict interpretation of the law was a profanation of the duty to secure the due administration of justice. By moving the previous question, there- fore, Government simply asserted that the matter was not one with which it was competent for the House to deal. They proposed to give nothing to Mr. Bradlaugh, but to allow him to act, as in the case of taking the affirmation' on his own responsibility. That was the sole object they had !in moving the previous question.—When the House divided the numbers were—For the resolution, 286; for the previous question, 228 ; majority against the Government, 58.—The resolution was agreed to without a dissentient voice. Mr. Bradlaugh advanced to the table, and the SPEAKER read the resolution which had been just passed, land informed the hon. gentleman that in pursuance of that ' ! resolution he had to call upon him to withdraw.—Mr. BRADLAUGH : I respectfully refuse to do so, the House hav- ing no power to compel me.—The SPEAKER: I again call upon the hon. gentleman to withdraw below the bar.—Me. , BRADLArGH : I refuse to withdraw, being here in the per- formance of my duty, and I have a right to take my seat.— Sir S. NORTHCOTE moved that Mr. Bradlaugh be ordered to withdraw.—Mr. GLADSTONE, who rose amid laughter and cheers, said he had not considered it a part of his duty to ' make any motion on the subject; but as the House bad declared its sense by a considerable majority, he could not offer any opposition to the consequential resolution now I moved.—The resolution was then agreed to.—The SPEAKER: I have again to call upon Mr. Bradlaugh to withdraw.—Mr. BRADLArGII: It would be undignified I for me to indulge in any unseemly conduct with the House, and I respectfully crave the House to allow me to withdraw below the bar.—The hon, gentleman then bowed to the Speaker, and withdrew amid cheers. NOTICES.—Mr. GLADSTONE gave notice that on Monday next he would move certain resolutions relating to the pro- cedure of the House, and the appointment of a Standing Committee to deal with bills of a certain class, in lieu of a committee of the whole House.—More than 100 other notices were given. THE IMPRISONED IRISH MEMBERS.—On the Speaker reading two letters from the Irish Office acquainting the House with the arrest of Mr. Parnell, Mr. Sexton. Mr. O'Kelly, and Mr. Dillon, members of Parliament, under the 1 Act for the better protection of life in Ireland, and of the I release of Mr. Sexton, Mr. E. D. GRAY moved that the letters of the Lord-Lieutenant be referred to a Select Com- mittee for the purpose of considering and reporting whether any matters rsferred to therein demanded the attention of the House.—Mr. J. MCCARTHY 'seconded the motion.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the Government would not have objected to the appointment of a committee to inquire into the way in which they had exercised their power; but he denied that the matter ought to be raised as a question of privilege.— After speeches by several Irish members the House divided. For the motion, 45; against, 174; majority for the Govern- ment, 120. DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—The SPEAKER having read the. Queen's Speech, the Hon. E. MARJORIBANKS rose to move the Address in reply.-I-Mr. FIRTH seconded the motion.
The House adjourned at 11.45. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair shortly before 12 o'clock. MR. BRADLAUGII.-Mr. Labouchere presented 763 peti- tions, signed by 170,000 persons, praying that Mr. Brad- laugh might be allowed to take his seat; and Sir Stafford Northcote presented 16 petitions, including one from North- ampton, signed by 10,000 persons. Other petitions to the same effect were presented from the Conservative benches.
