div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, FEBRUARY ILIBB2
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, FEBRUARY ILIBB2

THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—At a quarter to one, Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE rose in a thin House to renew the debate on the Address. Referring to Egypt, he took the opportunity of explaining that Lord Salisbury was not per- sonally responsible for the establishmeet of the joint control with France of Egyptian finance. It was the work of Lord Derby. The right hon. gentleman expressed some appre- hension that matters might drift into a position of danger. With respect to the congratulatory paragraphs in the Speech relating to India and the Transvaal, he thought it better to wait and see. He asked for information with respect to the French Treaty, and in dealing with the Irish questign, to which be devoted much of his speech, he also assumed rather an interrogatory than a denunciatory tone.—Mr. GLADSTONE, who was warmly received from the Ministerial benches, assigned the first part of his reply te affairs in Egypt. He took comfort from the fact that while Sir Staf- ford Northcote had expressed apprehension that the Govern- ment were "drifting," Lord Salisbury had spoken in a directly opposite sense, charging them with interfering too much. He dwelt upon the complicated nature of the task which had been bequeathed to the Ministry. There was the dual action with France aggravated by two changes of Administration which had taken place in that country since the Egyptian question became a " living " one. There were the dispositions of other Powers to be considered; the jealousy of. the Sultan,, the claims of the Khedive, the action of the military party, and the approach to sole amount of the movement of real political life in Egypt. The Government were doing their best amid these complicated circumstances, and he was glad to accept Lord Salisbury's description of the result as halanc ng Sir Stafford North- cote's. .As to the Commercial Treaty, he did not know that there was anything to add beyond what appeared in the Queen's Speech, though in this connection, touching on the question of tariffs, he struck some good-humoured blows at Mr. Lowther's Protectionest declaration and Sir Stafford Northcote's philandering with the heresy. Turning next to Ireland, and speaking with increased animation, the Premier contended that it was too soon to form an opinion on an Act of Parliament which was only a few months old. But he declared and showed in detail that the great conspiracy of the Land League had, by the joint action of the Land Act and the Coercion Bills, been not only confronted, but defeated. That, he said, amid loud cheers, was a result so great and so solid that it could not be broken down by any cavil. 'The payment of rent was going on, and was not now met by violent resistance. The circle of intimidation had been narrowed, and in some degree the judicial system of the country had revived. All this was done in spite of the relentless animosity shown by the Land Leaguers to the Land Act—a measure which had shown itself rn infant Hercules that Could grapple with the serpent that tried to kill it. Passages in this section of the speech were enthusiastically cheered from the Ministerial benches. 'The Leader of the House suffered great inconvenience from the action of Mr. Biggar, who accompanied his remarks by a running commentary—if ejaculations composed of jeers, snorts, monosyllabic contradictions, and other unparliamen- tary sounds, may be dignified by this description. After some remarks by Colonel Tottenham, Mr. P. J. Smyth moved an amendment, declaring that the ills of Ireland may be cured only by a " readjustment of the legislative relations estab- lished between the two countries by the Act of Union." The debate was continued by Mr. O'Connor Power and Mr. Daw- son, who was in the middle of an amusing speech when interrupted by the hour for closing the debate. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THUBSDAY. _

A SEDITIOUS PAMPHLET. Lord SALISDCRY moved for the production of the correspondence between the Chief Secretary for Ireland and the Secretary to the Land Com- missioners relating to the publication of the pamphlet re- ferred to in the debate on the Address, entitled "Flow to Become the Owner of your Farm," which Lord Carlingford stated was issued by the Secretary of the Commission on the recommendation of the Solicitor to the Commission.— The Earl of LONGFORD stated that in answer to a request from him Mr. Godley, the secretary to the Comtnission,•re- plied that the pamphlet was issued without the sanction or knowledge of the Commissioners in the belief that it con- tained nothing of a political character, but merely useful information respecting the purchase clauses of the Land Act, and that when the nature of the pamphlet was brought under the notice of the Commissioners, instructions were given for its withdrawal from circulation.—Lord LONGFORD asked for the production of correspondence on the subject, to which Lord Carlingford assented. THE JEWS IN Rl:sm.—Th:l' Duke of SOMERSET asked whether the Government had received any recent informa- tion respecting the treatment of the Jews in Russia.—Earl GRANVILLE, in reply, reminded the House that the Govern- menta had no right and no means of insisting upon anything like. searching or judicial inquiry into these matters, but their Consuls reported the facts as far as they came to their knowledge, and their reports should be laid on the table. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY.

AMENDMENT OF CRIMINAL LAW.—A number of bills were introduced and read a first time, one of them being by Mr. Hopwood, Q.C., for the amendment of the criminal law. THE CHDRCH OF SCOTLAND.—Lord COLIN CAMPBELL gave notice, amid much cheering on the part of the Opposi- tion, that be will move an amendment to Mr. Dick Peddie's motion in regard to the disestablishment and disendowrnent of the Church of Scotland.

PERNICIOUS JOURNALS.— Sir W. V. HARCOURT, whose attention was directed to a publication en- titled the "Freethinker," which the hon. member who brought the matter forward described as "blasphemous," expressed the opinion that it would be much better, instead of instituting a public prosecution, to leave such pernicious journals to the reprobation of all decent members of society. TarE DOTEREL EXPLOSION.—A question which was put to Mr. TREVELYAN on the Doterel explosion elicited the assu- rance that-the Admiralty is doing its,utmost on behalf of the personal safety of seamen. THE PERSECUTION OF THE JEWS—Replying to the member for Dewsbury, Mr. GLADSTONE, whilst expressing his horror of the outrages perpetrated on the Jews in Russia, pointed out that for him publicly to engage to make representations to the Russian Government on the subject would be likely to arouse an amount of jealousy which would be positively detrimental to the object which Mr. Simon had in view._

THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—The debate was then resumed on Mr. Smyries amendment to the Address, affirm- ing that the only efficacious remedy for the deplorable con- dition of Ireland is a readjustment of the political relations established between Great Britain ann Ireland by the Act of Legislative Union of 1800. Mr. SMYTH desired to withdraw his amendment, but the Parnellite section objected to such a course, and on being pressed to a division it was rejected by 93 to 37 votes.—Mr. JUSTIN WCARTHY also moved an amendment.
11 SCEL LAN MT'S.
The new Eddystone Lighthouse was lighted for the first time on Friday night. _ _ _
_ Two men were killed on Saturday afternoon in a Liver- pool dock by the explosion of a tank on board the flat Leander.
Lord Lyons and the French Minister for Foreign Affairs on Saturday siczned the declaration prolonging the existing commercial treaties until the Ist of March.

A floating dock, which is likely to prove of great advan- tage to the shipbuilding trade of the town, was on Saturday launched by the Barrow Shipbuilding Company. The failure has been announced in the London Bankruptcy Court of William Turner, of Estelle Road, Haverstock Hill, and Chelsea, builder and contractor, with liabilities to the amount of L'50,000. Sir James Ingham Las directed that a warrant should be issued against the Marquis of Huntly on a charge of ob- taining by false and fraudulent pretences from William Gardner the sum of £2,000. Damages to the amount of £lOO were given on Saturday by a Liverpool jury in a Welsh breach of promise case. The defendant, J. W. Peemuller, who did not appear, was said to be a German, now in Switzerland.

On Monday a presentation of a thousand guineas, accom- panied by an illuminated address, was mad to the Rev. Henry Postance, Vicar of Holy Trinity, Toxteth Park, in recognition of his educational and other work at the South- end of Liverpool. At London Bankruptcy Court, on Monday, application was made to commit The O'llonogbue, M.P., for contempt in not attending to pass his public examination. Counsel stated that the hon. member was negotiating to annul the bankruptcy. The case was adjourned. A fog of extraordinary density prevailed in London on Saturday evening, as a consequence of which traffic of all kinds was blocked, and a number of accidents occurred. In the theatres the occupants of the stage were but dimly seen by the spectators, and at one theatre the performance had to be abandoned.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, James Dickenson, a collier, was tried for the murder, at Pemberton, near Wigan, of another collier, named Middlehurst. This was a very bad case of kicking, and, the jury having found a verdict of manslaughter only, Mr. Baron Pollock passed sentence of 15 years' penal servitude. Mark Fahey Kavanagh, who was remanded by the Ham- mersmith police magistrate, last week, for causing the death of Helen Hawkins by administering poison, and on the charge of attempting to commit suicide at the same time, has committed suicide by hanging himself in the house of detention at Clerkenwell.

Writing to a member of the Monmouthshire Chamber of Agriculture, who had forwarded to the right hon. gentleman a copy of a resolution on the incidence of local taxation, Mr. Bright says that during the period of nearly 40 years that he has been in Parliament every increase of expenditure has been supported by the representatives of farmers, and that county members are the most eager supporters of what- ever extravagance our administrators have been guilty of. THE PIMLICO MYSTERY.—On Saturday, the murdered child, Georgina Moore, was buried at Brompton Cemetery. Upon her father leaving the house to follow the body, a large crowd of persons assembled outside the house in Winchester-street, Pimlico, made violent efforts to assault him, and were only prevented by the exertions of a large number of police-constables, who were stationed at each side of the mourning carriage which was to carry him. On arrival at the cemetery the father was apprehensive for his personal safety. He was not amongst the mourners at the last ceremony, and afterwards mysteriously disappeared from the cemetery, the mourning coaches returning without him.

TIIE MISCARRIAGE OF JUSTICE IN STAFFORDSHIRE.— The Home Secretary, writing to Mr. W. Craig, one of the members for North Staffordshire, who had addressed the , right bon. gentleman on the subject, states that after con- sulting with Mr. Gladstone he had come to the conclusion , that a sum of £5OO should be awarded to each of the two farmers, Johnson and Clowes, as compensation for the suffering they had undergone by their wrongful conviction and imprisonment on the charge , of unlawfully wounning Isaac Brooks; and that the two men on being informed of the compensation proposed to be given, ! had expressed their deep sense of gratitude for the considera- tion and promptitude with which he (Sir W. V. Hermit) , had dealt with this painful matter. THE SECESSION OF LORD ZETLAND. A Conservative banquet took place on Monday night, at Richmond, York- shire, to celebrate the return of the Hon. Guy Dawnay for the North Riding. Lord Zetland, replying to the toast of " The House of Lords," said no one rejoiced in the Conser- vative victory more than be did, and it was a proof, in his mind, that the people of this country approved the steps lately taken by the House of Lords with regard to certain extreme Radical measures which had come under this con- sideration within the last two years. He had taken up the Conservative cause because he was unable to swallow the Radical and revolutionary ideas which appeared to be ma- tured with so much care by those in authority in the so- called Liberal camp. DISESTABLISHMENT IN SCOTLAND.—A great public meet- ing in favour of disestablishment of the Church of Scotland was held on Saturday evening in Aberdeen. Upwards of 2000. persons attended, and the chair was taken by Lord Provost Esslemont, who delivered a vigorous speech, declar- ing that the time had come for carrying out the great work to which the Liberal party were pledged. The other speakers were Dr. 'Webster, M.P., Principal Cairns, and Principal Rainy. Resolutions were passed declaring that the continued establi4shment of any denomination in Scot- land is an ecclesiastical wrong and a political injustice, that the time has come for pressing the question upon the Legis- lature for early and final settlement, and that in view of the importance and urgency of the question the electors and community of Scotland ought to be prepared to give an unequivocal decision on this great subject. THE FARMERS' ALLIANCE.—The annual meeting and din- ner of the Farmers' Alliance were held in London, on Mon- day, Mr. Howard, M.P., presiding on both occasions. At the dinner the chairman said no association had been sub- jected to more strenuous and persistent misrepresentation than had theirs, but the objects of their association were not sufficient to account for the virulence they had met with. He was afraid the antagonism was to be traced to a fear of the effect which a combination of tenant farmers would have upon what was called the country party. Mr. Rowlandson, the late candidate for the North Riding, said he could not agree to all the proposals contained in the bill, but in the recent contest he kept straight before him the objects of the Alliance. , His great standpoint was the abolition of the law of distress, as he believed it would benefit small farmers the most. THE PERSECUTION OF THE JEWS IN RUSSIA. Letters from Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamberlain were read on Monday evening at a town's meeting held in Birmingham in reference to the persecution of the Jews in Russia. Mr. Bright stated that the frenzy which is born of ignorance and superstition cannot always be controlled by a Government, but he hoped the Governments of Russia and Germany would do all that could be done to put an end to the cruelty to which the Jews were being subjected. Mr. Chamberlain warmly condemned the many grievous outrages which have been perpetrated on a hapless people, " whom the local authorities have been either unwilling or unable to protect." He is hopeful that the force of pablic opinion will exercise a useful pressure in the matter, and adds that the movement in aid of the perse- cuted Jews is one which must command the sympathy and support of all lovers of freedom and justice, without distinc- tion of sect or party. At the Leeds Assizes, on Tuesday, John Tobin, an Irish quarryman, was tried on the charge of committing acts of treason felony at Bradford within the last 12 months. The evidence connected the prisoner with the Fenians, and showed that 40 revolvers, a large quantity of ammunition, and a number of treasonable documents were found in his possession. The jury returned a verdict of guilty. On Wednesday he was sentenced to seven years penal servitude. CENTRAL CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE.—A council meet- ing of the Central Chamber of Agriculture was held at the Society of Arts, on Tuesday. Colonel Paget presided. Several new members were elected, amongst whom was the Marquis of Salisbury. A long discussion arose on the working of the Educatfon Acts in rural districts, with special reference to the proposals for a new code. Mr. Owen Jones moved " Thas the council views the proposals for a new revised code as tending to lessen the Government grants and to increase the ordinary expenditure of the smaller schools in *rural districts, and thought their effect in many cases would be to increase the cost of education, only be justified by a larger capitation grant from the Impe- rial funds."—The resolution was carried. which could

„ .A.E.ROTINE SICCITIVE."—The trade, as well as the general public, have for some weeks been painfullr exercised about "Xerotine ” which apparently killed several people and wounded others, as well as endangered H.M.S. Triumph, and possibly was the cause of the loss H.M.S. Doterel. The explosion on the Triumph has luckily left survivors who knew the cause, and has assisted one of the very few who escaped death, to recall circumstances which suggest that the loss of the Doterel was caused by " Xerotine;" as also the explosion on board the Cockatrice previous to both acci- dents as far back as April; and also to prove that neither O'Donovan Rossa nor any other person procured any mis- creant (Irish or otherwise) to perpetrate the diabolical deed he is stated to have said to have been accomplished through the pay from the American skirmishing or any other funds. But what is "Xerotine ? " Nearly two months have elapsed since the last disaster without the public being made acquainted by the Admiralty what is its proper technical name. If it be necessary to send all over the world to order the commanders of our ships to return it to the store, or destroy it, why not let the public know what it is? If " Xerotine " is one of the mineral naphthas under another name, still to the general public unknown it is about one of the dangerous substances to put into the hands of people ignorant of its qualities. Gunpowder and dynamite polish you off at once. Naphtha may blow you against something and "shiver your timbers ;" nay, even cause as sudden death as the former; but it may unhappily prolong your sufferings, and burn you to death in a fiery furnace, or suffi- cient to prolong your agony for days, till kindly death releases you from possibly the most awful suffering flesh is —not heir to—but capable of enduring. These naphthas give off a vapour at a very low temperature, which on the application of a light, when combined with air, not only ex- plode with violence and flame, but carry the flame instan- taneouslv to its source, and set fire to, and explode the bulk of naphtha from which it is vaporizing. If this " Xerotine" is our well known petroleum or paraffin spirit, then the people of England will want to know how it was the Admi- ralty did not know the properties which are well known to the trade. Or if they did not know, then why the suppliers did not make the officials cognisant of it, that they might take prover precautions whilst in store or on board ship.— The Oil and Golourman's Journal.
FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE,
TRADE AND FINANCE IN INDIA.

Orders have been issued carrying into effect the policy announced in the last budget with reference to the sum of £1,500,030 to be provided annually as insurance against famine. This sum, instead of being considered as a surplus receipt for subsequent appropriation, will be treated as a fixed portion of the normal expenditure of each year. The budget is expected early in March. It seems certain that Major Baring will announce a handsome surplus, and the abolition of the duties on grey piece goods as well as the re- tention, if not extension, of the license tax. GUITEAU SENTENCED TO DEATH.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 4.—The court to-day overruled the motion for a new trial in the Guiteau case. Sentence of death was subsequently passed upon the prisoner, who will be executed on June 30 next. When Judge Cox concluded reading the sentence of death in the usual form;Guiteau shouted to the judge, "And may the Lord have mercy upon your soul." By an explosion of gas in a coal mine in Virginia, 32 men are entombed without any hope of rescuing them. The bodies of six have been recovered. RUSSIA.—THE PERSECUTION OF THE JEWS.

The Gobs prints a report from a province of Grodno of the brutal murder of e Jewish family in the village of No- vodvor. The father, mother, two sons, and two daughters were cruelly butchered by a band of Moujiks, and the Jewish population, fearing a general attack, were in a state of panic. The local authorities had warned the Jews to organise patrols and prepare to defend themselves. Further distur- bances are apprehended at Warsaw, where a patrol of Cossacks and infantry has been organised throughout the city, and orders have been issued enjoining the Jews to keep within doors and to close their shops. An official statement has been published at St. Petersburg enumerating the arrests of "Jewbaiters " in the various gov- ernments, with the view of showing that the authorities acted vigorously against the rioteis. The quession is declared to be "one of those matters of internal policy in which every country legislates accerding to its own views, and never admits cf foreign interference Or rithi iCe in any shape or form."

THE CRISIS IN EGYPT. A ne'w Egyptian Ministry has been formed, of Which the Fresident is Mustap.a Pasha Baroudi, the nominee directly of the Chamber of Deputies and indirectly of the military party. Ouraby—or as he is more generally known Arabi Bey, the leader of the military party—is the new Secretary for War. The semi-official Journal de St. Petersbourg says that the present state of affairs in Egypt cannot last, that a settlement will probably be effected through the concert of the Powers interested in the Eastern question, and refers to similar views expressed by German and Austrian papers. FRANCE.—THE SUSPENSION OF THE UNION GENERA.LE.

Some gentlemen, deputed for the purpose by the Society of Licensed Brokers, went, on Saturday, with MM. Bontoux and Feder, to the offices of the Union Gen6rale to examine the books and coffers of the company. The investigation lasted for several hours, and MM. Bontoux and Feder were afterwards conducted hack to the Conciergerie. No fresh warrants have been issued up to the present. The Paris, however, believes that some further arrests may poisibly be made.

It is confirmed that bills for sixty million francs entrusted to M. Bontoax, the president of the Union Gen&ale, by the Servian Government, is missing. The Servian Finance Minister has left Belgrade for Paris to look after the interests of Servia in this matter.

At the Foreign Office soirée, on Saturday night, there were not many women-of fashion and high unofficial rank. The Bourse crash was said to account for their absence. The monetary disasters of the last week have pressal most severely upon the aristocratic class. In the course of the evening the disappearance was announced of a noble rela- tive of Marshal Maculation, who, after pledging his mansion and his wife's jewels, is still said to owe 3,000,000 f. of dif- ferences which he is unable to pay.
THE INSURRECTION IN THE B,ILKAN PROVINCES.

The grant of 8,000,000 florins for the suppression of the insurrection in the Balkan provinces has been approved both by the Austrian and Hungarian Delegations. At a plenary sitting of the Hungarian Delegation on Saturday, to consider the Credit Bill, the Minister of Finance declared that statements published with regard to the extent of the insurrection in Bosnia had been exaggerated, and that the notion put forward by members of the Opposi- tion that the conquest had to be undertaken afresh was wholly groundless. He expressed the belief that with the increase of prosperity, peace and contentment mould return to the disturbed districts.

A telegram from Scutari reports the capture by the insur- gents of an important strategic position between Serajevo and Mostar. It is said that many soldiers have deserted from the Austrian ranks, but this ieformation is derived from Slav sources.

The Austrian Charge d'Affaires at Cettinge has asked the intervention of the Prince of Monteneoro, and the mediation has resulted in the conclusion of an armistice, or rather a cessation of hostilities, to last for 20 days, in the district bordering on the Montenegrin frontier. The insurgent leaders have resolved to continue the struggle, and the cessation of hostilities is of the most partial kind. _ .

A telegram from Vienna on Wednesday night says that as yet there is little hope of the insurrection being put down rapidly. The official reports of the encounters shows that the scene of action is gradually passing from the 'Montene- grin frontier into Russia, and that the insurgents are sur- rounding Foca. Intelligence has reached Vienna from Cracow of exten- sive movements of troops in Pocolia, Russian Poland, and Bessarabia. It is added that travellers coming from Russia tell Of war-like preparations all over Russia.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.
Twenty farms in Queen's county were sold on Saturday for rent, and were either bought in by the owners or the Emergency Committee.

. _ A shoemaker, named Kelly, was arrestad at Millstreet on Sunday, charged with being a sworn member of the Irish Republic. There are 35 persons awaiting trial in Cork on a similar charge. The Dublin Gazette notifies that _Kilkenny Gaol. will, from-Monday last, be used for male prisoners owly. ;This is regarded as indicating an intention on the part of the authorities to effect a large number of arrests in the southern counties.

The inquest on the body of the Cashel money lender, Phe- lan, has terminated in a verdict of wilful murder against some person unknown. The police on Sunday arrested two men who had been in the deceased's company, and one of whom had paid him a sum of £29. At Cork on Monday 16 men, reputed to be members of the Millstreet band of desperadoes, were committed for trial on the charge of treason-felony. lhe informer Connell gave evidence against them, alleging that they were members of the Irish Republican Brotherhood, and were sworn to depose the Queen in that country. At a meeting of the Dublin Corporation on Monday, 'a letter was read from Mr. Burke, Under-Secretary, to the effect that the Lord-Lieutenant could net comply with the request of the Council for permission to have the roll of honorary freedom signed by Messrs. Parnell and Dillon in Kilmainham Gaol.

In addressing the city jury at the Dublin Commission, on Tuesday, Lord Chief Justice May commented upon the great increase of crimes, the porpetratois of which were not discovored. On the other hand, he congratulated the county jury on the state of County Dublin, which presented a con- trast to the disturbed counties in the remote parts of the country. Seventeen men were brought up at Clonbur, on Tuesday, charged with the murder of Lord Ardilaun's bailiffs, whose bodies were found in Lough Mask. Six were discharged, and the others remanded, the police stating that there had been great difficulty in obtaining evidence, owing to the common cause made by the people in the locality with the persons believed to be implicated in the crime. They had, however, traced the movements of the bailiffs to within one hundred yards of the scene of the murder.

In Limerick, the relations between the military and cer- tain citizens, chiefly from the old town, have become so strained that a communication has been addresssed by the commander of the force in Limerick to the Mayor on the subject, pointing out that the soldiers cannot pass through the streets at night but they are pelted with stones. A warning is given that if such a thing is continued and the soldiers attacked by the populace, the military will be com- pelled to fire on the people in self-defence. ATTEMPT TO INJURE MR. FORSTER.—A diabolical attempt has been made to do serious personal injury to the Chief Secretary for Ireland. On Thursday week, a few days after Mr. Forster had left Ireland for London, a letter addressed to him was received at Dublin Castle. Upon the envelope were a number of dark stains, which were apparently caused, not by external contact, but by some substance contained within. The suspicions of the officials w:re at once aroused, and after partially opening the letter they sent the envelope , to an analyst for careful examination and analysis of the contents. It was discovered to contain two scruples of iodide of nitrogen—a dangerous explosive, which it is possible might have caused damage if opened without caution. The substance in the envelope was wet, in which state it is non-explosive. Certain chemical formula within the envelope, and the manner in which the dangerous compound was enclosed in- dicate that the persons guilty of the outrage must have been possessed of a high degree of chemical knowledge. The letter was addressed to "The Right Hon. W. E. Forster, the Castle, Dublin," and bore the capital letters of " 0.H.M.5.," as if to induce the supposition that it was an official com- munication. It was stamped with the Dublin postmark, January 31. The mere act of opening the letter might have caused an explosion and resulted in injury to the hands, or to the face, if close enough, or it might have destroyed the eyesight. The originators of the plot appear to have over- looked the fact that all letters addressed to Mr. Forster are opened by his secretaries.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

ENGLAND V. IRELAND—Favoured by fine weather and in the presence of some 5,000 spectators the above inter- national contest was played on Monday at Lansdowne-road, Dublin, when a very fast and well-contested game ended in a draw.

ST. ELPHIN'S JUNIORS V. ST. JOHN'S.-A match between the above clubs was played on the ground of the latter, on Saturday last, and resulted in a victory for the Juniors. Score :—St. Elpluns Juniors, two goals, and four minor points; St. John's, one goal, and three minor points. CREWE BRITANNIA V. RUNCORN (2ND TEAMS). This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and ended in favour of Britannia by three minor points tn Runcorn one touchdown. The forwards were equally matched, but the splendid back play of Skeldon and Gregory was very noticeable. A. Bebbington, T. Bebbington, Derby- shire, and Lightfoot were the pick of the forwards. Teams: Britannia—Back, Cook, three-quarter backs, Skeldon and Derbyshire ; half-backs, G (captain), and Iteillys ; ,9 Gregory forwards, Bettanny, A. Bebbington, T. Bebbington, Groves, Lightfoot, Lewis, Roberts, and Williams. Runcorn—Back, Windrigg ; three-quarter backs, Sherlock and Riley ; half- backs, Mason and Page; forwards, Dean, Dunbavan, Ford, Gittens, Borrtiws, Riley, Wright, Ase, and Roberts. RUNCORN V. CREWE BRITANNIA. - The first teams of these clubs played the return match at Runcorn, on Satur- day, when a very unpleasant and disputive match was played. Runcorn were the victors by one try and seven minor points, to one goal, kicked from a disputed try, and four minor points for Crewe. Teams: Runcorn—J. Pow- nall, full back; Larkin and Broady, three-quarter backs Hughes and Andrews, half-backs ; Bate (captain), Gatley, Cox, Bennett, Wright, Clarke, Crosby, Joule, Lewis, and C. Pownall, forwards. Crewe—W. Talbot, full back; Brookes, Halfpenny, and Talbot, three-quarter backs ; Moore and Bailey, half-hacks ; Carter, Harden, Dooler, Roberts, Nott, Heaps, Greensmith, and two others, forwards.

Information has reached Liverpool from San Franclsca of an affray on board the British steamer Anjer Head, in the course of which the second officer shot dead the cook, a Chinaman. The second officer had been arrested. The Home Secretary has intimated to Dr. Cameron, M.P., that he has given orders for the release of the girl Mary Jane Park, from Glasgow Lochburn Industrial School. This was the girl who was flogged naked in that school and after- wards put under the spray bath, by order of the matron, against whom she since obtained damages for as§ault. A young married woman, named Hannah Poppleton, living in Grenville-street, Stockport, on Thursday evening drowned one of her children, aged twelve months, in a bucket of water, cut the throat of another child three years old, and then committed suicide by cutting her own throat. The husband is employed as traveller by Mr. Oulton, sack dealer, Liverpool, and left home on Thursday morning. On his return at six in tae evening he found the children dead and his wife with a fearful gash in her throat, from which she died shortly afterwards.

TRADE NOTES.

The wages dispute in the Manchester and Salford en- gineering trades has been settled by an agreement between the employers and the workmen that the advance of 2s. per week shall come into effect on March let. On Saturday the chain-makers in the Cradley Heath, Old Hill, Rowley, Lye Waste, Halesowen, Walsall, and Tipton districts, numbering about 3000, gave notice for an advance of wages averaging between 10 and 15 per cent. The men clabo the 4s. Gd. list for common and the ss. list for best chain. _ _ _ _ _

At a largely attended special council of delegates from South and West Yorkshire, held at Barnsley, resolutions have been passed in favour of a general restriction of output or a stoppage of col- lieries in the event of the owners still declining to concede the advance of wages applied for. At a meeting of workmen's representatives in the iron trade, at Darlington, on Saturday, resolutions were adopted advising the men on strike to resume work, leaving the questions in dispute to be settled by the board of arbitration. On Monday that board passed a resolution that in consequence of the condition of trade an advance of 71' per cent. be given from the 30th January to the 20th April, and any claim for a further advance and the sliding scale be referred to arbitration. The men are to work full time as heretofore.

On the miners of Rowley Hall Colliery, Rowley, being ordered on Wednesday morning to remove bats from the tubs of coal, they struck work, and ascended the pits with their picks. Some men refused to leave work, and a general dis- turbance followed. In consequence of the great intimidation a posse of police was specially in attendance and quelled the disturbance. Upwards of 2'ooo men are employed, and the proprietors have been compelled to close the pits, Fifty of the men will be prasecuted. In view of the increasing business in the iron trade and disappointment felt at no increase in wages following the last meeting of the Ironmasters' Association at Birmingham, the North Staffordshire ironworkers have decided to appeal to their employers to return to the scale of prices paid before the late depression in trade set in especially as respects doubling, concerning which the puddlers of the district made great concessions some time ago. THREATENED STRIKE IN STAFFORDSHIRE.—On Tuesday night (says a correspondent), it had .become known to the officials of Ironworkers' Wages Board of Staffordshire that the ironworkers in Lancashire, Yorkshire, and Staffordshire, who acknowledge that tribunal, bad resolved that they must have a like advance to that conceded to the ironworkers in the north of England after last week's strike, and that if this should be declined they will stop work next Monday. Au immediate rise of Pd. per ton on puddling, 7A- per cent. on mill work, and further advAndeg after March are demanded. THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE. MANCHESTEn WEDNE- DAY.—The amount of new business coming into the market is still only limited in extent, but makers generally show very little anxiety to press sales as they believe that by . waiting they will do better than by attempting to force the market at present. There is, however, a weaker tone in the market, and both local and district brands of pig iron can be bought at lower figures than sellers have recently been ask- ing. Lancashire pig iron is still quoted at 525. GI less 2A- delivered equal to Manchester, but makers are open to entertain good offers at slightly under this figure, whilst deliveries would now in all probability be extended up to the end of Jane. Lincolnshire iron averages about the same as local brands, and Middlesborough has been quoted at 30s 4d net cash delivered equal to Manchester. Although finished iron makers are Pet bolding for the top figures lately quoted, they are generally firm in their prices on the basis of about £7 per ton for bars delivered into the Manchester district, with second-hand lots in some cases offering at a trifle under this figure. The principal Lancashire engineering firms con- tinue well employed, and a considerable amount of fire-proof work has recently been given out in comeeticin with the erection of new mills in the district.

I THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.—MANCHESTER, WED- NESDAY.—A. very quiet tone continues throughout the coal trade of this district, and although the recent colder weather has brought a little more activity into house fire qualities of fuel the increased demand has not been appreciably felt in the market, owing to the output of the Lancashire collieries being so much in excess of requirements. Where the pits are kept on full time heavy stocks are being put down, but except in the immediate neighbourhood of Manchester col- lieries, as a rule, are not working much beyond the orders which come in, and this represents an average of about four days per week. Steam and forge coals are in fairly '..olad demand for manufacturing and trade purposes, but are plenti- ful in the market. Engine classes of fuel move off tolerably well, but of these there is also no scarcity. Prices are with- out material change. Although it is only in a few excep- tional cases that there has been any officially announced reduction of list rates, there is still so much underselling that for the most part they are a little more than nominal, and at the pit mouth the average prices are about as under :—Best coal, 9s. to 9s. ed., seconds, 7s. to 7s. GI., common round coals from ss. to Gs., burgy, 43. GI. to 55., good slack, 33. Pd. to 4s. 3d., and common sorts, 3s. to 3s. 3d. per ton. There is still only a limited amount of business doing for shipment, and 7s. to 7s. tici. per ton remains about the average figure for steam coals delivered at Garston docks or the high level at Liverpool.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

MISSIONARY MEETING.—The annual meeting on behalf of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel; was held in the Town Hall, on Monday evening, when £l4 were handed in by the box holders. There was a moderately good atten- dance.

CONCERT.—On Tuesday evening, the Earlestown Football Club held a concert in the Infants' schoolroom, when an interesting programme was gone through, including "The ancient mariner," a cantata by Mr. T. Mee Pattison, of War- rington. There was a numerous audience.

I:I,'ESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE. An enjoyable entertain- ment was given in the Wesleyan schoolroom, on Thursday evening, in connection with the Band of Hope. The pro- gramme consisted of a piece, entitled "A teetotal chairman in a fix," given by nineteen characters, interspersed with singing, &c. A collection was made at the close to defray the expenses. INDECENT ASSAULT AT NEWTON. At the Liverpool Assizes, on Saturday. James Singleton, aged 30, labourer, was convicted of having, at Newton, on the 3rd December, feloniously assaulted Emma Broom. Dr. Commins, Q.C., M.P., prosecuted, and Mr. Shand defended. The prisoner was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment. ACCIDENT IN A PRINTING OFFICE. On Friday after- noon, a boy named Appleton had his hand crushed in the Printing and Stationery Office while " feeding " one of the " Tumbler " printing machines. It appears that in endea- vouring to prevent a sheet from slipping through so as to clog the machine he had snatched at it, and in doing so his hand was caught in the machine which mutilated half of his hand. He was immediately taken to Manchester Infirmary where the surgeon thought to save the hand by amputating one finger, but it was found next day that mortification had set in, find the band was amputated. The firm have done all they can for the lad's comfort, and he is progressing very favourably.

ACCIDENT TO THE SEWAGE VAN.—About noon' on Mon- day, as the town scavenger's van was crossing the bridge over the brook in Newton, the axle broke in two and the vehicle became immovable till another cart was obtained, and the contents of the derelict transferred. much to tie dis- comfort of the printers at that end of the town, who were returning from dinner.

I. 0. G. T., HOPE OF EiRLESTOWN LODGE. The usual quarterly meeting of the above lodge was held in the lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday even- ing, when there was a very good attendance of members; Sister M. E. Allison,W.C.T., presided. After the initiation of a candidate, the reports of the various officers were tendered and adopted, that of the W. Sec. (Bro. Ed. Newman), being a very encouraging one. The number of members considered good was 70, an increase of eight on the the previous quarter. One means of promoting this increase was the Saturday evening entertainments, and he urged the members to invite their friends and acquaintances to attend. He also urged the members to take more temperance litera- ture, as it would tend to make them better acquainted with the position and progress of the temperance cause, and would strengthen them in their principles. The report of the W. F. S. and W. Tres. (combined) Bros. John Taylor and Hy. Warburton, showed the finances to be in a very satisfactory state, there being a fair balance in hand. Bro. W. Mitchell, W. 111.. also gave his report on the state of the lodge property, and Bro. E. A. Newman tendered a report as superintendent of the Juvenile Temple, which showed a slight decrease of membership on the quarter, the number now being 33. The decrease was chiefly owing to the establishment of several new bands of hope, of which he was glad to say there were three in Earlestown, and one in the Crow-lane Congrega- tional school, Newton. After the adoption of the various reports, the officers for the ensuing quarter were duly installed by Bro. John Warburton, Lodge Deputy, assisted by Bro. George Warburton jun., as G.W.M.; W.C.T., Bro. John Taylor; W.V.T., Sister J. E. Warburton; W. Sec., Bro. E. Newman; W.F. bee, Bro. John Little ; W. Tres., Bro. George Warburton, sen., &c. It was decided to invite the District Lodge of South West Lancashire to hold its May session in Earlestown.

NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, Newton-.le-Willows, on Monday. Present, Mr. F. Gooch (chairman), Lieut.-Colonel McCorquodale, Messrs. - Pardey, Glover, Emmett, Forster, J. E. Worsley (clerk), R. Brierley (surveyor), J. Watkins (medical officer), and J. Ball (school attendance officer). THE APPOINTMENT OF CHEMICAL WORKS INSPECTORS. The CLERK said that in conformity with the resolution passed at the last meeting he prepared and forwarded a Petition to the President of the Locll Government Board,', with a letter explaining its purport and effect. He received ' on the 17th January a reply, which, referring to the portion of the memorial relating to the appointment of a separate inspector for each of the districts of St. Helens and Widnes, inquired whether the Commissioners were willing to take • advantage of the provision in section 19 of the Alkali, &c., Works Regulation Act, 1881, for the appointment of addi- tional inspectors, or w:lether they were prepared to unite with any adjoining authorities for that purpose. scnYlisaaoOdif the School Attendance Committee, held already eAN would been tnEad uElNdpe ebAeN unnecessary OL COMMITTEE. ess as the to reply, a piAplotrfnalAßet) mmeenDttEisg h on the 16th January, the school attendance officer read his report and the committee, on considering the same, together with the complaint from St. Peter's Schools, found in some cases that absence from school had been permitted on in- sufficient excuses. It was ordered that it be an instruction to Mr. Ball to be more particular in accepting excuses of

contagious or infectious sickness, unless certified by a medical practitioner. Mr. Ball was ordered to report monthly upon all absentees from each school in the district and the causes for their absence.

Mr. PARDEY drew attention to the case of a lad named Pullen, who was desirous of attending a school within this district as a half-timer. The Board would recollect that the boy was refused admission to Et. Peter's School, unless on the payment of a fine as they might call it. The Board passed a resolution instructing the Law Clerk to write to the Local Government Board for an opinion upon the case; btat the reply was that they could not give a reply in general but that they must have the case put before them. It was ordered that the boy present himself foradmission and tender the usual fee of 4d. The boy was, however, prevented from attending school owing to sickness at home ; but three or four weeks ago he was again ready to go to scheol. The school attendance officer then came to him as chairman of the School Attendance Committee' and asked him what he was to do. He (Mr. Pardey) took upon himself to say that the lad should go to the school and ask for admission and tender the usual fee of dd. per week. He believed the lad went on Monday and stayed half a day, but was told he would not be admitted again unless lie brought the double fee. He asked the attendance officer if the boy had attended at the school again but he said he had not. He thought he should have instructed the boy to go to school again next morning and seek admission. The father of the boy was called in and confirmed the above statement.

Mr. BALL, in reply to a member, said St. Peter's School was the only school which refused to admit half-timers. The custom at all other schools was for half-timers to paw the same amount as full-timers. At Ashton-in-Makerfierd the usual fee for a boy in the third standard was 3d. per week full time, but a half-timer only paid lid. After some conversation, the minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. PARDEY seconded by Mr. FORSTER ; and on the proposition of Mr. PennEy the Law Clerk was in- structed to lay the facts of the Puilen case before the Education Department.

div.p: HIGHWAYS, ETC., COMMITTEE.

A meeting of the Highways, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee was held on the 16th inst. Seven fresh cases of scarlet fever had occurred during the week, and 30 old cases still exNted ; three cases of measles Wel e also reported. Mr. Brierley submitted a statement of the trial holes made on the site of the proposed burial ground, when it was resolved that the members of the Board be summoned to attend a meeting on the land to inspect same, and for other purposes, Mr. Brierley, in the meantime, to peg out the proposed site. The committee recommended that the resolution passed at tire Board meetir- held on. the Th June, 1881, agreeing to the payment Of 1.-827. hi tndic4Trac:W.mers for each CalF.o of infectiotin disease reported by ineni Plans for seven cottages in Nelson-street for Mr. George Ratcliffe; one cottage in Houghton-street for Messrs. Green- all and Co., and an amended block plan of two houses in Cross-lane for Mr. George Tunstall, were submitted and approved.

- Mr. GLovEn moved, and Mr. PARDEy. seconded, the con- firmation of the minutes. Dr. WATKINS asked the Board to reconsider the resolution which the Board proposed to rescind. If they did not get all the co-operation they desired from the medical practi- tionerg, he beseeched the Board to get all the co-operation they could.

Mr. PARDEY moved an amendment that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of the last resolution, and that the payment of the 2s. 61 be only made in those cases of which-an intimation was received within three days of the time they came under the knowledge of the medical men. Mr. EMMETT seconded the amendment, NI hich was carried.

GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. A meeting of the Gas and Water Committee was held on the 16th ult. It was ordered that a 3m, gas main be laid across the Market Place. Mr. Brierley recommended that Mr. Dawson be paid the sum of £5O he discharge of his balance on contract ;or gas tank; and it was ordered that a cheque for the amount be issued. Mr. GLOVER mowed, and Colonel MCCORQUODALE seconded, the adoption of the minutes, and the motion was adopted.

div.p: FINANCE.

A meeting of the Finance Committee was held on the 16th ult., when acconots amounting to £795 183. 3d. were examined, and cheques signed for payment. The minutes were confirmed on the proposition of Mr. GLOVER, seconded by the CHAIRMAN:.

div.head: TILE MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: TILE MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT.

Dr. Weertems read his report for the year 1881, which stated there were ree,istred :—Births, 223 melee, 180 females, total 406; deaths, 95 males, 95 females, total 190; excess of births, 131 males, 85 females, total 216 The birth rate was 38 OD and the death rate 17.82 per 1,000 of the population estiniated to the middle of the veer. There were only two deaths registered under the head of "diarrhms and dysen- tery,"—one chronic case of ulceration of the bowels, and the other connected with dentition in an infant a month old. There was one case of confluent smallpox removed to the Infectious Diseases Hospital at Warrington, where the patient died. Scarlatina had prevailed throughout the whole year. It had been of a mild type, and almost entirely con- fined to children. Thirty-nine deaths-23 under and 16 above five years of age—were caused by the disease, either immediately or by its sequelae In proof of its prevalence almost entirely amongst children, out of the 16 deaths above five years of age the three highest ages were tespectively ten, nine, and eight years, the remaining 13 ranging from just over five years to Seven years of age. The various measures that had been adopted in the direction of curtail- ing the extension of the disease must be fresh in the remem- brance of the Commissioners. The mildnes of the type of the epidemic had been one cause of its wider diffusion, for so many of the cases had in the primary stages of the disease been so light and transient that too many parents had been deluded into a state of false security that all danger was over, and thus, by an indiscreetly early exposure, the double danger of injury to the convalescent and infection of those they commingled with was sadly to often incurred. There was no moral doubt that the epidemic might have been re- strained within narrower limits if .there had been more thoughtful care, more circumspection, more self-restraint, more thought for one's neighbours, with a greater disposi- tion to heed advice and regard authority in the place of so much recklessness and blind fatalism. The obvious Un- necessary amount of intercommunication between families west he explanation and the key to the problem of the dissem- ination of the disease that had been so terribly worked out. There was now reason to hope that the force of the epidemic was nearly spent. There had been great need of a place for the special disinfection of wearing apparel, or an efficient locomotive disinfecting apparatus for the purpose. The utmost care had been taken to distribute liberally the neces- sary disinfectants for the houses of the sick, and in those cases without medical attendance external agents to diminish or destroy the infective power of the skin in each convalescent. He strongly recommended the Board to purchase or hire an , apparatus, if they did not deem it convenient to erect one of a fixed and more permanent character. He was glad to record that the rate of infantile mortality, (i.e., of children under five years of age) had declined from 56.72 in the year 1880 without an epidemic visitation, to 43.68 per cent. in the presence of a serious epidemic prevailing throughout the year 1881. The removal of nightsoil by the contractor was on the whole well done. The removal, however, of the pail-soil in the ordinary liquid manure carts was obnoxious in the extreme; and he urged upon the Board the necessity of devising means to wholly reitove or mitigate this grow- ing nuisance. He again called attention to the subject of the burial ground, which, day by day, was becoming of greater urgency. The two Church of Eneland graveyards were both nearly full, and the day was but little distant when a new breadth in either would not be obtainable. These burial places were now, for all practical purposes, free for the use of all, irrespective of creed ; and this fact, in connection with another very important one, namely, that the population of the district increased by over 2,000 in the last decade, rendered it certain that interments in these existing places of sepulture would he in an increasing ratio , It was painful to contemplate the possibility, through un- necessary delay, of having to find a resting place for the dead only on sufferance. An extensive main sewer, deep and wide., had been constructed from the middle of High-st. westwards. He trusted this improvement would be further developed by provision being made for the periodical flush- ing of the sewers in dry summers. He was convinced this was an actual necessity.
Mr. EMMETT, referring to the burial ground, said the matter was under consideration, and he had no doubt it would receive every atteniion.

Mr. PARDET said Dr. Watkins had given them a very long and, he believed, a most valuable report. (Hear, hear.) He thoug•ht it was hardly competent for them to go into it that afternoon, and he therefore proposed that it be referred to the Sanitary Committee.
Mr. GLOVER seconded the proposition, which was carried. •

ARSON AT LIVERPOOL.—At the Liverpool Police Court, on Tuesday, William Shimmin, manifest clerk, in the employ of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal Company, was charged on his own confession with setting fire to a shed at the company's wharf in Great Howard-street, on Sunday night, by which £4,000 worth of cotton was destroyed. Th.e prisonerh c Coroner's gave r, s in inquiry himself ui uryp inattotthhee deeatnescetiovfe otflihece he t was drunk at the time, and did it for "devilment." The office, Saving explosionig prisoner had nothing to say, and was remanded. the Abram Colliery, Bickershaw, by which 48 men lost thei lives, was resumed on Tuesday. Evidence was given by two colliers to the effect thaC they had been in the habit, when their lamps became extinguished, of taking them to the pit-eye and themselves unlocking and relighting them. It had often happened, they said, that there had been no official present to see that the lamps were properly locked. A des- cription was given of the creceral working' of the mine, which han the reputation of being one of the best constructed and best managed in the country.-The enquiry was continued on Wednesday, and on Thursday evidence of an,interesting character was given. Samuel Aspinall, a collier, of Leigh, said that on the Friday before the explosion he saw a lamp which young Mr. CRONSHAW, the underlooker (one of the victims), had in the workings was not locked. The witness said he had not made this statement before except to his wife and the miners' agent, "for fear of being bagged." William Clare, another collier, said he had been allowed to go away from the pit-eve with- out having his lamp examined. On the day mentioned by the last witness, he saw the underlooker and the fireman come into his working place with their lamp tops off. This ' witness also had not mentioned that circumstanee before "because he feared he should lose his place" if he did. The inquiry was further adjourned till next Wednesday.

BACHELORS' BALL AT ST. HELENS. - The annual bachelors' ball was held on Friday night, in the Town Hall, St. Helens. Dancing was commenced to the strains of Mr. Goodwin's band from Manchester and kept up until late. Refreshments and supper were provided. by Mrs. Taylor, of the Fleece Hotel. SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 11, 1882.

THE day of the opening of Parliament was an excit- ing one. It was not anything contained in the Royal Speech which caused such a high pitch of political feeling at the beginning of the session as was ap- parent in the House of Commons, on Tuesday after- noon. No; what caused so many members on the Tory side of the House, to hurry into their places as if the fate of the Empire depended upon their pres- ence, was simply the circumstance that one solitary Member of Parliament, who has been the object now for nearly two years of a persecution on account of his opinion pretendedly Christian, but in its male- volent and intolerant spirit most anti-Christian, was known to intend again to seek to take his seat on the same terms as all the other members of the House. OAKLAND-STREET, WIDNES, WESLETsVi 'MUTUAL IM- PROVEMENT CLASS.—The weekly meeting class was held on Wednesday, when, in place of the customary paper or lecture, a miscellaneous entertainment was given. HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.-011 Monday evening, Mr. J. Looker read a paper to the members of the above society on "Temperance." The essayist dwelt chiefly on local option and the Sunday closing question, which he contended would greatly benefit the nation. A good dis- cussion followed.

SERIOTJS ACCIDENT TO A WIDNES MAN.—On Tuesday morning, a man named John Turner, who is in the employ of Mr. Thomas Sadler, builder:and contractor, of Widnes- road, was putting the belt on the fly-wheel of an engine while it was in motion when some portion of his clothing caught in the wheel and he fell to the ground, fracturing his ankle in the fall. Dr. O'Keeffe was sent for, and the injured. man was taken to the Accident Hospital. Turner is now stated to he progressing favourably. THE APPLICATION FOR AN 'INJUNCTION AGAINST THE WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.—Tchay v. the Manchester, Shef- field, and Lincolnshire Railway Company.—ln the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, on Thursday, Vice- Chancellor Hall ordered this motion for an injunction to re- strain the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, the Cheshire Lines Committee, and the Widnes Local Board, from interfering with the right of way over certain land, to stand over for a week in order to answer affidavits.

WESTON SONS OF TEMPERANCE.—On the evening of the 3rd inst., the annual meeting, in connection with this Order, was held in the Church schoolroom, Weston, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Norman. The society, which was only established at Weston three years ago, has now 40 adult and 43 cadet members. The chairman delivered an , address on the advantages of the Order, and the progress which the temperance movement is making throughout the , country. An entertainment followed, in which the Elles- mere glee party, Miss Clough, Miss Booth, Miss Horton, and Messrs. Fred. Nickson, John Holford, John Hopkins, and Peter Smith (drngsrist), took part. A comic sketch, entitled "Wanted, a confidential clerk," was given, the characters , being taken by Messrs. Moulton, Crosby, Williams, Hop- kins, Page, and Shaw. A vote of thanks was passed to the chairman, on the proposition of Mr. John Poole, seconded , by Mr. W. Norman. RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.—An adjourned meeting of the members of this body was held on Monday evening. Mr. Coventry occupied the chair The deputation reported that the directors of the Coffee and Cocoa Room Co., had offered to let the three rooms on the first floor of their building, at a rental of £32, including gas, coal, taxes and attendance. It was resolved that the offer be accepted, and that the removal take place on the 27th inst. A letter was read from Mr. Meadowcroft, agent to the Bridgewater Navigation Company, stating that on account of his duties, he (lid not consider he was in a posi- tion to take the presidency this year. It was unanimously decided that Dr. Steele be requested to accept the position. A vote of thanks was given to Mr. J. D. Jones for his ser- vices as treasurer, and Mr. S. C. Beckett was elected to the post. Mr. Charles Nickson was appointed secretary, in the place of Mr. B. Smith, resigned. RUNCORN AND DISTRICT TEACHERS' AsSOCIATION.— The monthly meeting was held on Saturday in Widnes National School (kindly lent by the managers), Mr. J. C. Crawford, the .president, occupying the chair. It was unanimously resolved to admit as members of the associa- tion Misses Clayton, Crake, Ellice, Hughes, Jump, Richard- son, short, Strong, Tyrie, and Messrs. Calland, Fitton, Hutton, and Minton. Through Miss Lee's generosity the party enjoyed an excellent tea. Upon resuming, Mr. Hunter read an amusing and interesting paper on Thackeray's " Pendennis," for which he received a hearty vote of thanks. Mr. Morris, of Weston, the defendant in a recent magisterial inquiry at Runcorn, detailed the circumstances that led to the alleged assault. The teachers deeply sympathised with Mr. Morris, hied expressed regret that such an unfounded charge had been preferred against him. A miscellaneous entertainment followed, Miss Williams, and Messrs. Lister, Hunter, Calland, and .Annett taking a prominent part, and Mr. Hutton and Misses Wilton and Ellice creditably acting as accompanists, whilst the president ably tilled the office of condnctor. , Votes of thanks brought the meeting to a close. The association now numbers 40 members. RUNCORN SOAP AND ALKALI COMPANY.—The sixteenth annual meeting of this company was heldron Thursday, at the Law Association Rooms, Liverpool. Mr. A. P. Fletcher (chairman) presided. In the annual report, the directors said they regretted that it was not more satisfactory. The gross profits (including transfer fees) amounted to £13,527 lOs 11d, from which had to be deducted office expenses, salaries, commissions, rates, income tax, audit, &es £5,249 11(1.7d, and bank commissions, interest on debentures, and balance of trade discounts, £2,217 13s 11d, which left £6,060 5s 54. After adding £2,071 3s, the balance from last year, less directors' fees, there was left an available balance of £9,131 8s sd, which it was proposed to appropriate as follows :—Proposed dividend of lOs per share, £6,000; balance carried forward, £3,131 8s sd—total, £9,131 8s sd. The report was duly adopted, the retiring directors, Mr. Fletcher and Mr. Hayes, were re-elected, and Messrs. 11ar- mood Banner and Son were appointed auditors for the ensu- ring Tear. THE FRODSHAM Gas COMEANY, LIMITED—The annual meeting of the shareholders of this company was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Monday evening. Mr. James Rigby presided. The report of the directors stated that the business during the past year had been satisfactory. The income frcm all sources amounted to £987 ss. 61-d., being an increase of £6B 9s. B.lid. on that of the previous year, due to an increase in the consumption of gas and larger sale of ammoniacal liquor. The expenditure amounted to £Ol7 103. 4(1., leaving a balance of profit of £369 15s. sd. Of this £2OO was taken to pay off loan capital, the re- mainder, together with the balance brought forward from the previous account, amounting to £382 Is. 7d., being available for distribution. A dividend of 7 per cent. for the past year was declared, and the retiring directors, (Messrs. S. Walker and Jno. Robinson,) were re-elected. ACTION BY THE WIDNES ASEISTANT OVERSEER.—At the ! Liverpool Assizes, on Thursday, the case of Rigby v. Edwards was heard. This was an action to recover £2O upon a ckeque drawn by the defendant, who is a farmer liv- ing near Bala. Mr. Woolton (instructed by Mr. Beasley, of Widnes) represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Kennedy the defendant. The defendant had drawn a cheque upon his bankers, payable to John Knight and Co., of Widnes. The cheque was endorsed by J. J. Knight, who was acting as manager in his father's absence, and it was cashed by Mr. Rigby, the plaintiff. When Mr. Rigby forwarded the cheque through his bankers to the bank at Bala, it was found that payment had been stopped. The only way in which lie could get his money, therefore, was to sue the drawer of the cheque. Mr. Knight who was at the head of the .firm at Widnes, had, it was dated, absconded, and had been made a bankrupt. The defence was that the cheque was endorsed under such circumstances as to give the plaintiff no right of action. The questions left to the jury were-1, whether J. J. Knight had authority to cash the cheque ; and 2, whether, in going so, he knew that he was defrauding the defendant. The jury answered the first rfuestion in the affirmative and the second in the negative. His Lordship thereupon gave judgment for the plaintiff. FUNERAL OF Mn. P. R. CHADWICK, OF RUNCORN.— The funeral obsequies of Mr. Philip Richard Chadwick, of Crofton Lodge, took place, on Tuesday, at Daresbury church. The procession left the deceased's residence about eleven o'clock, and was headed by the police, under the command of superintendent Williamson, assisted by Inspec- tor Hollingworth. They were followed by the following members of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows, of which deceased was an honorary member:—Messrs. T. Lydiate, J. W. Woodland, A. Riley, J. Tonks, Joseph Owen, W. 11. Tonks, S. Armstrong, H. Briscoe, W. Appleton, John Wilson, W. Brown, D. McLean, J. Riley, W. Ford, Joseph Slade, and H. B. Toone (secretary). Immediately following was a car- riage containing the Rev. Canon Barclay, Dr. McDougall, and Dr. Mouritz. The next carriage contained Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P., brother, and the Rev. J. E. Hughes, brother- in-law of deceased. In the third were Messrs. C. W. Hazle- hurst, J. A. Reid, G. S. Hazlehurst, and G. L. Wigg; in the fourth, Messrs. J. Brundrit, Thomas Banks, W. Sharp, and J. E. Wortley (deputy coroner); and in the fifth, the Rev. Thomas Chambers, Rector of Halewood; Mr. Ches. Jack, of Liverpool; Mr. E. A. Chorlton, and Mr. Charles Chorlton. The following were the bearers:—Messrs. S. Sutton, J. Ball, J. Carroll, M. Rathbone, Thomas Dutton, and J. Collings. As the procession passed through Runcorn and the imme- diate neighbourhood, most of the shops were closed, and the blinds of the principal reeklences were drawn. At Dares. bury, the body was met by Messrs. Robert Davies (of War- rington), John White, Denis Brundrit, and a large number of the tenantry ein the Daresbury estate. They preceded the hearse to the church doors where it was met by the Rev. Mr. Spencer and the Rev. T. S. Jones, who walked before the body to the chancel, the mourners following. Inside the sacred edifice, the service was read by the Rev. J. E. Hughes, and at the vault, which was placed at the east end of the building by the Rev. Canon Barclay, Vicar of Runcorn. Wreaths were sent by the following :—Mrs. Chadwick, Misses Hazlehurst, Mrs. John Brundrit, Miss Barclay, Mrs. Silver, Miss Jefferson, and others. The coffin was an oak one, with brass mountings, and the inscription stated that deceased was in his 32nd year. Mr. W. H. Rogerson acted as undertaker. The hearse and carriages were supplied by Messrs. S. Yarsvood and Sons, of Runcorn, and the coffin by Mr. F. Brown. The private carriage of Mrs. C. Hazlehurst was also in attendance.

CIIARCIE AGAINST A NV/ CRINGTON MAN.—At Whit- church, on the 3rd inst., William James Addis, timekeeper to Messrs. Collin and Son, builders and contractors, of War- rington, was brought up in custody charged with obtaining from Mrs. Hayes, the Railway Inn, Whitchurch, a sum of money under the pretence that it was for his employers. After a lengthened hearing, the Bench discharged the prisoner, considering that he intended to return the money, and only required the temporary use of it. A crowded court applauded the decision, Nr. Percy Davies, of Warrington, appeared tor Addis.

PRIMITIVE METnODISTS' SPECIAL SERVICES AT WIDNES. —A series of special services were commenced, on Sunday, in the Simes Cross Primitive Methodist Chapel, the preacher being Miss Griffiths. WARRINGTON CEMETERY.—Returns of interments in the Warrington Cemetery during the week ending yesterday : Adults, 4; children, 15; total, 19. VALENTINES.—A severe strain is put upon the post- office in dealing with valentines which tare sent in such large numbers. The post-office does all in its power to ensure the due despatch and delivery of correspondence at the valentine season; and it is hoped that the public will assist the department by posting their letters, Sze., early on Monday next. _ _

Cinous TIIEA.TRE or VARIETIES.—A. capital enter- tainment has been provided at this place of amusement during the week. In addition to several of last week's attractions, the programme i included a ventriloquial entertainment by Mr. Vernon Grey, whose performances kept the audience in a roar of laughter, some clever bicycling; feats by Sydney and Alphonze, buprising acts of legerde- main by Professor Devon°, and comic songs which were provocative oi much amusement by Mr. Harry Gill, who was repeatedly recalled. The performances throughout seemed to be greatly enjoyed.

LIQUIDATIONS BY A.RDANGEMENT.—James Newton, Manchester-road, Warrington, licensed victualler; Thomas C. Pierpoint, Bold-street, Warrington, architect; Robert Davies, Foregate-street, Chester, licensed victualler; George M'Fall, Tollemache-street, New Brighton, slater; Clementina Yarwood, Hurdsfield-road, Macclesfield, provision dealer; Enoch Pace, Swanlow-lane, Over, grocer; Samuel Brace- girdle, Leftwich, near Nothwich, wood and iron ship- builder.

WARRINGTON PEOPLE'S COLLEGE.—MiSS Jesse Cruick- shank, late a pupil teacher in this school, who obtained a first-class Queen's scholarship, at the July examination, for admission to the Training Colleges, was presented by the Head Master, on behalf of the pupils, with a handsome olive-wood writing desk, and also with a dressing case from the teachers, on Thursday last, as marks of esteem and re- gard on the occasion of her leaving to become a student in the British and Foreign School Society's training college for mistresses at Stockwell, London. PADGATE WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SO - CIETY.—On Thursday, Mr. J. Wilde read an interesting paper contrasting the greatness of England with the great- ness of ancient Rome. An animated discussion followed, Mr. Arthur Bennett contending that if ever England fell, like Rome, the fault would be her own; and that if her people were true to themselves, they might so consolidate and establish the British Empire as to make it impos,ibla for any other empire to rival it in greatness. Mr. F. Wright thought that the chief danger England had to contend with was the drunkenness and immorality that are so prevalent; whilst Mr. S. Shakeshaft and Mr. John Hankey expressed grave fears that Romanism was gaining ground in this country, and might ultimately work out her decay. WARRINGTON CASES AT THE LIVERPOOL ASSILES. —On Monday, at the Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. J. B. Aspinall, Q.C., John Austin, John Nicholls, and Alice Smith, who had been out on bail, were acquitted of a charge of hav- ing, at Warrington, on the 19th September, unlawfully con- spired to defraud John Wilding of the sum of £s.—John Kearns 18, bottle blower, Darby Rohan, 28, labourer, and Michael Flanagan, 18, factory hand, were convicted of hav- ing, at Warrington, on the let January, unlawfully assaulted' John Lee, and stolen from his person 'is., a. pocket knife, and ,other articles. They were sentenced to nine mouths' im- prisonment each. William Moran 19, labourer, and Charles Pollard (on bail), who were included in the charge, were sentenced—the former to four months' and the latter to three months' imprisonment.

SUDDEN DEATHS AT WAERINGTON.—A widow named Jane Plumpton, 78 years of age, residing at 6, Regent-street, died suddenly at 2 p.m. on the 3rd inst. Deceased had been suffering from a slight cold for several days, during which time she had talz-en very little food. On Thursday, the 2nd inst., she went about the house as usual, and seemed to be getting better when she retired to rest at night. However, at one p.m. on Friday, deceased began to sink, and Dr. Starkey smith was sent for, but she died before the doctor arrived.—The infant son of James DeloQze, warehouseman, 1, Lilford-street, also died suddenly at 2 a.m. on Saturday morning last. Deceased was suffering from dentition, and about midnight on Friday he became convulsed and died before Dr. Cannel could be called in. The Coroner referred the cases to the registrar.
