CHANCELLOR ESPIN ON THE REVISED VEESIONOF THE NEW TESTAMENT.—On Tuesday, a lecture was delivered by the Rev. Chancellor Espin, at Liscard, the subject being " The Revised Version of the New 'estament Its need." Chancellor Espin, after referring to the great responsibility involved in the revision of the authorised version of the New Testament, said it was the strongest link that bound together nearly 100 millions of English-speaking Christians throughout the world, and it had been supreme for nearly three centuries. Dealing with the •question as to whether there was any need to meddle with the authorised version at all, he pointed out why the question should be answered in the affirmative. He glanced at the provision which the Almighty had been pleased to make for the pre- servation and transmission of His holy word, and pointed out that there were three sources of authority for 4t—first, the Fathers, who ,quoted copiously from holy scripture; second, the ancient versions, such as the Syriac and the Coptic, which were as old as the second century; and many others. In conclusion, he described and classified the ancient manuscripts of the Greek Testament, illustrating his remarks by diagrams, and showed that the full authority of manuscripts was not understood when the present authorised version was made, and that this fact, together with the im- proved knowledge of the Greek language, formed weighty reasons for revising our translation. ,

THE RE-OPENING OF ST. PAHL'S CIIIIRCH.—The special services in connection with the re-opening of St. Paul's Church, Warrington, were continued on Sunday. There was a large attendance at the morning service, an the Dean of Manchester preached from the words, "For the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead "—Romans 1. 20. The church was crowded in the evening when the Rev. T. P. Williamson, vicar of Thelwall, preached from the words, "I was glad when they said unto me, let us go into the house of the Lord "—Psalms cxxii. 1. The preacher, in con- cluding his discourse, congratulated the congregation on the alterations and improvements that had been so happily car- ried out in their parish church. It must, he was sure, be a source of pleasure and satisfaction to them all to see how much better, and brighter, and more cheerful the church was, and how much more convenient it was for the render- ing of divine service. It must be a great happiness to them all to feel that they had a hand in it—that it was the result of a united effort. But while they justly prided themselves upon the improvements which had been made in that temple of the Lord, they must remember that there was another temple in which the Lord dwelt, a temple not made with bands—the temple of their body, which it was their bounden duty to cleanse, and beautify, and ornament with the graces of a meek and holy spirit—to adorn with the flowers of a godly and Christian life. WARRINGTON OVERSEERS' MEETlNG.—Alderman Kean presided at a trieeting of the Warrington overseers, held on Thursday evening, at which there were present, Messrs. Bowden, Mackie, Blackhurst, and J. L. Tunstall (deputy assistant-overseer). A letter was read from Mr. H. J. Hagger, vestery clerk, of Liverpool, informing the overseers that a meeting of those interested in obtaining an amend- ment of the law relating to the rating of successive oc- cupiers, would he held in London, on the 15th inst. The draft of a bill which appeared calculated to meet the require- ments of the case was appended. It was proposed that, if the name of any occupier did not appear in the poor-rate when made, the overseers should, as soon as this should be- come known to them, enter his name in the rate; and if the occupation commenced prior to, or at the date of the rate the overseers should also enter the date of the rate and if the occupation commenced subsequent to the date of the rate, the date when the occupation commenced. Such occupier should henceforth be deemed to have been rated from the date so entered, subject to any remedy of appeal which he would have had, if his name had appeared in the rate when made. Every occupier whether he was assessed in the rate when made or not, and every occupier who suc- ceeded or came into occupation, should be liable to pay such portion only of the rate as was proportionate to the period to his occupation. If any occupier should cease to occupy premises, in respect of which he had, paid a greater portion of the rate then he was under the provisions of that Act liable to pay, the overseers might, on demand, refund to the occupier the amount paid is excess.—After some conversa- tion, the Chairman, Mr. Mackie, and Mr. Tnnstal were appointed a deputation to attend the meeting in London.
CONGREGATIONAL TEA MEETING.

The congregational tea party in connection with Widnes Parish Church, which took place on Wednesday evening, was most successful. Over 400 persons sat down to tea which was served in the Waterloo-street schoolroom. The trays were given by the following ladies :—Mesdames J. Wright-Williams J. White, Tarbuck, Ankers, Kilcross, Crawford, F. Neill, W. Treacey, jun., H. Burton, Boardman, Littler, J. L. Briscoe, H. Mather, C. Jones, T. Davies, T. Balmer, J. Lord, and Hunt. After tea a meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, who was supported by the vicar (the Rev. J. Wright -Williams) and other gentlemen. The CHAIRMAN, remarking that he was present to show his sympathy with Mr. Williams in the work he had in the township, said in striving to make people better and happier they might regard the work from different standpoints, but whether Churchmen, Methodists, or Roman Catholics, the end was the same, and those who strove honestly to attain it richly deserved sympathy and respect. In a large parish they wanted a man who could not only work himself but make others do so, and Mr. Williams was thus qualified. Mr. Williams had monthly temperance lectures, and sought to aid in overcoming the sin of drunkenness. He, (the speaker), did not feel very hopeful of the present generqtion in this respect, but had great hope in the education of the children, especially in that of the girls. He did not consider total abstinence a sound remedy, and did not thlnk too much should be expected from legislation. The sobriety of the people must come from the feeling that drunkenness was degrading. He tcok great interest in all that concerned Widnes, and as far as he could would help to make the people better and happier. (Applause.) The Rev. J. WRIGHT-WILLIAMS said that they worked as a Church ow the parochial system, and took in all who were willing to work under their Church organisation, Speaking of the unsatisfactory condition of the Church, he said that the wardens had to contend with a poor fabric, a bad roof, and very bad churchyard, but they had endeavoured to keep the interior of the Church clean and comfortable. The de- pression in the chemical trade had prevented the completion of the new wall around the Church. The schools were doing very good wcrk, under the capital teachers and good- hearted managers, but the number on the trolls had been limited by the accommodation. In the Sunday schools they had a most regular, numerous, and true-hearted band of teachers; and at the branch school at Sirnm's Cross he had always received willing assistance. They had now a tem- perance society, of which they were exceedingly proud, and under the able management of the president and secre- taries it was likely to have a very successful career. The glee class had done good work, and had by their efforts largely contributed to the class-room fund ; and a number of good-hearted, self-denying women had come to his help as district visitors, and had in that capacity had a kindly reception on their rounds. He afterwards acknowledged the efficient services of the choir and church officers, particu- larly the sidesmen. (Applause.) Mr. IMISON acknowledged the compliments paid by the vicar, and subsequently votes of thanks were passed to the choir, day and Sunday school teachers, glee class, sub- scribers and providers of the tables, and the chairman. During the evening sons were effsctively rendered by Misses Jones, Fairlev, Cook, and Davies, Messrs. Large, Walker, Davies, and Wilkinson ; a duet by Misses Jones ; a violin and pianoforte duet by Messrs. Fairley and Imison; and three glees by the choir; each contribution eliciting hearty applause.

WESLEYAN METHODIST TEA • MEETING AT WIDNES. The annual tea meeting in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Sunday School, Lacey-street, Widnes, was held in that building on Tuesday evening, when from 200 to 300 people were present. The following ladies presided at the trays :—Mesdames Romney, Robinson, T. Sadler, B. Brown, Swale, J. Sadler, Forsbaw, Abbott, and C. Brown ; the Misses M. J. Sadler, Lizzie Jones, L. Lyons, and P. Bal- sbaw. Mr. Thomas Sadler presided. • The CHAIRMAN, in a brief opening address, dwelt upon the work of Sunday schools, which, he said, were often the nursery of the church. He believed that hundreds and thousands had found their way to Heaven throught the in- fluence of sabbath schools. In conclusion, Mr. Sadler said he should like tr see abetter attendance in the morning, as they could accomodate as many scholars again as they had at that portion of the day. The Rev. J. H. CUMMINGS (superintendent minister) ex- pressed hearty sympathy with the teachers in their noble work. (Applause.) He could never forget the impressions made upon his mind when a boy in the Surd:ly school. Speaking of Channing, the great Unitarian orator, he said ; that if Channing had been led to think of Christ at the time a preacher impressed upon him the terrible punishment reserved for the impenitent, these gifts of oratory which were the admiration of the Unitarian Society, might, instead, have been an ornament to the Christian cause.; From the story of Charming, he learned the lesson that 1 when the conscience was yet unseared, and impressions werel likely to be permanent, was the time to hit often, to hit I hard, and to strike successive blows, until the child's heart was broken, and he was brought to look to God, the Light of the World. He regarded the Sunday school as an irite- ' gral portion of the church, and held that no church was complete without it. He asked his brethren there that night, who were working, and, in many cases, working hard for the church, that they would give their interest and sympathy for the Sunday school, as an institution belonging not merely to the office bearers, but to the congregation. He afterwards adverted to the system of canva.,sing which had been established in connection with the Lacey-street school, with the object of bringing the hundreds of children in , W;does who at present attended no saoli institution under reiigious influence ; and Observed that the conduct and de- portment of .the teachers in the school, as regarded tneir classes, was a most important factor iu the training of the children. Discipline was important ; training was impor- tant, but disposition and behaviour were the most important of all. If the teacher came in late he undid, by such con- duct, all the good he was likely to-do that day. He wished to see scholars and teschers mutually courteous. As to the subject matter of the teaching, he remarked that we lived in an age of great intellectual activity; books were as plentiful as snowflakes in winter, and were so cheap that every cot- tager could buy them—there were simple books for children, racy stories for men and women, books of travel for all, and scientific books for the learned—and in such circumstances there was no excuse for the teacher going to the class un- prepared. He strongly denounced the practice of teachers reading story books to their classes, and asked if it were meant . that the training in their Sabbath schools should be merely a method of killing time. He abhorred the idea of "killing time," for time was pregnant with the issues of eternity. When exhausted with labour they did not want Ito kill time, but to have recreation, change of thought, and change of occupatima. The importance of work in the Sab- bath school was increasing. This was an educational age— there were orphanages for our street a.rabs, Board schools for I the children of the working classes, better schools for the ' middle classes, and universities where the young men be- longing to the families of Dissenters were admitted, and colleges were being built all over the country. There was intellectual friction; mind was coming in contact with mind, and moral influences were becoming more power- ful. In the midst of all this, what was the feeling of Eng- land ? Where were they to find an honest tradesman, a brave soldier, a citizen who would go to the ballot box and record his vote according to his conscience, without fear of the anger of his employer? Where were their ministers s,nd missionaries to come from; and whence were their office- bearers and teachers to come? From the Sunday school. (Loud applause.) He wanted them, as Wesleyan Methodists, in conjunction with the Congregationalists and the Baptists, to do their duty; to look to the future of their country, and see to it that it was one of increased morality and greater spirituality. (Loud applause.) Mr. BENJAMIN BROWN read the treasurer's report, which ; showed that the income had been £54 75., and the expendi- I ture £6l 7s. 11d.
The Rev. J. Tessyman and other friends also addressed the meeting, which passed off very successfully.

but the audience, after the comical efforts of Mr. Antonie, did not appear to be in a sufficiently serious frame of mind to appreciate it. The glee party then sang "Silver moon- light winds are blowing," after which Messrs. T. and A. Holt and T. Burrows rendered a selection on the cornet, saxhorn, and harmonium. Mr. Antonie appeared as Jolly Jack, "a gradely Lancashire chap," in which character he sang "Jolly Jack, the carter," which caused roars of laughter. On being cncored, he sang "Blow ye wild winds, blow." The glee, "Gaily launch and lightly row," was very well rendered by the Glee Party, after which Mr. Alfred Holt performed a solo on the cornet in very good style. Mr. Antonie then appeared as Betty Scrub, a victim to soapsuds and damp attics, and gave an account of her complaints in a song entitled "Rheumatics." His imita- tion of an old woman subject to that complaint was capital, and the contortions of his face might have led anyone to believe that he was suffering the most fearful agonies. He received a well-deserved encore, and in answer to it sang a nigger song, entitled "Skedaddle," which was also loudly applauded. The Glee Party next gave with good taste "The singers' good night." The usual votes of thanks were then passed, and the singing of the National Anthem brought the meeting to a close. Mr. Antonio laboured under the disadvantage of having to appear in evening dress.
ST. PAUL'S AND ST. BARNABAS' CHURCHES, WARRINGTON.

The annual gathering of the congregations of these churches was held in the Public Hall on Tuesday evening, and, as in former years, was attended with much success. Round the front of the gallery bannerettes bearing scrip- tural mottoes had been suspended, and the Sunday school flag occupied a position in the centre of the platform, which was decorated with a number of greenhouse plants. There were upwards of 700 persons present at the tea, which com- menced the evening's proceedings, and it was necessary to have a second sitting. Trays had been given by about a hundred ladies of the congregations. After the tea tablgs had been cleared away, a musical entertainment was held, presided over by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., who was sup- ported on the platform by the Vicar, the Rev. W. Wilkinson, the Revs. E. St. A. Duke and H. G. Smith, curates, E. C. E. Carleton, Alderman Harrison, Councillors Sutton and Pier- point, Messrs. T. Jalley, D. W. Finney, Rice, Sec. The united choirs of St. Paul's and St. Barnabas' during the evening sang a number of glees with spirit and precision. Miss Wycherley, a member of the choirs, made her debut, and she was heartily applauded for her rendering of "Happy be thy dreams." She poSsesses an excellent voice, which showed, however, a lack of training. In his comical songs Mr. Joseph Cantor, was very successful, each of his efforts earning him a hearty encore. The audience showed a flat- tering appreciation of Mr. Eaton Batty's rendering of "The Yachtsman," "The Raft," and "True till death ;" and Mr. Reddish was deservedly applauded for his singing of "Mig- nonette." Mr. Pattison presided at the piano and organ. Sir GILBERT GREENALL, who was cordially received, said ! lie had great pleasure in coming there, mainly because he was in immediate association with his old and beloved friend, Mr. Wilkinson. (Hear, hear, and applause). It required very little pressure to induce him to accept Mr. Wilkinson's invitation, and he should always be ready and willing, as long as God gave him vigorous and healthy life, to give the hand of friendship to Mr. Wilkinson. (Applause). It was impossible not to feel upon these occasions how very quickly time passed. It was, as it were, but yesterday since they met together upon a similar occasion, and yet really twelve months had passed. He knew the anxieties of the past year to Mr. Wilkinson he knew the heavy %sink he had to do, and how he had imposed upon himself the works which he had accomplished. (Hear, hear). He thanked Mr. Wilkinson for what he had done in the past year, which would encourage him and entitle him to wish that other people might have the same God speed. t•Hear, hear). The Vrcat. (the Rev. S. Wilkinson), after a few prelimi- nary remarks, said he stood there that night with especial pleasure, and with grateful feelings towards the parishioners and friends of St. Paul's, because they had been enabled to accomplish by God's help the work which they had determined to do nine years ago. When he took charge of the parish it was with the determination, with Divine help, to supply Bank Quay district with a place of worship, and they had been enabled to do it. They had there a beau- tiful church, a 'good congregation, excellent Sunday schools, and a capital choir. In speaking of St. Barnabas. he was happy iledeed to express his thanks to his friend and fellow- worker, Mr. Duke, for all his labours in that part of the parish. (Applause). During the past year there had been an addition to the clergy of St. Paul's of a gentleman whose talents, eloquence, and goodness had endeared hilts to them all. (Hear, hear) He referred to Mr. Smith. They had ' also been able to accomplish the restoration of the mother church of St. Paul,—(hear, hear)—and he must confess that it had been a great and anxious work, and, thank God, a most sUccessful work. (Hear, hear). When they compared the present beautiful structure with the old church, the vast difference in their appearance was striking. But while speaking of improved St. Paul's he must not forget that they loved the old church even in its dirty state. They had the old building there just the same, except that. it was tieautified and made more meet for the service of Almighty God. He was sere the work reflected the greatest credit upon the architects, who had carried out the work to perfection and I made them a church of which they need not h ashamed. Mr. Wilkinson referred to the ingenuity and skill displayed ' by those pc-sons engaged in the restoration, and the expedi- tion with which the work had been carried out. All the seats in the church were now alike, and a comfortable seat was obtainable in every part. The church was now suitable for the worship of the Almighty God, but he should ;lice theni to remember that having completed the material fabric, they must begin with increased energy to build up a spiritual building., for, though they. might have a beautiful church and service, unless rise,: had a spiritually-minded, God-fearing people connected with it, all was in vain. He trusted their principal object had been to beautify God's house, because they loved the God who was worshipped there and wished men to learn to love and worship Him also. (Hear, hear.) He was pleased to say that the same kindly feeling existed amonst ministers and people now as existed twelve months ago, and had it not been for the loving and kind help of the parishioneers and the inhabitants of Warrington, the work of restoration could never have been accomplished. Much was heard at the present day about the education of young people. Too much importance could not be attached to that work, and to carry it on they had two great instruments in operation,-the Sun- day schools and day schools. He had to thank the teachers and superietendents of the Sunday schools of both churches for their work. They had during the past year lost the services of Mr. Hough, who for 111 my years was a most faith- ful and dilligent superintendent in the girls' school, and whom he thanked for his kindness and attention. His place had been kindly filled up by Mr. Lawless. (Applause.) They bad exceedingly large day schools at Heath-side, of which Her Majesty's inspector said:—" The boys' school is in a very efficient state of discipline. Neatness of execution and accuracy characterises the exercises of a majority of the scholars. The special subjects are creditable as a rule. The geography of the fifth and sixth standards are remarkably advanced and intelligent. Ido not remember seeing better Penmanship than that of these classes. The girls' school is in excellent order and has made very satisfactory progress in sound instruction during the year. The special subjects are well known : needlework in particular being very good. Much thoughtful care and energy have been bestowed on the school by the mistress. The infants were well ordered and taught." At present there were 1,407 scholars on the books, which was a very large namber. He thanked all who had in any way laboured in the parish during the year. He could not help feeling that they must to a certain extent rest a while after their labours of the past five years —(hear, hear)—but he hoped that as time went on they would have other works to do in the parish. He should like to have some Sunday schools built at Bank Quay, which might in time also be used as day schools; and in connec- tion with the large population over Bewsey Bridge, a room where mission services could be held. The enormous popu • lotion of 4,000 had sprung up in Bewsey Bridge district since he went to St. Paul's, and it was the dream of himself and his wife, to obtain the services of a mission woman, who had done so much good in many places, to work amongst the parishioners. He asked them to remember that if they were to get on in the parish, everyone must pray God to bless their work, and everyone must put their shoulder to the wheel. (Applause.) The Rev. E. St. A. Dur.E said he liked the Warrington people when he entered the town, and did so still after five years experience of them. He had received great kindness at the hands of Mr. and Mrs. Wilkinson, and from many he saw present that night, which had made his sojourn amongst them pleasant indeed. It was two years since St. Barnabas' Church was consecrated, and from that time to June last was one of incessant hard work for the clergy of the parish, and he rejoiced in the help given by Mr. Smith. He spoke in terms of praise of the choir at St. Barnabas's and said that, under the leadership of Mr. Evans, they were second to none in the town. He couldtot approve of Mr. Wilkinson's sentiments that they should rest from their labours. While they endeavoured to change the religious condition of the people, he considered they should continue forming material fabrics Holding the Sunday school in St. Barnabas's was most in- convenient and troublesome, and no one would rejoice more than he should when he saw Sir Gilbert Greenall laying the foundation stone of a school near the church. (Laughter and applause.) The Rev. H. G. Slum then delivered an appropriate address, referring in terms of praise to the noble ministra- tions of his Sunday school class. Mr. T. JOLLY proposed a vote of thanks to Sir Gilbert Greenall for presiding, which was carried with acclamation. Councillor SUTTON, churchwarden, moved a vote to thanks to the ladies who had presided at, and supplied the tables; and also to those ladies and gentlemen who had so generously contributed towards the success of the musical entertainment. (Applause.) Mr. }teem seconded the motion, which was carried. On the motion of Mr. D. W. FINNEY, the thanks of the meet- ing were accorded to Mr. T. Jolly for occupying the post of Sir Gilbert, who was obliged to leave before the conclusion of the entertainment.
Mr. JOLLY in replying remarked that the services of Mr. Pattison, Mr. Heald and Mr. Evans were deserving of their best thanks.
The entertainment concluded with the singing of " God save the Queen."
THE RAILWAY BRIDGE STEPS AT RUNCORN.
CLAIM AGAINST THE COMPANY FOR DAMAGES.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Thursday afternoon, before Mr. Justice Chitty, John Widders brought an action against the London and North-Western Railway Company to re- cover £5OO for injuries sustained by him owing to a fall on the defendants' steps, which he alleged were in a defective condition, at Runcorn Bridge, in July last. Mr. Russell, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Mattinson; (instructed by Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., of Warrington), appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Potter, Q.C. and Mr. Moon (instructed by Mr. Roberts, solicitor to the London and North-Western Rail- way Company) for the defendants. Mr. 111attinson, in opening the case, said the plaintiff was Mr. John Widders, and he sought to recover damages for personal injuries to himself by the negligence of defendants' servants; but the defendants denied their negli- gence. I Mr. Russell said the plaihtiff lived at 17, Eastside, I Queen's Dock, Liverpool, and held the position of fore- man quay porter to the Bridgewater Trustees, in whose employ he had been for 25 years. He was 60 years .of age, and on the day in question he was paying a visit to some relatives at Runcorn. He had Co cross Runcorn I Bridge, for which a charge of id. or 2d. was made, and as he was descending the flight of steps on the Runcorn side, owing, as they alleged, to the imperfect lighting and imperfect condition of the steps, he fell and was severely injured. The accident occurred on the 19th July, be- tween eight atld nine o'clock, and it was then not posi- tively dark. There was no light on the steps, and the only light was inside the ticket office. Evidence would be given to show that the steps had been much worn away, and that no doubt added to the accident, they being actually scooped out in the middle. Where the steps used to be six inches high some had been reduced to 31 inches. Ihe plaintiff had not been able to resume his employment since the accident, and now claimed compensa- tion.

His Lordship : Is contributory negligence set up ? Mr. Potter : Yes, my lord. Mr. Russell : I know not what the contributory negli- gence can be, because the plaintiff took every possible care of himself. It was not owing to his negligence that he fell.

Mr. John Pierpoint, architect and surveyor, Warrington, stated that from the top of the fourth flight downwards all the steps were more or less worn, down to the bottom one, and dangerously so. Plaintiff, in the course of his evidence, said there was no light on the stens, except from the ticket office. He fell from the top to the bottom step, and his leg was severely injured. He was carried to the house of his nephew, and he was confined to his bed for three weeks.
The hearing of the case, which was not concluded At the rising of the court on Thursday, was resumed yesterday, and the jury found for the plaintiff, damages £l5O.

div.head: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
The thirty-ninth half-yeatly meeting of the members, was held on Tuesday evening, at the Co-operative Hall. Mr. Win. Rhodes presided.

On the motion of Mr. Holt, seconded by Mr. Bradley, the report of the Committee of Management, for the six months, ending December 31st, was adopted. It showed that the total sales amounted to £28,414 14s. 6H., being in increase of £1,373 ss. id., over the corresponding period of last year. The profits realised, after paying interest and trade expenses, were £3,752 2s. BN., and the balance in hand, £1,014 Os. 101-d.

A discussion took place as to a proposal to give compensa- tion to the parents of a child which had been run over by one of the society's carts. Several propositions were made, which gave rise to an animated debate. One member moved that a sum of £3O should be given to the father (Mr. Tittle) in settlement of the claim but he refused to accept it. The parent was then asked if he would consent to his child being examined by a doctor, in order that it might be accurately ascertained what injuries it bad sustained. Mr. Tittle saide he would not; and during the debate described 'one of the members as a clown, and told him not.to let his face become so red. It was resolved that as Mr. Tittle would not come to terms, he should be left to his remedy—the county court. On Wednesday evening, a public tea meeting in connection with the society was held in the Public Hall. A substantial tea was provided, to which about 700 persons sat down. The tables were presided over by ladies belonging to the society. After tea an entertainment was held in the same buildin,c, and the hall was very well filled. Mr. W. Rhodes occupied the chair, and stated that Mr. J. H. Greenwood, who had been expected to take part in the entertainment, was unable to attend owing to ill health. A substitute had been provided, however, in Mr. Harry Antonie. The first piece on the programme was a glee entitled "Queen of the night," which was well rendered by the Ellesmere glee party, after which Mr. Harry Antonio gave an amusing song entitled The tailors' feast," and on receiving an encore substituted "Ireland's emerald hills." Mr. Alfred Holt next gave a cornet solo, and was loudly applauded. A song entitled "The dying child" was sung by Miss Whitlow,

div.head: STRANGE SUICIDE AT ACTON GRANGE.
div.p: STRANGE SUICIDE AT ACTON GRANGE.

At the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-street, on Thursday, the county coroner (Mr. C. E. Driffield) held an inquest on the body of an old man named John Savage, 78 years of age, who died in the Infirmary on Monday.—Sarah, wife Of Charles Massey, platelayer, Acton Grange, said the deceased was her father, and had lived with her for 14 months. He had done no work for about 12 years, as he had injured his hip, and was very subject to rheumatism, He could not walk without the aid of two sticks. On Friday morning be got up at about 8-30, and with the exception of complain- ing that be bad had a very bad night, he appeared in his usual state. In the course of the morning he made a great " slop " in the yard whilst washing some " peelings," and she sent her daughter to tell him not to make such a mess.l He then went to her in 'a bit of a temper, and said, "Sarah, I think I've been here long enough." Witness replied that he bad not, but should not make such messes. Without any further remark her father walked from the house. He was a man of a very hasty temper, and got himself in a passion for a very little thihg. At half-past 12 he had not returned, and she went to the door to look for him. She saw him coming up the lane, apparently to his dinner, which she placed on the table. Some minutes passed, but he did not make his appearance, and she again went to the door, when she saw him scramble on the railway embankment, and place his head on the line. She knew a train was due, and she shouted to some platelayers to take him away, hut before they could get to him the train passed. Her father was picked up, and taken in the van to the 'Warrington Infirmary.—The Coroner said her father ought to have been privileged to make a slop at his great age, and see ought not to have sent the girl to scold him—Witness: I didn't scold him.—:The Coroner: He would consider it as such. You cannot undo it now, but it has evidently caused the old man's death, and you will have it to think over all the days of your life.—John Mottershead, of Chester, said he was the driver of the 12-0 noon passenger train from Chester to Manchester. When near the Walton junction distant signal, two platelayers signalled to him to stop; and be whistled and applied the breaks. He saw a man throw him- self on the line and place his head on the rail, but be was unable to stop the train, and the life guard of the engine struck the man's bead.—Evidence was also given by John Millington, platelayer, Moore, who stated Mrs. Massey told him there was a can on the line. He looked round and saw the deceased crawling on his hands and knees on the rail- way embankment. When he reached the metal he laid himself down, and put. his head on the line. The train was approachiree from Chester, and he signalled the driver to stop, but the head of the deceased was struck by the engine , guard before the train was pulled up. There was a wound on the back of the deceased's head which penetrated to the bone, aud rendered him insensible. Witness placed deceased in the van, and accompanied him to the Infirmary.—The Coroner : Have you heard that deceased was not treated well by his daughter ?—Witness said he had heard people say that deceased did not appear comfortable, but he had no reason to think that he was as comfortable as he would be with anyone else. He had never heard that deceased was neglected.—The coroner having summed up, the jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased committed suicide whilst in a state of temporary and mental insanity, more or less the reeult of old age.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

LIVERPOOL CORN. TiniushAv.—There has been very little passing in wheat t,day, but in view of the small stocks of soft American new on spot, holders of these qualities are very firm. East Indian, however, is dull and easier to buy. Maize quiet and in buyers' favour. Flour remains unchanged. Beans and peas steady at the quotations. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, TIII:RSDAY.—Beef firm, but quiet, at the quotations. Pork steady, at late peces. Bacon dull. and easier to buy. Hams without change. Shoulders slow. Lard quiet, al.:el weak in value. Cheese meets a moderate demand. Butter fiat, at late figures. Tallow unaltered. LAMENTABLE ACCIDENT TO A BOY AT HITYTON QuAßEL—About Hine o'clock, on Tuesday night a boy named William O'Neill, about 14 years of age, whilst en- gaged at the shears for cutting iron, at the Huyton Quarry Iron Works, accidentally got his fingers on the right hand cut off. He was conveyed to the Liverpool Royal In- tirrsary.
NOTES FROM "THE LOBBY."
LONDON, FRIDAY NIGIrr.

lam able to state that before many weeks, the gentle- men of the long robe in Westminster Hall are likely to be engaged in a trial, which, I venture to say, will be the sensation of the season, Parliamentary and social. It will be a suit for breach of promise of marriage, brought against the prominent member of the Irish active party in the House of Commons, who of all other men that assembly and the outer world would most relish to see in the witness box on such an occasion. This is what comes of escaping Mr. Forster in Ireland, and falling into the toils of Cupid in Paris.

From St. James's Gate to the Guildhall, London is vocal with comment on the Prime Minister's speech last night in reference to local legislation in Ireland. The opposition journals have sprung upon it with:alac rity, and one and all call attention to the momentous significance of what he said. The Daily :Tors seems to reflect the feelings of the less advanced portion of the Liberal party, and is evidently perplexed. The Pall Mall Gazette on the other hand boldly applauds Mr. Gladstone for the wisdom and far sightedness displayed•in this speech. It is in the clubs and lobby, however) that the discussion is hottest. The Premier, in brief, stated that whenever the Irish members could lay before the House a proposal for a local parliament in Ireland which would exclude all idea of weakening the control of the Imperial Parliament over imperial affairs, and cosfine an Irish legislature to strictly Irish business such a proposal ought to receive and would receive full and ample consideration in that House. Although no doubt some of the Home Rulers, who lean towards the American or Separatist party in Ireland, would not Car- dially welcome this, yet the spirit in which it would be received in Ireland by the great bulk of the popular party was evidenced by the warm manner in which Mr. Sexton, one of Mr. Parnell's most prominent lieutenants, thanked the Prime Minister for the words he had spoken, and confessed that it was incumbent on Irish members to satisfy. the House of Commons that no ideas of separation lurked beneath the Irish demand for self-government. It is not apparently the intention of Government to confer any exceptional renards upon Sir Evelyn Wood on account of his services in South Africa. He has been made a Major-General, and he has been also granted the boner of G.C.M.G. The first is substantial, the second honorary, and both together are thought to constitute a sufficient reward for the recent services which Sir Evelyn Wood has rendered to his country. There was a

rumour current in military and political clubs some time since that Government intended to confer a peerage upon this young and fortunate officer. The rumour, however, appears to have been without foundation, and I am not sur- prised that it is so.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.
MESSAGE FROM THE QUEEN.—EarI RESMARE brought up the ,Queen's answer, thanking the House for its Ad- dress.

THE IMPRISONED SOLICITORS.—Lord STANLEY asked why the Government did not accede to the memorial pre- sented on behalf of the imprisoned solicitors, Messrs. May and Mair.—Earl of ROSEBERY said that no memorial bad been presented which would induce the Home Secretary to interfere.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

NEW MEMBER.—Lord Algernon Percy tool: his seat fo Westminster. MR. LABOUCTIERE AND THE HOUSE OF LORDS.—Mr. LABOUCRERE gave notice that that day month he should move a resolution relating to the House of Lords. __
THE NEW RULES OF DEBATE.—Sir STAFFORD NORTH- 00TH repeated his notice to move a negative to Mr. Glad- stone's first resolution on the business of the House on Monday. _ _
THE ALLEGED MISSION TO ROME.—Sir CHARLES DILSE stated that Mr. Errington had no official appointment in Rome.

MAJOR BOND IN IRELAND.—Mr. FORSTER replying to Jesse Collings, said it was quite true that Major Bond, lately chief constable at Birmingham, had been temporarily ap- pointed stipenaiary magistrate in Ireland. The testimonials he had from Birmingham were of the highest character. THE TRA.NSVAAL WAR.—Mr. CHILDERS stated that dis- tinctions had been conferred upon the commanding officers for gallant conduct in the Transvaal. The conduct of the non-commissioned officers and men, was now under the con- sideration of the Commander-in-chief. • THE PRIIPOSED CHANNEL TUNNEL—Mr. C HOLDERS stated it was quite true that several military authorities had been examined before the committee now sitting with regard to the Channel tunnel. Sir G. Wolseley had given an opinion adverse to it, and Sir J. Adie an opinion of the oppo- site character. The whole subject was under the considera- tion of the Government. The late Government, he believed, approved of the scheme. A COMPLAINT.—Mr. CALLAN complained of the conduct pursued by the Government whips in getting the House counted out last night.—Lord GROSVENOR denied that he had anything to do with the circumstance.
AFFAIRS IN BASUTOLAND.-Mr. COURTNEY, replyina. o. Sir M. Hicks-Beach, said the telegram published in to-day's papers from the Cape, relative to affairs in Basutoland, was not true.

THE DEBATE ON TITF. ADDRESS.—The adjourned debate on Mr. M'Cartby's amendment to the Address was resumed by Mr. REDMOND, who said the Government message of peace to Ireland had proved nothing but ruin and desolation. He justified the issuing of the" No rent "manifesto, and denied that there was anything like a general payment of rent in Ireland. He censured the manner in which .the Coercion Acts had been enforced, and the treatment extended to the Ladies' Land League.—Mr. GIBSON pointed out the difficulty f the situation the Government had had to meet in Ireland, and the lavish manner in which they had been trusted by Parliament with all the power they asked for. Ha then enquired whether the action of the Government had been defencible, and said he felt certain .the greatmajority of the House and country would be satisfied from the abundant extracts read and the painful record of outrages described by the Irish Chief Secretary, making allowance for misrepresentation and exaggeration, that they had proved ten times Over the necessity for the vigorous action which had been taken by the Government. The point, however, that he strongly insisted on was that the strongest measures were not adopted early enough, and that had the Government acted with energy sooner than they did, the present state of affairs would never have existed. He thought the Land League ought to have been suppressed earlier than it was and he wanted to know why the golden opportunities presented to the Government for energetic action had not been taken .advantage of, and why the sup- pression of that illegal body was reserved until the very day the land courts opened? He thought the Land Act was not fulfilling its object, and the appointments made under it were greatly in favour of tenant interest and against those of the landlord. He, however, took a hopeful view of the future in Ireland, and said he should vote against the amendment.—Major O'BEIRNE complained ofthe manner in which the Land Act was being administered, as unjust, both to landlord and tenant—Mr. DALY admitted that there had been outrages in Ireland, but said they had been much exaggerated. He thought the present policy of the Govern - meat ought to make Libeaals blush for shame. [LEFT SITTING.]
At Leeds Assi;2s, yesterday, John Ross was sentenced to death for the murder of John Manley in a drunken quarrel, on Christmas Day.
As a result of the War Office inquiry into the administra- tion of the Royal Hibernian.l4ilitary School, at Dublin, the Commandant, L. S. Cotton, has sent in his resignation.
Yesterday afternoon a house in course of erection ia Oxford-street, London, fell to the ground killing one man and injuring several others.
The following telegram was received yesterday from Mr. Stillman, the correspondent of The Times, w'ao was reported to have bun murdered :—" Canard. All right Mr. Stillman is at Athens."

At the Birmingham Police Court, on Thursday, James Gethin,g, engineer, was charged with fraudulently conspiring with Mary Jane Fearneans (who had passed in male attire as Lord Pelham Clinton),and obtaining £2OOO from Edward Beynon, of Selly Oak, and £3,000 from a Mr. Screen, of Brades Vilage, near Oldbury. The prisoners were remandei for a week.
AUSTRIA.—UNITF.RSITY AT PRAGUE. VIENNA, Friday.—The Upper House has today accepted. by 82 against 55, the Government proposal for the estab- lishment of a Czech lan University at Prague.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIGAN.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIGAN.

A fatal accident took place shortly before noon, yest2rday, at the Meadows Colliery, Wigan, belonging to Messrs. Lamb and Moore. Two men, a metal contractor and his assistant, were ramming a shot, when from some cause unknown the powder exploded. Dempsey, the metal man, was killed in- stantaneously, and the other was seriously burned. Dempsey was a married man, and has been employed at this pit nearly three years.

BURGLARY AT HALE. —On Friday week, at the Liverpool Assizes, Robert Hel4by, 35, joiner, for having at Hale, on the 31st of December, burglarously broken into th, dwelling-house of William Turton, and stolen a number silver spoons and other property, was sentenced to tv of months' imprisonment. - - - - - - THE RECENT CONSERVATIVE SOIREE. Sir,—l had not the—pleasure, I was about to say, of attending the Conservative soiree; nor the questionable i felicity of hearing dear Sir Gilbert expound, n his usual lucid, profound, and statesmanlike manner the burning questions of the day. But, sir, I consoled myself for this loss by readicg. your report of the striking oratory of the i wcrthy Baronet. What a breadth and a depth there s about the thoughts! So much so that even the orator himself seems sometimeo overhead, and his meaning and relevancy lost to our meaner capacities. •Mr. John White may dis- claim the merit of "making funny speeches "—though even he. if not funny himself, may be the cause of fun to others —but Sir Gilbert cannot deny that his speeches are fnnny," at least in one sense of the word. For it is funny how any man calling himself a politician could stand upon a pluoil9 platfcrra and unblushingly utter such a string of sesule inanities as did the man whom Captain Reynolds hopes "at no distant period to see fulfilling his duties as heeetofore." Does he? As an elector I shall do what lies in M:7 power to prevent such a calamity. What the Con. servative Association can be thinking of in pushing poor Sir Gilbert into a position for which he is so evidently unfitted as that he occupied on Thursday evening, I am at a loss to Conover. Surely they do not think that the exhibition of Thursday evening last will win over any votes from "the vulgar Radical herd" who have the unheard-of temerity of calling the food-taxing Lowther "Jim ? " A member of Parliament need not be a man of very brilliant talents, but he should be a man of sense, and one who can refrain from talking the feeble twaddle jerked out by the chairman of that meeting. We are told on every hand that these are very momentous political times, pregnant with great issues. And this is the kind of man the Conservative Association propose to send to deliver them! One beside whose diluted platitudes even the blatant balderdash of "the rising crop" becomes respectable; and one so pre-eminently fitted to shine in the congenial atmosphere of a tea fight that it seems a pity he should ever be called away from this sphere of usefulness to navigate waters wherein he is so soon out of his depth as when tampering with Imperial politics. What . dcee this old man eloquent mean by that delightfully mean- anything, if not meaningless, phrase, "We will fight for a good cause—a cause that is true, loyal, and constitutional"? Can he refer to the land law reform, or the extension of the ' County franchise, which is to make the men of the county p&itically equil to the men of the town? Both of these objects would be true, loyal, and constitutional, but they are not dear to the Tory heart. We never hear this man of vague sentences mention such things. The political world might be in a state of perfection, and unstained by political .in justice, to judge by his silence on that theme. Perpetual pensions, alias perennial robberies—the inequality of the franchise, and land law reform are topics upon which Sir Gilbert was conveniently silent, but upon which, if we were foolish enough to place him in the position he is weak enough crave, he would give a silent vote for the retention cf these to abases. The display of that evening enables one to guage the estimation of the Conservative leaders for the Conserva- tive workingman. They evidently think that any kind of Dabble will do for him,. Were I a Conservative workingman, and not one of "the vulgar Radical herd," I should feel astamed and indignant that my leaders should thus commit so gross a breach of good taste and good sense as to drag the old gentlernaa from his chimney corner to make an exhibi- tion of himself on a political platform. If this be the kind of education the party is to receive, it is not likely to lose it title of " stupid " just yet. Ido not wonder at Sir Gil- bert regretting that his wife was not there. She might have plucked at his coat tails when nobody else would.—l am, &se JOHN PEERS. Warrington, February Gth, 1882.

div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.

MClMAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickrnere), Coun- cillors Crosfieldand Fairclough, and Major Cartwright. PITCH AND Toss.—John Shields, a young man, was charged under a warrant with playing pitch and toss in Cicth Hall-yard, on the oth No-rember last, and he was fined 2s. 6i. and costs, or in ,default, seven days' imprison- ment.

Cerrene- or DESERTERS.—JO9eph Derby and Geo. Bal- linger were charged with being deserters from the 7th brigade -Of Her Majesty's Seth Regiment, stationed at Curragh Camp, Ireland.—Whilst visiting the common lodging-houses -le the town, P.C. Bowe-n discovered the prisoners' who were wearing military boots, and when questioned by him ad- mitted being desertere.—They were remanded to Walton gad to await an escort, and the Bench allowed the officers the usual reward. ASSAULT ON .THE POLlCE.—Edwardler was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Long-ford-street on Saturday night, and also with assaulting P.C. Evans whilst in the execution of his duty.—When requeeted by the officer to go home quietly, the prisoner, who was very drunk. struck him a violent blow on the chest.—A fine of 53. anti cost was imposed. A DARING Yor7.—Thomas Rush and Martin Kelly, yeeths, were charged with having been on the premises of Elijah Skelton, Bank-street, with intent to commit a felony. —From the statement of the Chief Constable it appeared that adjoining the premises are two cottages occupied by two families, who keep cows. These persons arose shortly after two o'clock on Sunday morning for the ipurpose of reilking the cows, and then sat dozing in the house. Whilst the people were in this condition a girl ten years of age "saw a face creeping downstairs," and then crawl towards the fire place, where was a watch. She recognised Rush, and awakened the people of the house, who distinctly heard the sound of two persons running upstairs. The would-be robbers, however, made their escape by the hay loft. Sergt. Berry at about 3-30 went to the house of Rush's parents, and found him in bed, where he said he had been since 11-30. His coat, however, was covered with hay seed, and his shoes were found at the bottom of the loft. When charged with the offence he said that Kelly was with him, and the latter was then apprehended.—Mr. Runt said he had no evidsnce against Kelly.—Rush said he was "suffering from drink" at the time.—Mr. Hunt remarked that a drunken person could not remove a window sash and climb a hay loft like the prisoner had done.—The Mayor said it was a serious offence, and amounted almost to burglary. There was not sufficient evidence against Kelly, and he would be discharged. Rush would be committed to gaol for three months with hard labour. DAMAGING ST. ANN'S CHURCH.—A youth named Patrick Ryan was charged with unlawfully throwing stones in Winwick-road on the 26th Jan.—P.C. Hitchtnough proved that the defendant had sent a stone at a pigeon which was etm the tower of St. Ann's Church. There had he said, been meny complaints of thedamage done to the church by stone throwing.—The Mayor said he had heard that the windows of the church were completely riddled.—Mr. Hunt: There are 50 panes a week broken.—Major Cartwedght: 403. and cests a time or two would do a great deal towards stopping this.—Mr. Hunt said it was lads like the defendant who did the damage.—Defendant was fined 103. and 63. costs, or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment.—The Mayor remarked ;hat if there were any more cases of a similar character the offenders would be severely dealt with. ETREET OBSTRUCTION.—Thomas Hughes was charged with having, on the 31st January, obstructed the free pas. sage of Wellington-street, by allowing his cart to stand there from 11 p.m. to 6 o'clock a.m. He was ordered to pay the costs (3s 6d). as was also William Plinston for a similar offence committed at the same time and place. ALLEGED BREACH OF THE LICENSING ACT.—James Gleave, landlord of the Barle,ymow public-house, Market- place, was charged with keeping his premises open during prohibited hours. It appeared that at 12-20 midnight, on the 2nd instant, P.C. Hollingworth saw three men enter the defendant's house: The officer acquainteti P.S. Spinks with the occurrence, and they entered the house. The three men were sat at a table with two glasses of spirits and one of Leer before them; and on another table was a glass of Leer which appeared to belong to the landlord. The defen- d-lit stated the men were his private guests, and that no money had been received for the liquor ; a statement which was confirmed by his wife. The defendant had kept the hr use for five years, in which period there had been no com- P'aint against him and his father had kept it 15 or 16 years e e previously; anti 'Mr. Hunt from enquiries he had made Lad no doubt the defendant's statement iivas true. Under these circumstances he would offer no evel..mce..—The case was dismissed. VIOLENT WIGANERS.—MichaeI Nolan, Thomas Hough, and John McDermott, all of Wigan, were charged with being drunk and disorderly at Bank Quay station at half- past one that morning. At that time the prisoners, who were in a very drunken state, went to the station and stated they wanted to go to Wigan. They kicked Mr. Smith's Leokstall, and threatened the railway detective. Hough, it was stated, was much quieter than his companions.—Nolan aed McDermott were fined ss. and costs, and Hough ss. SCTIOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—Mr. Riley, the school attendance officer, summoned a number of parents for CF. Tiecting to send their children regularly to school, and they were dealt with as follows :—Robert Cade, joiner, Lord Nelson-street, 2s. 61; Jno. Nixon, Edward-street, 55.; Smith, wiredrawer, Aiken-street, Sc.; Michael Smith, labourer, 'Turner-street, ss. ' • John Frangleton, labourer, Eldon-street, 5e.; John Maloney, baker, Bowes-street, two children committed to the Industial School ; M. A. Bailey, dressmaker, Manley-street, dismissed on promising to send the children regularly to school. TUESDAY.—Before Major Cartwright and Councillor Monks. ROBBERY AND ASSAULT : EXEMPLARY SENTENCE.— John Kilcourse, labourer, 9, Garden Row' was charged with having, on Monday, stolen a quantity of bacon, about 811 be. in weight, value Sc. 6d., the property of John Williams, pro- vision dealer, Bridge-street. About 25 minutes past six c'clock on Monday night, John Hatton, a butcher, in the employ of Mr. W. Gill, Bridge-street, noticed the prisoner loitering about on the opposite side os the street. Prisoner seddenly disappeared, and Hatton was about to cross the street to speak to Mr. Shaw when the prisoner came out of the entry between the prosecutor's and Mr. Shaw's shops, ran across the street, and took off up the Swan entry. Eigniry was made as to whether anything was missing from the entry, and the prosecutor found that two sides of bacon hid had pieces cut out of them. Mr. Wrliams followed the prisoner up the Swan entry but he got lost. Hatton went r)und Market Gate, and met the prisoner near Mr. Percival's s'mp with the bacon produced in his possession. Prisoner resisted Hatton, seized him by the throat, and dragged him tp the entry. Another butcher, in the employ of Mr. Pres- ton, seeing the struggle, seized the prisoner who then, according to the Chief Constable, found them "full work." A policeman arrived, he was followed by two others, and then the Chief Constable came up and identified Kilcourse. Prisoner said "I will go with you Mr. Hunt, if they will take these things off." The police took the handcuffs off the

prisoner, who reluctantly walkerl to the police sthtion where he committed an assault upon P.C. Chantler ; with which offence he was further charged.—The Chief Constable said that within the last month there had been three or four robberies from this particular entry. Prisoner, who had a long; , " character " sheet, was sentenced to three months' imprison- ment for the robbery, and four months for the assault, in all , seven months' imprisonment, which the Bench said would perhaps be a lesson to the prisoner and other desperate ; characters.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Councillor Fairclough (chairman), Alderman Chandley, and Councillor Monks. YOUTHFUL PIGEON STEALERS.—Frederick Massey (12) and William Ward (15) were charged on remand with steal- ing two pigeons, the property of Thomas Peacock, forge- man, 20, Bostock-street.—On Monday evening, when defen- dant arrived home from work, he found the staples of his pigeon cote drawn, and his two pigeon stolen. He went round to the different pigeon dealers in the town, and called upon Mrs. Shaw, of Haydock-street. There he saw the prisoners about to receive is. 4d. for the pigeons, but on seeing him they ran away. They were subsequently appre- hended by P.C. Hennessy.—The mother of Massey said he was unmanageable, and he was committed to gaol for a month, and afterwards to a reformatory for five years. Ward was fined 10s. and costs, or in default, 14 days. THEFT or CLOTHING BY BOYS.—Three ragged looking urchins named Samuel Bate, Thomas 'l`.Toc'fs-ton, and Septimus Naylor, were charged with stealing a quantity of under- clothing, the property of Michael Grey.—Mrs. Grey, on the previous day, placed a quantity of wet clothing on the ground in the yard of the house, 13, Edward-street. At seven o'clock she missed the articles, and about that time the prisoners went to the marine stores of Peter Taylor, and endeavoured to dispose of a quantity of wet clothing. In- formation was given to the police, and the prisoners were apprehended. Mrs. Grey identified the clothing, some of which had been torn to shreds with the object of selling it as " rags."—Bate stated he and Naylor watched outside the yard whilst Nockton stole the clothing.—Bate was sentenced to receive 12 strokes with the birch rod, and Nockton and Naylor si each. A THIEF CONVICTED BY HEE CHILD.—EIIen Savage, a married woman, was charged with stealing a 21b. loaf, of the value of 3!2(1., from the shop of John Ashton, in Cartwright- street.—At nine o'clock on the previous day the prisoner's young daughter was found behind the counter of the shop with two haddocks in her hand. She was taken into the house and questioned as to why she had §tolen them, when the prosecutor's son, who had been in charge of the shop , during the day, said a 21h. loaf had also been stolen from the counter. "I didn't take it," said the child. "Mother took it." The prisoner was in consequence taken into custody, and she admitted the theft. She said she took the loaf be- cause she could not pay her way.—Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs, or seven days. ABSCONDING FROM A HOME.—Henry Jenkins and Henry Hargreaves were charged on remand with absconding from Allsop'a Boy's Home, but as they had not been claimed they were discharged. THußsDlY.—Before Alderman Webster.
A DRUNKEN CRIPPLE.—AR old woman named Isabella

Kelly' who hobbled along by the aidof crutches, was charged with being drunk in Horsemarket-street on Wednesday night—P.C. Cokely said he found the prisoner in Horse- market-street with a large crowd around her. She was very drunk. She was dischargrd on promising to leave the town. USING TIII2EATS.—Patrick McDonald' a hawker, was bound over in his .own recognizances of £lO, to keep the p2ace for six months, for using malicious threats towards his wife, Mary McDonald. . NEGLECT OF FAMlLY:—Patrick Conway was charged with having, on the 9th January, run away f.tom the borough and left his wife and child chargeable to the common funds of the Union.—The Master (Mr. Mackey), said on the 10th November last, the prisoner was admitted to the Workhouse Hospital; and five days afterwards his wife and child were admitted. He remained in the hospital until the 14th November, and then asked for his discharge which was granted. He was sent to the healthy part of the workhouse, and a few days afterwards obtained. his discharge from the house, promising to take his wife and child the following Saturday. The prisoner was allowed to go, but they had seen nothing of him until that morning.—Prisoner said he was taken ill the week he left the workhouse, and P.C. Neil, who received the prisoner into custody at Prescot, said he had been in the Whiston workhouse for a month.—The case was adjourned for a month. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds, Mr. Ziba Armitage and Mr. John White.

GROSS CRUELTY TO A HORSE. Thomas Stubs was Charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse by allowing it to work, and Wm. Slater for working it, in an unfit state, and unmercifully beating it. Inspector Harper, R.S.P.C.A., stated that on the 3rd inst. he saw Slater in charge of a brown mare, attached to a cart of cinders, in Folly-lane. Slater was beating the animal very severely with a whip, but thinking it was perhaps a " gibbing " horse he (witness) passed on. Shortly afterwards he again saw the horse with the empty cart, and unable to walk more than 15 yards , without stopping, and Slater was beating it. An examine- , ticn showed that the animal was an old one, and a mere skeleton. There was a laceration on the inside of the thigh, a crack in its hoof, and it was badly lame. The horse was in such an exhausted condition that it could not walk home. although that was only half-a-mile distant. During his 13 years' experience of these cases he had never seen a horse in such a condition before; it was totally unfit to walk.—Mr. Wall, veterinary surgeon, gave evidence of the state of the horse, and said he had ordered the defendant to destroy it. He had never during his 20 years' practice seen a horse in such a condition, and he was surprised that anyone could allow such a horse to be worked.—Mr. Stubs stated that he gave £lO for the horse a short time ago, and he did not think it was in such a bad condition.—Stubs was fined £3 and costs, and the driver Slater la.---John Barrow was chorged with having, on the 3rd February, cruelly illtreated a horse by working it in an unfit state.—lnspector Harper proved the case, but as there were some extenuating cir- cumstances, the Bench only ordered defendant to pay the costs. .

ROBHING CLOTHES LlNEs.—Mary McKenna, wife of a f.rgeman, was brought up, on remand from Tuesday, charged with having stolen clothing of the value of 155., from the clothes lines of Wm. Marney, James Williams, and John Hogan.—Prisoner pleaded guilty to all the charges.— Mr. Hunt said eight tobberies of this nature had occurred during the present month. The prisoner had sold the goods much below their value, and be suggested that the persons who had purchased them should be prosecuted for receiving stolen goods.—Mr. John White said in future cases pro- ceedings should be taken against the receivers as well as the thieves.—The prisoner was sentenced to two months' hnpri- sonment on each charge ; in all six months.

The Cardiff steamer Cosmo has foundered in the Black Sea. She had a crew of 27 men, the only information es to whom is contained in the statement that "a portion of wreckage and 10 men have been washed ashore." Amongst the Parliamentary representatives of the farming districts there is stated to be disappointment that the Queen's Speech should have contained no mention of the subject of agricultural reform' especially in regaud to the law of distraint in England and Ireland. A solicitor from Liverpeol is engaged taking evidence on behalf of Mr. Simpson, the defeated candidate, with respect to an alleged attempt on the part of a Preston town councillor to vote twice, contrary to the statue. The affi- davits will be presented to the Mayor, who will then be asked to prosecute. The Board of Trade returns issued on Tuesday show that the imports for month ending January 31st exhibit an in- crease of £5,276,505 as compared with the same month of 1881. The exports for January show an increase of L'2,501,7772 as compared with the corresponding period of last year.

A correspondent who has asked Mr. Gladstone if he would repeat, on behalf of_the Russian Jews, the intervention which was so effectual in rezard to Naples and Bulgaria, has been informed that the Premier "will take no step ex- cept such as may seem to him to be productive of real good ;" and that under all circumstances of real or imputed cruelties he will act on the same principles as those which have guided his conduct in the past.

MR: BRADLAUGH'S FUTURE Acnox. Mr. Bradlaugh, after his return from the house. on Tuesday evening, in- formed the representatives of the Press that it is his inten- tion to present himself at the earliest convenient moment at the bar of the House of Commons to claim to take the oath and his seat for Northampton. Mr. Bradlaugh considers the house has illegally deprived him of his right as the duly elected representative of the borough of Northampton to sit in the house, .and is determined to loose no oppor- tunity of claiming his right to take his seat. Only one consideration will prevent him from again seeking the suffrages of the electors of Northampton, and that is in the event of the seat being again declared vacant. He does not give the precise date upon which he will next claim to be admitted. THE SITEFEILD POISONING CASE—At the Leeds assizes, on Monday, Felicia Dorothea Kate Dover, spinster, aged 27, was charged with the wilful murder of Thomas Skinner, artist, Sheffield, to whom .she was housekeeper, on the eth December last. The prisoner pleaded not guilty. The pro- secution alleged that arsenic was administred by the prisoner to the deceased, and evidence was called showing that the prisoner had purchased arsenic before the clay of his death, saving that it was for the purpose of colouring wax flowers. She had stated that there had been •frequent quarrels be- tween herself and the deceased. The case was continued on Tuesday, and after two hours consultation the jury retnrned a verdict of manslaughter. On Wednesday the prisoner was sentenced to penal servitude for life, the judge remarking , that the circumstances of the offence were so grave arid atrocious that they were separated but by a very thin line from the offence of murder. The sentence appeared to take the prisoner quite by surprise, and she fell fainting in the I dock, and bad to be assisted out.
