THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 11, 1882. LIBERAL MEETING AT LYMM.

SPEECHES OF MR. G. W. LATHAM, MR. J. TOMKPNSON, AND OTHERS. Under the auspices of the Mid-Cheshire Liberal Associa- tion, a public meeting in support of the Government, and in furtherance of legislation important to the farming in- terest, was held in the Congregational schoolroom, Lymm, on Tuesday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. Wm. Long, of Grappenhall, who was supported by Mr. G. W. Latham, the Liberal candidate for Mid-Cheshire; Mr. Jas. Tomkinson, of Tarporley, the Liberal candidate for West Cheshire ; Messrs. Kenworthy, Killick, Broadbent, Wm. Milne, J. C. Falden (Grappenhall), T. Davies, Brewtnall (Thelwall), Hudson (Grappenhall), T. Hodgson (Bowdon), J. Swanwick (Lymm), G. Worthington (Altrinchatn), J. A. Swanwick (Lymm), Todhunter (Lymm), Ford (Heatley), Watson (Lymm), Bickley (Heatley), and the Rev. J. Bedell (Lymna). There was a moderate attendance. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, observed that Mr. Geo. Dewhurst, whose heart and soul were with them, had to avoid the excitement of public meetings at present, or he would have presided that evening. Speaking of the reason for holding the meeting, to give them an opportunity of judging between the Government and their opponents, he said he held that each man should for himself decide his political views and not accept them at second hand. Every man should read the history of his country for the last half century, and he was convinced that the result of such reading, if undertaken without bias, must make a man a thorough-paced Liberal. (Applause.) Looking back for that period they saw that the action taken for the good of the masses of the people, had been the action of the Liberal party—(applause)—and even when, as in the case of the last Reform Bill, had not been directly instrumental in passing the measure, it was done indirectly to them. (Renewed applause.) The Conser- vatives, in the instance named, opposed the measure tooth and nail until they found that the country would have it, , and then they passed it, though they had before condemned it in the strongest possible language. If the non-electors of the district wished to have the franchise—which he hoped they would soon have conferred upon them—they must look to the Liberal party. ("Yes"). They had had a great deal of abuse and villificatiou of the Governmentlately but they could afford to stand by and smile, remembering the great sadness and disappointment of the Tory party at their summary dis- missal from power. There was not much reason in the virulent and bitter abuse of our noble Premier, Mr. Glad- stone—(cheers)— one of the greatest statesmen England has ever known, whose name would be remembered with honour when those of his vilifiers had been forgotten (Applause.) Turning to their own neighbourhood, they found that one of their neighbours, a most mild and courteous old gentlemen in ordinary life, speaking at a Tory meeting in Warrington the other night could find no better words in his vocabulary to apply to the. Liberal party than "that vulgar Radical herd." (Laughter.) They might all smile at such epithets, which were almost beneath notice. The greatest part of the abuse and scurrilous language used in speaking of political subjects came from the Conservative side. If those present would take to heart what the speakers said he would have no fear of the next election in the Lymm and Grappenhall polling district. (Applause). Mr. KENWORTHY moved the first resolution, which was as follows :—" That the meeting desires to express its con- fidence in Her Majesty's Government, believing its action to have been thoroughly consistent with the professions of its leading members when in opposition, and to have tended to increase the strength and prosperity of the United Kingdom; that it further desires to record its full approval of the Irish policy of the Government." He declared that the present Government was the best that had been in existence within his memory. He was not sur- prised at the attacks on Mr. Gladstone, for a man of emi- nence was always abused. There was no subject Mr. Glad- , stone did not thoroughly examine, and whatever he pro- posed was for the welfare and prosperity of the United Kingdom. The late Government was well qualified to squander public money, but they hardly knew what legisla- tion meant. He considered that there was required not only an extension of the franchise, but a redistribution of seats, and for that they must look to the Government. The position of the Liberal party had much improved in that district, and he had no doubt that at the next election Liberal mem- bers would be returned for the division. (Applause.) Mr. KILLICE: seconded the resolution. He said the Go- vernment did not act upon any chance suggestions for ex- pediency. but upon fixed principles, and hence there was not now the sense of insecurity and uncertainty that existed under the late administration. The improvement had con- duced to the prosperity of the commercial and industrial classes. He consideied the conclusion of peace in the Transvaal was the greatest instance of courage shown by the Government in their administration of the nation's affairs. As to Ireland, if the people of that country had any cause to complain of England this country had certainly reason to complain of Ireland. The Irish were said to be a warm-hearted race, and they might be asked to show so:ne gratitude to Mr. Gladstone for what he had done for them when previously in office. The Irish were a quick-witted race, but they had not shown their wit in combining with the Tories to obstruct the Liberals, who alone could remedy their wrongs. (Applause.) Mr. Tcrawrersosa, who was received with great cordiality, supported the resolution. He said he was present that he might help on in any small way he could his friend Mr. Latham, to whom he was very much indebted for his great and disinterested services. Through good report and evil report he (Mr. Latham) had championed the Liberal cause throughout Mid-Cheshire, and as a return for those labours he (the speaker) hoped he would be rewarded with a seat as one of the members for Mid-Cheshire. (Cheers.) The Par- liament which had met that day had as many important subjects before it as any Parliament which had met for many a long day. Thanks to the policy which it distinctly stated its intention to carry out when returned to power. The Government had no foreign complicstions now on hand. (Applause.) Of domestic subjects the most pressing was the state of Ireland. He need hardly remind them that the history of Ireland up to fifty years ago was a history of suppression and repression. The Irish had unrivalled water power. which gave them an advantage before the introduc- tion of steam, and they could work their mills cheaper. But no sooner had the Irish stuffs come into this country and competed with Manchester, Bradford, and other English towns, that deputations went up from those places, and it was attempted to prevent the introduction of these fabrics. As early as 1829 the Liberal Government passed that great Act of Catholic Emancipation by which Ireland was re- lieved from those abominab. le penal laws which were a dis- grace to any country imposing them upon another. , (Applause.) Since then the Liberal party had, according to' its lights, tried to do the best for Ireland. In the year 1869 that alien Church which was imposed upon the nation, in opposition to the majority of its inhabitants, was abolished —(applause)—and that was followed in 1870 by Mr. Glad- stone's Land Act. (Applause.) That Act took the Ulster custom as it found it, and legalised it, and recognised throughout Ireland the joint proprietorship of landlord and tenant. The fact was that the tenant had created an un- deniable property in the soil, inasmuch as for the most part he had made the improvements and furnished the equip- ments of the farm in the shape of house, draining, wells, reclaiming bog, &c. The Act prevented the landlord turn- ing out the tenant without compensation for improvements. In 1879 and 1880 it was found that, owing to bad harvests, many tenants were not able to pay their rents, and Mr. Gladstone introduced a bill which passed in the Lower House, but was thrown out in the House of Lords. (Hear, I hear.) That Act was called the Compensation for Disturbance Act. Under the existing law the landlord could not turn out a tenant as long as he paid his rent, and under that bill he would get paid for his improvements. (Applause.) In certain districts of Ireland, a famine was then existing, and it was enacted that those who were evicted for non-payment of rent should get compensation for improvements. (Ap- plause.) That Act was thrown out by the House of Lords, though it passed through the House of Commons, and Mr. Parnell told Mr. Rylarals that if that measure passed it would take nothing out of his agitation. A flaw having been found in the Land Act of 1870, the Act of last session was necessary. lie cotald not do better in connection with the matter than read them an extract from the Richmond Commission, which was appointed by a Conservative Government, and was composed in part Of Conservatives, to consider the question of Irish land. That Commission re- ported that, "bearing in mind the system by which the im- provements and equipments of a farm are very generally the work of the tenant, and the fact that a yearly tenant is at any time liable to have his rent raised by the increased value given to his holding by the expenditure of his own capital and labour, legislative interference to pro- tect him from an arbitrary increase of rent does not seem unnatural, and we are inclined to think that by the majority of landowners a measure properly framed to accomplish this object would not be ol;- jscted to." Mr. Kavanah, an Irish member, speaking of the matter said, "A sufficient. number of cases of the unjust raisine. of rent have been proved to show that the Land Act ,of 1870 is not a sufficient safeguard against the exercise of thiis power. I must frankly confess that, when I entered on s work of this Commission, I did not believe that there iv-as any valid ground for the discontent which has been and is so rife. However, as the inquiry proceeded, I found there was, I could Fee, an element of hope in the fact that all this discontent was not the fruit of political agitation." (Ap- pla.rise.) Then again there were the remarks of Mr. McNaghten. He spoke of the bill which the Government had introduced in this language :—" I.know that there is a pressing necessity, and I believe the bill, 7ith all its imper- fections, is an honest attempt to deal with that necessity. Et erybodv agrees that things cannot long remain as they are. There is a very general feeling: at least in the north of Ireland, that any measure to be satisfactory and acceptable must be based on the lines of what are called 'the three F's.' Everybody is agreed that there ought to be a tribunal to regulate rent." (Applause.) That was the evidence of the Richmond Commission, and of two Conservative members for Ireland. The result was that the bill was framed which empowered a court to fix a fair rent and give the tenant security if not fixity of tenure, and power to sell his in- terest in the farm if he wishes to leave it. If the bill was the measure of spoliation that Lord Salisbury alleged, Lord Salisbury was guilty of the worst form of political cowardice in allowing, it to pass into law when he had an obedient and m i overwhelming majority at his hack n the lloue, of Lords. What would Tories have done if they had been in the same position? Thsv had before them the evidence of the same Commission. Would they not have done the same? He ventured to say that they would have introduced a weak bill that would have worked their supporters in Ireland—(hear, hear,

—and he further irritated their enemies, who left a worse state of affairs for the Liberals to take up. He believed that throughout the whole of the bill Mr. Gladstone never swerved from those splendid words with which he concluded his opening speech when he said _ . . . .

"Justice, sir, is our guide ; walking in that path we cannot err. Guided by that light, that divine light, we are safe. Every step that we take upon our road is a step that brings us nearer to our God, and every obstacle, though it seem for the moment to be insurmountable, can only for a little time retard, and can never defeat the final triumph." (Cheers.) Turning from remedial legislation let them look for a little while at the other side. It must have been a

very hard thing for men like Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Bright, and Mr. Forster, men with the utmost warmth of heart, to have to introduce measures of coercion. Mr. Bright said that had it not been accompanied by a great act of remedial legislation, which, he believed, would remove the last shred of injustice from Ireland he could not !aave voted for it. (Applause.) He (the speaker) considered that the Govern- ment did quite right to adopt extraordinary measures in order to protect life and property in Ireland, which it was the duty of every Government to do. (Applause.) The agitation in Ireland,_ was. not one merely on a question of
rent. Mr. Parnell had said to an Irish au.dience.-not in the

House of Commons, that if it had not been with the view of the separation of Ireland from England, he would not have taken off his coat to help the Land Bill. The state of Ireland, he was glad to say, was very much quieter. Even Captain Boycott had been allowed to return, and was now living at peace among his old enemies. In places where the papers had said the hunts were stopped by crowds hunting was now resumed. As an instance of tint there was the

Limerick hounds, which were stated to have begun hunting again, and have enjoyed good sport. They met a few days since at a place where they bad previously been stopped, and were wiplcomed by the people. (Hear, hear.) After touch- ing upon foreign affairs, the speaker adverted to future legislation, and said there were many pressing measures of importance which the Government only wanted time and opportunity to carry, and amongst them the county fran- chise. The absurdity of the present arrangement was only equalled by the absurdity of Woodstock, Malmesbnrea Chippenham, and Colne returning members, while Crewe, St. Helens, Barrow-in-Farness, and other great industrial centres were left without. The first thing to be done was to reform Parliamentary procedure. An objection was raised againet the cljture, but he must call their attention to the fact that it was in actual use in its worst form at present in the House of Commons in, the shape of an obstructive minority, who by talking could stop the passing of any measure. (Cheers.) Mr. J. C. FIELDEN also spoke in support of the resolution, 'which was afterwards carried unanimously. Mr. G. SV. I..ATITAM, who was introduced by the Chair- man as the future member for the division, had a very cordial reception. He moved the second resolution as follows :—" That this meeting hails with satisfaction the prospect of a strong bill for the amendment of County Government 3nd the re-adjustment of Local Taxation, and that it earnestly anticipates at the hands of Ministers a measure for the complete protection of Farmers' improve- ments; it ale° sincerely trusts that the Government will, at the earliest practicable date, bring in and carry a bill to give the franchise to all householders in counties." , Standing as he did in the centre of a large agricultural district, he said, and speaking to a large number of those who were interested in land, he wished to discuss the question—Why are the tenant farmers of England usually ranked as Conservatives? He did not believe they were really so. A man whose occupation was upon the land, and who from the very nature of that occupation must be an intelligent man, see- ing the progress of the seasons, must believe in progress:; and therefore the tenant farmer from his observations must be a Liberal. Besides from the occupation of farming they found that the representation of the country was not at present satisfactory. A man who knew that change of seed was sometimes necessary was not likely to be satisfied with a representation confined to a few leading families, who simply settled amongst themselves who should be members for the county. And if observation led a farmer to be a Liberal, how much more was it his interest to be so? Surely everybody knew that the prosperity of the agriculturalists round Lymm depended upon the prosperity of Manchester, Liverpool, and Warrington; and that the greatness of those towns was due to the measures of Liberal Governments. The reason that farmers were classed as Canservatives was this—up till 1332 tenant farmers had no votes as a class. Of course; some farmers—many more than at the present moment—were freeholders, and consequently had votes, and a large number of farms were then held on life leases, the holders of which were freeholders, with votes. But it was not until the Chandoa clause was passed in 1832 that holders of farms worth £5O and upwards had votes. That clause was inserted in the bill as a compromise in, order that the leading families of England might have influence in Parlia- ment when they thought they were going to be deprived by the laws. The consequence was that landlord and agent drove these tenants to the poll like flocks of sheep, and farmers were considered Conservatives because they thought it better to have no politics, as they knew the day would come when they would not be allowed to express an opinion of their own; and in many cases they became unreasoning and unreasonable politicians. But now, he believed, all that was changed. Farmers ware beginning to think for them- selves. They were findine out that the ballot was secret, and they well knew that whatever the opinions of their landlords were they had the right as Englishmen to hold their own opinions or to express thew at the poll without fear. (Applause.) Up to his ' time the agriculturalists of England had had no reason to be grateful to either political party. Probably the Liberals had neglected him because they had thought him hopeless, and the Conservatives had done nothing for him because they were pretty sure they had him whether' they did so or not. (Laughter). lie asked them, how- ever, to look at what the late Government did and what the. present administration had done for the farmer, and say whether they could not draw some hope for the future from what had past. What did the late Government do for the tenant farmer? They gave him the Agricultural Holdings Bill, which seemed very satisfactory, giving perfect security, only there was a clause which allowed the landlords to get out of it if they liked—(laughter)—and get out of it they did from the great lords of the State to the smallest landlord. The bill might as well have been put in the fire before it received the Queen's assent for the good it conferred upon the tenant farmer. Then they gave him what they called "Grants in aid." The grant for police was increased from one-quarter to one-half, and they gave something' towards the maintenance of lunatics. But were the rates one farthing less since that was done? (" No.") The reason the rates had not decreased was that the "grants in aid" led to extravagance. If a man knew that he could get a thing at half-price he was very apt to buy it even when he did not require it.. So applications were sometimes made to the governing authorities of Cheshire for additional policemen, and some magistrate, who thought hiS rabbits were not looked after well enough, said "Oh! the Government will pay one-half ;" or some old woman was very troublesome in a workhouse, and was sent to a lunatic asylum, because the Government would contribute towards her maintenance: and thus "grants in aid" were simply aids to extravagance. What had the present Government done for agriculturalists ? They had repealed the malt tax. That was not of much interest in Cheshire, but for years when the Liberals were in power the Conservatives were always aeitating for its repeal. They had given a Hares and Rabbits Bill that allowed the farmer to keep down the ground game on his farm and prevent the crops being ruined—by stock that was not his own. (Applause). In the Queen's speech, too, the Government promised to intro- duce a County Government Bill. He did not think many of them had an idea of how, they were governed. A few days ago he was reading some statistical papers drawn up at the bidding of Messrs. Rathbone and Whitbread, and he found that their friend Mr. Broadbent lived in a borough, a parish, a union, and a county, none of which were co- terminus with one another, and had different boundaries and areas. He (Mr. Broadbent)ewas governed by a council, a vestry, a school board, a burial \board, board of guardians, and quarter sessions; and he was liable to be called upon to pay borough, district, burial, poor, and county rates. Mr. Swanwick lived in a Local Government Board district, a parish, a union, and a county, and was governed by the Local Government Board, a vestry, possibly a school hoard, union authorities, a burial board, and quarter sessions. (Lauehter.) Mr. Long lived in a rural parish, and also in a union a highway board district, and a county, and he was governed by the authorities of a union, a vestry, a school board, a highway board, and quarter sessions. Everyone of those bodies borrowed money, ran into debt, and paid in- terest on its debts. But he 'did not think any gentleman present could tell how much the county, the parish, or the union owed ; what the rates were, or upon what system those rates were raised. It was necessary. before economy could be secured in the management of local affairs, that we should have one unit as the area, and the large body be made of a collection of those units. Then when we had a local Chancellor of the Exchequer we might hope to get such an annual statement of affairs as would make the rate- payers look after them. How was it possible at the present moment, with confusion of accounts and overlapping areas --some of which might be in two or three counties—to hope for economy ? He heard the other day of a farm of 300 acres in Worcestershire that was in 12 parishes, and was liable to 50 rates. The only hope of economy was in sim- plification of county government. When men could see how they were governed, and get a thorough knowledge of the area in which they lived, they might hope to return such representatives as would ensure economy in their Govern- ment. (Applause.) He was excessively grateful to the Government for not, in the scheme as had always been suggested, associating ex-officio magistrates with the elected representatives of the people. Surely such a thing could hardly be advanced at the present day. Fancy the people of Liverpool, Manchester, or Warrington, being told that amongst their elected governors must it some 20 or 30 gen- tlemen who had not been chosen by the electors, but who had been appointed from political motives or by a party Lerd Lieutenant (Applause.) He did not hope for any great land measure this session, for he believed a satis- factory measure of that nature could not be carried until we had the extension of the county franchise. (Applause.) The one thing needful for agriculturalists at the present moment was that they should have security for their capital. That was necessary, because owing to cheapness of transit the great prairies of America were now practically close to Eng- land, and food was poured into the country in competition with that here produced at almost a nominal freight. The British tenant farmer, who had to pay rent for his land and live in an oldcountry, could only hope to compete with farmers of the virgin soil of America by growing larger crops on the acre than was done on the other side of the Atlantic; and he could only do that by the expenditure of capital, which he must be perfectly sure he would receive back before he could

be expected to expend it. (Applause.) He would like best to see continuity of tenure, farmers holding their land as long as they paid a stipulated rent, and living on them from generation to generation. But he did nol, expect that could be obtained at present; and he therefore desired, first of all, that the law of distress should bq abolished—(applause)—
and that agriculturists shoald have perfect security for their improvements. They might think that because they paid

their rents and were not likely to have a distress put in that the law in this respect did not affect them; but owing to the law of distress the landlord was able to accept as a competi- tor for a farm a man who, though witbourcapital, offered a high rent, because at the worst the landlord could sell him up and cheat all the other creditors. Thus rents were in- creased to an uncertain degree, but no doubt to the extent of 10 or 12 per cent. "But," a farmer might say, "if the law of distress is abolished my landlord will want security, he will want bondsmen l" At the present time bondsmen were required on the third or fourth large estate in Cheshire. "Then," the farmer might say, "he will want my rent in advance !" But if they paid money in advance they would get discount. A third Conservative argument was that young men would be prevented from going upon farms. He was certain, however, that the son of a good farmer, known to be respect- able, would be preferred by a landlord, even if there were no law of distress, to a man who had capital but svho had had no experience in farming. The landlord, being dependent upon the liability of his tenant, would take the best man he could get. Besides, the law of distress being abolished, there must be a law for compensation for improvements. The members of the Farmers' Alliance believed that would be best secured by allowing the tenant to sell his improvements, as it was unfair both to tenant and landlord to lay down a fixed scale on the basis that drains and bones were exhausted in so malty years, when their duration depended in a measure on the nature of the soil. The fairest arrangement would be to allow the tenant to go into the market to get the best price he could. Then the landlord, instead of having an out- going tenant who wished to make ,things unpleasant for the incoming tenant, would have a mh doing his best to let his farm to a solvent and respectable man. (Applause.) That would be a grand reform to secure capital. The landlords said the tenant would sell something beside his improve- ments, but he did not think that would be the case, and, if it were, the question might be asked—have the landlords never taken that which was somebody else's—the property of the tenants? (Applause.) He wanted the Farmers' Alliance proposal carrying, because it would afford protec- tion against landlords selling their tenants property, and pre- vent, what was equally unjust, the rent of a tenant who did not wish to leave his farm, being increased for the value of his own improvements. He had received a rather amusing; letter, bearing the NiTarrington post mark, from some gentle- man who wished him to say a few words on tithes. That gentleman's idea of tithes was rather a strange one, as he seemed to say that if a tenant farmer was willing to take the risk of going to the arch-enemy he should not pay tithes, because the parson was merely cheating the devil of his due. (Laughter.) He was afraid his correspondent had not studied the history of the incidence of tithes very much. They all knew that practically, the origin of tithes was lost in obscurity—they having been first imposed in Saxon times —and that every acre for. which tithes were paid had been bought and resold, settled and unsettled, mortgaged and redeemed over and over again, and the burden of tithes had been taken into account. A very large portion were not paid to those gentlemen who were supposed to be trying to rob Satan of his just due, but to lay proprietors; and another large part were paid not only for works of religion, but also for works of education. He considered it would be thorougly unjust to abolieh tithes without compensating the tithe holders ; but all tenant farmers and tithe payers had just cause of complaint at the way averages were taken at the present time—on the price of corn of the best quality in certain market towns' the price being often increased by the merchants' profits. He would like to see the tithe owners paid out of some national fund raised and paid for—say for 40 or 45 years—by the tithe payers of the present time. That would be a better arrangement for the owners, while in it short time, by a very little extra payment, those who paid tithes would get rid of the burden. As to rates he would only say they would be less when county government had been secured. He believed it would be a great measure of reform if, as was the case in Scotland, the landlord and tenant divided the rates between them. (Applause.). ViThen those improvements were made they might hope to see something like free land—land free from the trammels of entail and settlement, so that a landlord could do what he liked with it; land free for the tenant to deal with, so that he could grow what crops he pleased, and not be fettered by stipulations, which prevented him from cultivating the land ar.d selling the produce in the way he would like. Referring to the recent election in the North Riding, he said the result was a misfortune to agricultural reform. But they knew how bit- ter was the feeling amongst landlords when a farmer stood against a landowner, when the landowner felt he was fight- ing to the cleath for his peculiar privileges; and knew that in such a district as the North Riding it was impossible to prevent an agent riding into the yard next morning and asking the farmer how he had voted. He was afraid that was done extensively in the recent elec- tion. But the result was that the public believed the farmers were opposed to reform, to tenant right, to enfranchisement of the soil, and to county government; and Lord Salisbury, MY. James Lowther, and their supporters would think that if they could get a dissolution those reforms could be post- poned. He hoped, however, that good would come of the evil—that it would be a lesson to the Cabinet, and lead them to accelerate the passing of the equalisation of the county and borough, franchise. They might depend upon it that the tenant farmer would vote much stronger when he had a strong force of emancipated men at his back—(ap- plause) ;—that the influence which was now used so power- fully would fail entirely when there were multitudes of voters present. He cared little or nothing how those voters exercised the franchise, only let us have a Government elected by the voters influenced by their opinions, and not by their fears. (Applause.) He believed we were on the verge of great changes, and he prayed for a happy issue out of all our troubles, and that the nation might be settled upon a certain foundation. (Hearty cheering.) Mr. MILNE, in seconding the resolution, spoke of the ridiculous clauses in farm leases which prevented tenants from sending to the Manchestetsmarket produce from which they might derive great profit; and Mr.. W. DAIIBTSHIRE, in supporting it, expressed an earnest wish for the abolition of tithes, and declared that in the present state of the law he would not lend money to his own brother to sink in a farm. The tenant farmers, he added, wanted to be in a position .to grow food as cheaply as it could be obtained anywhere else, and thenPthey would be satisfied—(applause); and the pre- sent Government were more likely to enable them to do that than any he had ever known. (Renewed applause.) Mr. BIZOADRENT (Latchford) also supported the resolu- tion and observed that the government of the counties had hitherto been conducted with a fair amount of ability and economy, but or. quite an antedeluvian system, and repre- sentative government would be advantageous in many ways. The CHAIRMAN, recommended those interested in the land question to study the observations of Mr. McMinnies, as reported in last Saturday's Examiner. The resolution• was carried unanimously, and the proceed- ings terminated' with the passing of a vote of thanks to the chairman.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Board was held on Wed- nesday, at the Workhouse. There were present Mr. Joseph Harrison (chairman), Rev. John Yonge, Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Blackburst, Darbyshire, Woolfall, Appleton, Hunt, Houghton, Greenell, Fairhurst, Cooper, Cartwright, Jeans, Heaton, Garnett,;Kilsball, Swinton, and J. C. Sutton (clerk).

THE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee were as follows:—At a meeting of the Schools Committee, on the 7th February, Mr. Napier applied for an overdraw beyond the allowance of 15 per cent on hand, and held by the Board of Guardians. Resolved that a certificate for £350 be granted. The archi- tect submitted a letter from Mr. Daniel, in reference to the proposed give-and-take line on the west boundary,.which was as follows :—" Holly Bank, Wellington-road, 25th January, 1882. Gentlemen,—Your note of the 13th to hand, and in answer I may say that the price named in my last is fair and equitable, it being front land, and I shall not take less."

Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved, and Mr. COOPER seconded,. the adoption of the minutes. The CHAIRMAN said it appeared the committee had.gmnted Mr. Napier privileges beyond what were agreed upon. Mr. lAnnvsainE said they had partly assented to Mr. Napier's request. The committee felt they could with safety grant a certificate for £350; but Mr. Napier wanted more. Mr. BLACKHURST said Mr. Napier told them on Tuesday afternoon he would be able to hand the schools over to the Board at the latter end of March.
The minutes were passed. A VACCINATION STATION WANTED AT HAXDOCX.

The CLERK read the following letter from Dr. Watkins:— "Dear sir,—We are being kicked about from pillar to post' for a vaccination station in Haydock. I had A long interview last Monday with the Local Board, in the hope of inducing them to let us have one of their rooms, but they refused. I enclose a letter received from Mr. Turnbull making an offer. We have no place to meet next Saturday." The enclosure was as follows:—" Lyme House, Haydoek, Feb. lst,lSB2. Dear Sir,— The managers of St. James's Church School, Haydock, re- quest me to say that they are willing to allow you the use of their infant school for vaccination purposes, provided the Guardians are agreeable to pay to them the sum of £lO per annum for the use of the said school. Awaiting your reply, I am, Sc.,e THOMAS TURNBULL." Mr. APPLETON: How often is the room wanted—once a quarter? The CLERK: Oftener than that. You only pay ;elO per annum for Warrington, where there is more room required. It was decided that the question be left in the hands of Dr. Watkins, and that the Clerk write to that gentleman inform- ing him the Board was of opinion £lO a year, for so small a township as Haydock, was too much, but the Guardians were willing to pay r.

THE CATTLE PLAGUE RATE IN CHESHIRE. The CLERK read the following letter :—" Clerk of the Peace's Office, Chester, 23 January, 1382. Dear sir,—As provided by section 101 of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, 1869, no specific rate is made for cattle plague rate in this county, but the expenditure is defrayed out of the county rate or out of any other monies applicable under Act of Parliament or otherwise for the public charges or uses of this county. By the 3rd sub-section of the section above referred to, in lieu of the provisions in other counties that tenants should be authorised to deduct half of the

cattle rate from their landlord, it ia provided that in this cousaty where the actual amount of cattle rate cannot be ascertained, there being no separate rate, the occupier of premises, in respect of which he is rated to the poor, but of which he is not the owner, may in each year until let November, MN, in which he duly pays his poor rate, deduct from the rent payable to the owner, one penny in the £ on the annual rateable value of such premises. IVe hope this information will answer your purpose. We are, 6T.c., POTTS ik ROBERTS." THE MAINTENANCE OF INFECTIOUS PA.TIENTS. Mr. DABBYSHIRE said a bill was presented by the Rural Sanitary Authority in respect to the maintenance of five
patient's who had been sent from their district to the In-

iectious Diseases' Hospital at Warrington. The total. amount was £23 Ps. 7d., and he proposed that it be paid. The in- spector of the Rural Sanitary Authority had been to see the persons, and reported that none of them were in a position to pay. _ _ _

Mr. COOPER seconeed the proposition, and said the persons referred to had been before the Authority and claim exemption on account of their inability to pay. There were only a few townships comprising the Authority, and by pay- ing the amount as proposed the cost was thrown over the whole of the Union.
On the suggestion of the Clerk, it was agreed to obtain the opinion of the Local Government Board as to the form of payment in these cases.
THE FURNIMING MISSION.-THE DIFFICTTLTY SOLVED

The minutes of the House Committee having been read, The Rev. J. YONGE said the Board would recollect that at the last meeting there was a very interesting and somewhat amusing discussion in reference to the purchase of some furniture, and he asked if it was referred to the House Com- mittee. If so, should there not be some record on the minutes of the House Committee respecting it ? Major CARTWRIGHT : I think I shall be able to explain the matter if you will wait patiently. The Rev. J. YONGE : I will wait as patiently as Job. Major CARTWRIGHT then moved, and Mr. APPLETON seconded. the adoption of the minutes. Major CARTWRIGHT said, in reference to the furniture, the committee deputed him, along with Mr. Woolfall, to wait upon Messrs. Johnson and Mr. Marsh to see if they could not make an am' cable arrangement in regard. to certain portions of the furniture. The first place they went to was Mr. Marsh's, and in regard to what the gentlemen selected, and he presumed ordered, there, he considered the articles, with the exception of the bed, bolster, and pillows, were not at all out of the way. He verily, believed they were worth the money charged', but they were a little too expensive. The half-tester bed they considered was rather too high in price, but Mr. Marsh met them fairly and said they could select any other in its place that would suit them, and they agreed to do so, but at a less cost. The bedroom suite they ',E2O was not extravagant at all; he con- sidered there was nothing unreasonable in that, and he recommended that the purchase of these things should be completed. _

The Rev. J. YONGE : What would the cost amount to? Major CARTWRIGHT said about £33 altogether. The fur- niture he saw at Messrs. Johnson's was excellent, but the price was too high. He asked Messrs. Johnson whether they would allow them to make another selection of furni- ture that would probably meet the Board's requirements, hut they positively refused to do so. He tried them in every way, but there was numoving them except as to the dining-room table, simply for the reason that the order was given and they had to take wen from another job to execute the order. He told them they had better write him a letter, and if he had been put to, any expense in preparing the articles the Board might use them. Mr. Johnson said that was a secondary consideration, but he (the Major) told hitn to write to him officially so that he could lay the letter before the Board. and.. get their opinion on the subject. He had . . .

received the folliiwing letter, dated 26th January :—" Major Cartwright.—Dear Sir,—With reference to the furniture ordered for the Warrington Union, and the conversation we had with you yesterday afternoon, we very carefully went through the other articles, and alth oug.h it will be at in- convenience to ourselves we will exchange the table for a less expensive one—say about £6. The one ordered being part made, we shall have to put it in stock. But with re- ference to the other things, we cannot entertain the idea of taking them into stock, part of them being made to measure and the remainder upholstered work. They are goods that we never do stock, and we cannot see why we should do it in this case. 'We may add that being told to deliver them. without any delay, it necessitated several hands leaving the work they were engaged upon to commence these; then by instruction we stopped them again, thus puftin!, us to both inconvenience and expense. As the amount is but small we shall be glad to know that this is satisfactory, and that we may deliver the goods."• He (Major Cartwright) thought the best plan would be to get out of the matter as well as they possibly could. Mr. BLACICHURST said he would like to know what orders , were given to Messrs. Woolfall and Heaton, whether they exceeded those orders, and whether the Board was com- promised by those gentlemen. The CHAIRMAN said there was no doubt that inasmuch as• the Board deputed those gentlemen to do a certain thing, and they went to these tradesmen and in the name of the Guardians ordered these things, the Guardians and not those gentlemen were liable for the purchase. They evidently thought they had the authority of the Board and in pur- suance of that authority they ordered the goods. rhe Rev. J. YONGE supposed it was a fact that these gentlemen were deputed by the House Committee to (lo this work for the Board, so that their authority was a doubly, deputed authority. Bat seeing it was a recognised prin- 7,iple that when there was a large expenditure of money to be undertaben it should be done in the way of estimate submitted to the Board in the first instance, he very much questioned whether the House Committee had the right to give an order, and still less whether these gentlemen, had the right to give _an order for the goods. He felt very _ _ _
much—sympatiiy with Major Cartwrighi in reference to the matter, because they all knew:how much he prided himself

on the management of the House; and when they found 'two of his most trusty lieutenants selling him in this way, he deserved their sympathy. It was strange that two gentle- men who were sent to the Board 12 months ago as represen- tatives of a. party who came there pledged to economy should so remarkably overstep the limits of economy in the administration,of that House. He did not object to every comfort being provided for the master and matron. Mr. Heaton said; he had acted in the matter in the same way he would do for himself. He questioned whether that was the principle upon: which they might go. He thought the rate- payers sent them there to spend their money on.principles which they would approve,—not on principles of their own preferenoe,.or even on their own personal comfort and en- joyment. He thought they were bound to provide all reasonable comfort for the master and matron of the house and every other officer,:andihe hoped they would always do it; but whether they should go to such extravagant expense as in this- instance was-a very doubtful matter indeed. Ho- did not know what the auditor would say. He might, per- haps,.surcharge their friends. Major CARTWRIGHT :• Oh, dear, no. Mr. HEATON: I hope he will. Major CARTWRIGHTI• There are a good many worse hills pass muster. The Rev. ,T. roNGE•thought they might take the matter in the best way they could, although he questioned whether these gentlemen could again claim the suffrages of the rate- payers on the ground of economy. Mr. JEANs asked if there had been any special resolution authorising the gentlemen to pledge the credit of the Guar- dians. ("No.") If nct, the Guardians were in no manner bound. He thought Mr. Heaton and Mr. Woolfall had rather overstepped the mark in ordering new furniture, be- cause if he had been going to seleet furniture he should have selected what melted him, and not have ordered new. Mr. GARNETT said the question he took up at the last meeting was the question of principle and it was a gross impropriety ta send Or permit any member of that Board to go and make a purchase to anything like the amount of £lOO or £l2O without bringing a list of what they had seen and selected, and getting the consent of the Board. (Hear, hear.) He, however, saw a way out of the difficulty. Mr. Heaton stated the goods were nothing like what he had been pur- chasing for his now house, but if he could find room for them it would be a way out of the difficulty, and the Board could start de nom. (Laughter.) Mr. HEATON was much obliged to Mr. Garnett for his sug- gestion, and said if the Board were so dissatisfied with the bargain he would not object to adopt it. He received his instructions by note, and when he had anything to do with Mr. Woolfall he always took it for granted it would be right. ("Oh.") The only thing Mr. Woolfall objected to was pur- chasing the furniture from one place. He did not consider , the furniture at all too good. He thought when they gave people something like £3OO a year they did not want them to sit upon wooden chairs; and that the least they could do was to make the master as comfortable as possible. He con- sidered the furniture was about as good as the commonest Mr. Garnett made. Mr. BLA.CKIII;RST: I should like to know how the clerk is to get the bill passed by the auditor. The CLERK: It rests with the gentlemen who sign the cheque. Rev. J. YONGE: I should suggest that the Major, Mr. Woolfall, end Mr. Heaton sign it. Mr. HEATON: I will sign it with the greatest pleasure. Major CARTWRIGHT: I have not signed a cheque for a long time. Rev. J. YONGE: Are you too old a bird? Major CARTWRIGHT: Yes. Mr. JEANs said it was his private opinion that the Board were not bound by the transaction. There was an order which provided that estimates and tenders should be given, and if the auditor asked for the estimate, and it was not forth- coming,. would he allow the account? He thought Messrs. Johnson had taken a position which they could not main- tain, and the Guardians might set their letter at defiance if they were not bound by the order. It was for the Board to say whether they would take that position or confirm what had been done. Rev. J. YONGE said the question was not simply whether the Board would confirm what had been done, but whether the auditor would pass it after-the Board had confirmed it. Mr. BLACKHURST remarked that, so far as he was con- cerned, he should repudiate the transaction altogether. The principlc in which that transaction had been carried out was open to any abuse they liked to turn it to; and it was evident, from the clerk's ruling, the whole thing, was illegal from beginning to end. They had no right to spend the ratepayers' money in the way proposed, and he protested against it. They should commence again to do the thing in a legal manner. Mr. DARBYSHIRE thought they should move in this matter according to law, and he hoped that would be done. There had been a good deal said in reference to spending the rate-

payers' money. He might say the ratepayers in some Part 9, of the Union. were very different to those in other parts, cause the ratepayers he represented were entirelY against pe expenditure being incurred for that furniture. GRASSHOPPER HtrxTim—Spearing salmon by moonlight on the rivers is as exciting a scene as a similar sport in the quiet bays of the North. The poor savage has an abiding belief that the Creator will send salmon in the stream and grasshoppers on the plain for his food, and year after year he leads his precarious life, buoyed up by the confidence his ' simple faith inspires. Certain portions of the north-west and central regions of North America swarm with several species of grasshoppers—veritable locusts—which cover the country and eat up every green thing. The farmer looks upon Chem with dread, and many and ingenious are the in- ventions to keep them out of his fields. The Indians all through the region between the Rocky and Cascade Moun- tains, and throughout Nevada, Utah, and California, regard them as one of the most unqualified blessings from " the Great Spirit"—illustrating the old and homely proverb about one man's meat being another man's poison. They are eaten either fresh or preserved for winter use, just as the Arabs do locusts, and with equal gusto. The grasshop- per season is almost equal in importance to the acorn one. To procure the former luxury, a hole is dug deep enough to prevent the insects jumping out. The Indians, old and young, then form a circle, each person being armed with a piece of bush. They then commence beating the grasshop- pers towards the hole, in which, when once driven, they are prisoners. Altogether, hunting this small game is an active and moderately-exciting exercise. Sometimes the grass and weeds round are set on fire, so that the grasshoppers are disabled and afterwards picked up.—The Peoples of the World.

„ FOWL ROASTED ON A STRING.—ON one occasion M. Dumas thought fit to prove his culinary acquirements by cooking a very complicated dinner, one dish of which was a pair of fowls roasted on a string. His vice, or assistant cook, had hitherto been obedient ; but at this she rebelled, standing up for the•jack, until he threatened to get her paid off and turned out of the house forthwith. She yielded, and five minutes afterwards the fowls, each on its string, were spin- ning like a couple of spindles, side by side, before the fire.' M. D Limas' plan is based on physiological facts. Every animal has two orifices, an upper and a lower one. To roast a fowl in first-rate style, the upper orifice must be stopped, after the Belgian fashion, by thrusting its head into its crop and sewing the skin over it with needle and thread. By the lower orifice the fowl will have been emptied. Its liver, chopped small with parsley and other sweet herbs, and mixed with butter, will be returned to the place of the absent intestines. And now, what ought to be the cook's grand object? Decidedly to retain in the creature she is about to roast the greatest quantity of gravy possible. But if she thrusts a big spit through it from end to end, and a small one across it to keep it in place, she makes four holes, instead of two, for the gravy to escape from. But if, on the contrary, you tie its feet together with a string, and suspend it vertically by that string, with its lower orifice upwards and its upper orifice closely plugged ; if you dust it slightly with salt and pepper, and baste it with the very best fresh butter, pouring a spoonful in now and then, you then fulfil all the logical conditions for having an excellent roast chicken. You have only to watch it while it roasts, to cut the string which holds it when the skin is covered with little blisters out of which issue jets of sweet-smelling steam. You then deposit it on its dish, and pour over it the contents of the latchpan, with which not a drop of , broth must have been .mixed during the whole process of basting.—Cassell's Household Guide.
