div.p: RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COM- MISSIONERS. The monthly meeting was held on Monday, at the Board- room, the Town Hall. Dr. Steel presided, and there were present Dr. McDougall, Messrs. -Norman, Williams, Taylor, Fisher, P. Speakman, Lake, Hazlehurst, Shaw, Handley, Whittaker, J. J. Speakman, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), and Barker (surveyor).

_ RESIGNATION,OF MR. LYON. The CHAIRMAN read the fallowing (copy) letter : "Mersey House, Runcorn, February 6th, 1882. To the Chairman of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, Dear Sir,—Feeling that I cannot properly attend to the duties devolving upon me as one of the Runcorn Impreve- went Commissioners, I beg to tender my resignation. Thanking you and all the members of the Board, for the unifcrm kindness which has always been shown towards me, I remain, dear sir, your faithfully Was. LYON." Ma. tionarAN said he was very sorry indeed to hear such a communication read, for a better man than Mr. Lyon never sat round that table since he had been a member of the Board. The CHAIRMAN thought the resignation of Mr. Lyon would prove a very a great logs to the Board of Commis- sioners. Dr. McDouGALL was of opinion that it must be a matter of sincere regret to all of them, that a gentleman who had always acted nith uniform courtesy, with a great deal of knowledge, and without giving rise to the shadow of a suspicion that he had any personal end to serve in acting as a commissioner, should have felt it nec;ssary to discontinue his attendance at their meetings, and so deprive them of the benetit of his valuable services. He was sure it must have been apparent to all of them that Mr. Lyon had but one object in view, and that of a most disinterested character, viz, to do the greatest possible good to the greatest possible number. (Hear, hear.) He was convinced they all wished Mr. Lyon every geed wish in his retirement. He should have been glad to move that Mr. Lyon should be asked to reconsider his decision, but he did not think he was a gentleman who would have come to so important a decision without giving it the most serious con- sideration. lie would move that an expression of the regret of the Board at the receipt of the intelligence, be placed upon the books. Mr. NORMAN most cordially seconded the motion, and it was carried unanimously.

THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The monthly report of the medical officer was read, and showed that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month :was 21, and one death had occurred in Halton-within-Runcorn, making a lotal of 22. Of these five were da-i to pulmonary diseases, three to brain affec- tions, three to cardiac affections two to natural decay, and two to premature birth. Scarlatina, jaundice, erysipelas, apoplexy, phthisis and fever accounted for one death each, representing a death rate of about 17 per 1000 per annum. Nine deaths had occurred amongst children of one year and under, and three inquests had been held. Dr. Mouritz also presented his annual report for the year ending Dec. :31st. The number of deaths during the year had been 239, besides 22 cases in which inquests had been held. The total number of deaths was, therefore 261, and the Medical Officer congratulated the Board that this was a decrease of 31 on the previous year, when the total deaths numbered 292. Of these 71 occurred in the first quarter, 69 in the second, 43 in the third, and 56 in the fourth. The death rata was 16 per 1000 per annum. Whooping cough, owing to severe easterly winds in the first quarter, was very prevalent, and accounted for no fewer than 32 deaths during the year. Thirty-nine deaths were due to pulmonary affections, 21 to general decay and exhaustion, 27 to abdominal affections, 36 to diseases of the nervous system, 27 to bronchitis, 5 to cardiac disease, 15 to brain disease, 4 to marasmus, 6 to phthisis, 4 to cancer, 4 to premature births, 2 to mesenteric disease, 3 to measles, 2 to scarlatina, and the remainder were due to dropsy, child-birth, debility, dentition, gangrene, convulsions, erysipelas, hemorrhage &c. Eighty deaths occurred amongst children under one year old. In his last annual report he remarked that the Board's Building Bye- Laws required revision. Since that time the work had been carried out, and appeared to meet with general satisfaction. In March last also, he also reported that the arrangements for combating the spread of infectious disease were far from satisfactory. The question of providing suitable hospital accommodation for the treatment of cases of a infectious nature had several times occupied the attention of the Board, and he trusted would certainly result in permanent good. Happily during the year, cases of zymotic disease had been very few, which might be attributed to the preventative -steps which he, in conjunction with the inspector of nuisances, had taken to prevent importation from other districts. There were three cases of scarlatina in Sept. on canal boats, but the measures taken were effectual in prevent- ing the spread of the outbreak. The fountain water was still contaminated by large quantities of vegetable and animal matter, and was rendered totally unfit for use. He had been assured by Mons. Clolus that everything would be done to prevent a future mishap. As far as he was aware, the lodging houses in the town were free from nuisances. The general health of the town was now very good. On the proposition of Dr. I‘IcDorGALL, seconded by Mr. NORMAN. the annual report was referred to the Highway and Sanitary Committee. THE BRIDGEWATER TRUSTEES AND THE BOARD. A CLOSE VOTE. The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, showed that a report had been presented by the Surveyor stating that the pollution of the Sprinch water still con- tinued. It had been resolved that Mr. Barker should turn the water off at the eye-hole in Ellesmere-street. A letter had been received from the Bridgewater trustees with reference to their plans of proposed streets on the Sprinch, on land near to the Old Quay, and in Cooper's field. The Committee recommended that the plans should be approved. —The report of Mr. R. B. Abbott, of St. Helens, as to his inspection of the Glycerine Works, was laid before the Com- mittee, on the 2nd inst., and it was resolved that the con- sideration of the document be adjourned until the following meeting.—The Surveyor was instructed to adopt such means as he might deem advisable for cleansing the Sprinch water pipes. Mr. Barker had been requested to write to Mr. T. Cliff concerning the street cleansing.—A correspondence had taken place between Mr. Beasley's solicitors and the Law Clerk, as to a request for permission to inspect the minute books, which had been refused. Mr. NORMAN moved the adoption of the minutes, and Mr. WILLIAMS seconded the motion. Dr. McDouGann asked for an explanation in regard to the plans of the Bridgewater Trustees. Mr. NORMAN said that he understood the plans had been passed. The streets referred to were already partly made. Dr. McDoroann requested the Surveyor to explain the matter. Mr. BARKER said that two of the streets referred to— White and Haworth—had been laid out and built upon a great many years ago. Dr. MCDOUGALL: Is there any resolution on the books with regard to them? The 6URVEYOR : I should think so, but it is 20 years ago. Mr. NORMAN : I say distinctly that every street referred to, so far as I understand the matter, is partly built upon. It would be utterly unreasonable for you to ask people to make a 331 t. street in places where the street has been laid out. Mr. P. SPEARMAN : We discussed this matter very fully at the meeting of the committee, on Thursday last. The CHAIRMAN intimated that he did not recollect it being

discussed. Dr. McDouGaLL moved that the plans be referred back for consideration at the next meeting. He considered that there had been unnecessary haste in adopting them, for he attended the meeting, and was present within five minutes of the commencement, but he found that the plans and some other matter had been already considered. Under these cir- cumstances, he was at a loss to know how Mr. Speakman was able to say the plans had been fully discussed. He (the speaker) also be:ieved that the plans mentioned, or some similar to them, were submitted to the Board a short time ago, at the time when Mr. Fereday Smith wrote to the Local Government Board about the new building bye-laws. The plans under discussion were not those of buildings, but of streets. Mr. NORMAN said be must object to the insinuations of Dr. McDougall that time had been taken by the forelock in discussing the plans. Everything done at the committee was taken in its proper order. The CHAIRMAN: He is not referring to that. Mr. NORMAN: I maintain that he is distinctly referring to that, and he was not present at the meeting within ten minutes of the time when it commenced. Dr. McDougall Las no right to cast reflections upon the manner in which the business of the committee is conducted. Dr. McDouGALL : I must ask you, Mr. Chairman, to pro- tect me, and keep the chairman of the Highway and Sani- tary Committee in order. (Laughter.) We ought not to pass any ground plans until we have the plans of the build- ings before us. The Law CLERK remarked that he saw there were no levels or sections on the plans. McDonwiLL said that such a fact ought to have been pointed out to them by the surveyor. Mr. BARKER (surveyor) explained that the streets bad already beeo formed. Mr. HANDLEY was decided of opinion that if the Board committed themselves to the passing of the plans "they would be agreeing to accept the termination of a plans, 12 feet in width." He seconded the amendment. Mr. SHAW supported it, on the ground that it was not good policy to pass plans of streets without having those of the buildings laid before the Board. Mr. P. SPEARMAN contended that there was no precedent for not passing the plans. Mr. Lake having briefly spoken in favour of the original motion, the CHAIRMAN said be considered there would be no harm in passing the amendment. On the amendment being put, six members voted for it and seven for tne original motion, which '!-vs, therefore, declared carried. The minutes, as they originally stood, were then adopted.

THE NEW HOSPITAL. The Canal Boats' and Hospital Committees minutes were approved, on the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Taylor. It appeared from them that an application had been received from the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Compapy to register a boat at Weston. The secretary had been in- structed to reply that the examining officer was not allowed to inspect vessels outside die district. The tracings and specifications of the proposed hospital had been forwarded to the Local Government Board for approval. ATTACK ON THE ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE. The Finance Committee's minutes stated that Mr. Parry Isad been instructed to assist the secretary in the preparation

of the rate book and demand notes. Instructions had been given to the officials to arrange for some one to be in atten- dance at the Commissioners' offices from nine in the morn- ing until five in the afternoon. The Secretary (Mr. Brookes) reported the result of the appeal against the assessment of Waterloo House; and the committee recommended that the portion occupied by the caretaker should be separated from the other portion of the premises, by bricking up the door- ways, after which the appeal should be renewed. lib% J. J. SPEAKMAN proposed that the minutes be adopted, and Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion. Mr. SHAW observed that if the Assessment Committee of the Runcorn Union were really such a red-tape body of individuals as to make a request such as that referred to in the minutes, before they would meet the requirements of the Commissioners by striking out the rates for the house, the sooner the ratepayers knew what sort of men the Board had to deal with and the better. There was no beneficial occu- pation of Waterloo House; and it seemed exceedingly singular that, under such circumstances, the Commissioners should be called upon to pay rates for it. Indeed, it appeared to him perfectly absurd. He hoped that there would be another application made on the subject to the Assessment Committee, so that they might be made aware of the grounds on which the Board were expected to pay rates for property which was not tenanted. The CHAIRMAN said he thought it was the custom in some towns. If, however, the Board adopted the recommendation of the committee, they defeated their own object. The caretaker was put in the house to look after the premises; but if they bricked off his part of the house from the main portion, then they might as well take him away altogether. Mr. NORMAN wanted to know what Mr. Handley, who was a member of the Assessment Committee, had to say about the question. (Laughter.) Mr. HANDLEY remarked that when the question first came before the Assessment Committee he told them frankly that he was a member of the Board of Commissioners as well as an overseer, and he preferred not to say anything on the sub- ject. tle (Mr. Handley) saw the difficulties of the Assess- ment Committee. At a previous meeting of the committee, Mr. Norman, in answer to the chairman, very pointedly told him that they could not let Waterloo House. The chairman of the committee said that if the Board were not in a position to let the premises to a tenant of course there was an occupa- tion, and, therefore, whether they bricked it up or not, the I assessment could not be reduced. It was quite possible within the next few days that they would have the matter further under discusision, so that they might defer the question of the assessment until that time. Mr. SHAW: Because you are not in a position to let it, that does not make it tenantable. Mr. HANDLEY: It is so far as this Board is concerned. It is an infectious diseases hospital, and nothing can alter that yiew of it. Mr. SHAW: I beg to differ from Mr. Handley. That house has never been an infectious diseases hospital. It was a dwelling-house. The CHAIRMAN : There have been cases in it? Mr. SHAW: There have been no cases there since Mr. Beasley left the house. If it was a hospital before, it has not been one since. Mr. HANDLEY said the Local Government Board bad never admitted its use as a dwelling-house. They always referred to it as an hospital. After a short conversation, Mr. SHAW moved that the minute be expunged. Mr. SPEAKMAN seconded the amendment. For the amendment the following members voted:— Messrs. Handley, Shaw, Hazlehurst, Lake, Whittaker, and P. Speakmam. Against :—Messrs. Williams, Norman, and J. J. Speakman.

div.head: FREE LIBRARY QUESTION.
div.p: THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION.

Mr. NORMAN wished to know how the Free Library was proceeding. Mr. HAZLEIMRST.—It is all right Mr. Chairman. (Laughter.) We shall be receiving the approval of the hospital plans shortly, when the question can be discussed. Until that time I do/lit chink we can do anything. The CHAIRMAN.—I am rather glad the question has been asked, but Ido not see any connection between Waterloo House and the Free Library. Ma. HAZLEHURST.-At the present time the Local Go- vernment Board regard Waterloo House as an hospital They will cease to do so when the plans are passed for the hospital on Runcorn Hill. We can then have the whole question be- fore us more definately. Mr. SHAW thought Mr. Hazlehurst had made a mistake in supposing that the Commisioners could devote a certain sum of money besides the amount collected by the rate for a particular purpose. If any gentleman in the town would give them a building to be used as a library, they could accept it, but for the library they could only use the money which was collected for it.
Mr. HAzLEHunsT.—Very well, we could rent a portion o: Waterloo House.

Mr. HANDLEY.-If Mr. Shaw will allow me, I will quote that portion of the Act, which says "that the governing body can appropriate any surplus loans or buildings they may possess for the purpose of a public library."
. . . . The CHAIRMAN.—The Act also saws that the rate must not exceed one penny in the L, and I don't see how Waterloo House can be kept up on that.
. . HAZLEHURST.—We should not want the whole premises. The subject then dropped.
THE VACANCY ON THE BOXED.

On the motion of the Chairman, the meeting was then adjourned to Thursday, February 16th, for the purpose of filling up the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. Lyon. This terminated the public business.

div.head: FRODSHAM,
div.p: FRODSHAM,

POLICE CASES.—At the Occasional Court House, Frod- sham, before Mr. E. A. Wright, on Saturday, Wm. Davies was charged with frequenting Bridge-lane with intent to commit a felony. P.C. Fellows stated that he met the pri- soner at one o'clock in the morning with a sack of coals on his back. The prisoner was committed to prison for 14 days with hard labour.—On Monday, John Ainsworth was charged with stealing three cabbages, value 6d., from open land belonging to Mr. John Challoner. P.S. Johnson proved the case, and stated that he saw the prisoner in the field with the cabbages at midnight on Saturday. The prisoner was committed to prison for 14 days with hard labour. A NOVEL CLIENT.—The other day a cow belonging to Mr. John E. Bate, visited the office of Messrs. Ashtpn and Jolliffe, solicitors, Frodsham, and after upsetting the furni- ture in the entrance office proceeded upstairs for a consulta- tion with the principal. Not being in possession however, of the simple fee, its instructions were not taken, but advice tendered gratis to beat a retreat was accepted with good grace, and safely accomplished, notwithstanding the unusual proportions of the unwelcome client. UNION CHURCH, SUTTON WEAVER.—The annual tea to the parents of children attending the Union Church Sunday School was given on Wednesday afternoon, and a meeting was held in the evening, when Mr. J. 0. Jackson presided. Mr. Arthur Rigby read the report of the Sunday school , work during the past year, after which a long programme, consisting of recitations, songs, &c, which were excellently rendered and loudly applauded, was gone through by the Sunday scholars and choir. The names of the scholars who took part in the programme were Mary Lawrinson, Sarah Worrall, Ada Boden, Jessie Thomas, Sarah Boden, Sarah Bennion. Sarah Moores, Emily Froo•gart, Lizzie Hayes, Martha Savage, Ruth Foyer, Jessie Grasspole, Annie Hunt, Joseph Millar, Samuel Wilkinson, Ernest Caldwell, William Thomas, Joseph Froggart, and Samuel Helsby. "ARE THE STARS INHABITED ? "—OR Friday evening, a lecture on the above subject was delivered in the Town Hall, Frodsham, by the Rev. J. Jones, of Brecon. The chair was taken by the Rev. F. F. Edmonds. There was only a moderate attendance, as usual on such occasions in Frod- sham. Having regard to the sparseness of the audience, the rev, lecturer volunteered to give one of three lectures which he audience might choose. viz.:—"Are the stars inhabi- :ed ? " " President Garfield," or "Rules of Life, illustrated

With the fables of Esop." The first lecture was selected by a majority of five, and the audience were treated to an in- teresting and scientific lecture. Mr. Jones gave his opinion in the affirmative, and maintained with all the force of logic from analogy and scripture, that the stars are itfhabited. He based his arguments from scripture upon Genesis ii. 1, Nehemiah ix. 6, Psalm viii. 3 and 4, Psalm xxxiii. 6, and Isaiah xlv. 12 and 18. The astronomieal discoveries were ably treated by the lecturer. At the close a vote of thanks, proposed by the Rev. D. Schofield, and seconded by the Rev. R. P. Borwick, was accorded to the lecturer, and a similar compliment paid to the chairman on the motion of the Rev. R. Trotter, seconded by the lecturer. A collection was made to defray expenses. WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS.—The annual sermons in aid of the Wesleyan Home Missions Fund were preached in Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, on Sunday last, by the Rev. T. Butcher, of the Wesleyan College, -Didsburv. A public meeting was held in the same chapel on Tuesday evening, when Mr. Proud, of Frodsham, presided. The meeting was opened with prayer by the Rev. J. M. Bamford, and the Chairman gave an address in which he advocated the cause of home missions, and made some very practical remarks as to the necessity of extending the work in Frodsham.—The Rev. J. M. Bamford read the report and stated that the home mission fund had aided 272 circuits during the past year, in addition to those receiving special grants, and supported 100 home missionary ministers. The total income of the society during the past year was £31,212, and the expenditure ' £33,947 4s. id. The juvenile collectors had collected the sum of £l6 183. 42d. The names of those who had col- lected upwards of £2 were Miss Ellen Simcock, £3 Ils. 3d. ; Miss Alice Edmunds, £3 Os. id.; and Miss Emily Proud, a 9s. 51-d. The total amount contributed by the circuit was £2l 12s. 5d., being a slight increase over the previous year.—The Rev. F. W. Briggs, M.A., chairman of the Liver- pool district, presented each of the juvenile collectors with a book, and afterwards addressed the meeting, giving par- ticulars of his experience in home mission work in East London.—A selection of anthems was given during the evening by a number of ladies and gentlemen who are mem- bers of the congregation, and Mr. Pickering presided at the organ with his usual ability. A vote of thanks to the chair- man and lecturer brought the meeting to a close. The total collections at the sermons aud meeting amounted to , 7s. 4d.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Thursday, John Mee, machinist, who had been found guilty of maliciously wounding Ellen Briercliffe, barmaid at the Ship Inn, Bolton, by shooting at her, was sentenced to penal servitude for five years.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, FEMWARY 11, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, FEMWARY 11, 1882.
RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
IMPORTANT MEETING.

On Wednesday afternoon, the monthly meeting of the Runcorn Burial Board was held at the cemetery offices. Mr. Coleburn presided, and there were also present Messrs. Moss, Handley, Norman, Littler, Briscoe, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary).

STATISTICS. The monthly report of the Secretary showed that the interments for the month ending the 25th nit, had beela 20, against 25 in the corresponding period last year. The burials for the ten months en4ing January 25, were 200, as com- pared with 251 in the same time in 1881. The fees received from the 25th March last year, to the 25th January, amour ted to £196 15s. 2d., as against £2OB 12s. 2d. in the corresponding period last year, being a decrease of £ll 17s.

THE DEPUTY CORONER AND THE BOARD. Mr. SALKELD reported that the Deputy Coroner (Mr. Worsley) had expressed his satisfaction at the arrangements which the Board had made for holding inquests at the cemetery offices in the case of bodies taken to the mortuary. The CHAIRMAN remarked that he was very glad to know that the Deputy Coroner had expressed such an opinion. THE REV. CANON BARCLAY AND THE PAYMENT OF FEES TO ; DISSENIING MINISTERS. The SECRETARY said that as a little difficulty had arisen in respect to the payment of fees to Dissenting ministers, the Vicar of the Parish was in attendance, and desired the Board to grant him an interview on the subject. A child named O'Neil, ard two years, was buried at the cemetery on the 12th December, and previous to the funeral he received an order from M. Wright, relieving officer, stating that the body must be interred in unconsecrated ground. When the mother brought the order to the office, it was read over to her, and she said the child "must be buried in Roman Catholic ground," as she belonged to that body of Christians. He said "Very well, if the parents say that the child must be buried in Roman Catholic ground, it must be done." The , mother said that the funeral must be conducted by the Rev. Father Fennelly (Catholic priest). He (the speaker) con- sulted with his clerk aud Mr. Ford, and said "Well, the matter must be conducted in the usual way, and Father Fennelly must bury the child and receive the fees." The funeral accordingly took place, and the body was interred "in the Roman Catholic ground," and the fee was paid to Father Fennelly. The next case arose on 11th ult., when Mrs. Hewitt, of Wivern-place, was interred in the consecrated part of the cemetery. The Rev. Evan Williams (St. John's Presbyterian Chapel), stated that he should claim to con- duct the service in the consecrated chapel. A short time previous, he (Mr. Salkeld) had seen a report to the effect that a Dissenting minister had claimed the right of reading the burial service in the consecrated chapel, if the inter- ment took place in the consecrated part of the cemetery. Under these circumstances, he considered that it was a ques• tion not for him, or Mr. Ford, the sexton, to settle. He accordingly told Mr. Ford that if Mr. Williams demanded to go into the consecrated chapel, he must be allowed to do so, but the matter must be brought before the Burial Board. On Mr. Ford telling Mr. Williams the decision arrived at by him (the speaker), that gentleman answered "Well, I don't wish to give any offence to the Burial Board, or to the Rev. Canon Barclay. My desire is simply to state that I claim the right." Under the circumstances of the Rev. E. Williams not enforcing his claim, the ceremony was read in the unconsecrated chapel, and the body buried in the conse- crated ground. Mr. Moss observed that the only question which itappeared to him the Board had to consider, was, whether the secretary required any instructions for his future guidance in a matter of this kind. Mr. SALKELD said he should be glad to receive such in- structions, as he did not like to take the responsibility of

acting without them. Mr. HANDLEy (Congregationalist), did not think the Nonconformists had any right to the use of the consecrated chapel, as it had been consecrated by special deed, under the seal of the late Bishop of Chester. If the chapel had not been consecrated, it would have remained a part of the cemetery grounds, and the Nonconformists had no right to the ground under the Burial Laws' Amendment Act, 1880. Mr. BRISCOE quite agreed with the remarks of Mr. Handley. Mr. Moss: But the Act does not mentiork the consecrated _
Mr. HANDLEY.replied that. Mr. Moss was quite correct,

but seeing that the place had been consecrated by special deed, that met the case. The 7 and 8 Vic., c. 101, sec. 31, gave the Guardians power to pay for the expenses of pauper burials out of t%,e poor rates, and also conferred authority

upon the husband, wife, or next of kin of the deceased, to choose in which ground the corpse should be buried, the fee, or fees, to be paid according to the custom of the place. The duty of the Board was simply to carry out the instruc- tions they received. Mr. BRISCOE observed that the vicar was taking the course he had adopted in order that the matter might be properly settled. Mr. Moss remarked that if the vicar stated he had a legal claim to the fee, it was a question whether the Board ought not to have withheld it in Father Fennelly's case. Mr. LITTLEu thought it had been decided on a previous occasion, that the fee should be paid to the minister who officiated, and if the vicar thought he had a right to it, it should be left to him to take legal proceedings. Mr. HANDLEY was of opinion that the vicar could not proceed against the Burial Beard, as they had received a proper notice. If the vicar had received an order to bury in the unconsecrated ground, he would have received the fee. The CHAIRMAN pointed out that if the vicar thought he had a case, he could take it to the County Court. He saw, not long ago, that Mr. Horatio Lloyd had given his opinion in a similar case, tried at Carnarvon. In that action the Parish Clerk had claimed the fees for officiating in. the un- consecrated portion of the cemetery, on the ground that he received them for burials in the consecrated portion, and his predecessors had been paid them from time immemorial. Owing to the Parish Clerk not being able to clearly prove the immemorial usage, he was nonsnited. The Rev. Canon Barclay, who had been requested to attend by Mr. Whittaker, then entered the room. The CANON first excused himself for intruding upon the business of the Board, but added that having always been treated very courteously by the members, and there never having been any hitch between them and himself—which was a very different state of matters to that which existed in some parishes—he thought it better to state what he con- sidered his grievance to them, so that if they thought proper they might redress it. The case he had to bring before them was one in which a child had been buried in uncon- secrated ground, and the burial fee had beerepald to a Dis- senting minister. They were aware that when the original "Burial 'Acts Beyond the Metropolis" was passed—under which the Runcorn cemetery was constituted—the tees and rights of the incumbent of the parish as regarded the inter- ments of paupers' were protected. As he read the 18 and 19, Vic., he alone had the right to receive the fees as Vicar of Runcorn, and he did not know of any Act which altered that law. He strongly maintained that his right to receive the fees arose from a custom which was immemorial. The CHAIRMAN asked whether this custom had been un- broken from time immemorial, because if it had been it would be abrogated? Mr. HANDLEY was of opinion that the Burial Board had really nothing to do with this question,as they had received proper instructions to bury the child in the unconsecrated part of the cemetery, accompanied by an expressed wish that the Rev. Father Fennellv should inter it. Those in- structions were carried out, and the secretary, as he was hound to do according to the law, paid the fees over to the Catholic priest. • Canon 03s..ncLA.v said the only course open to him was to enter a friendly suit against the secretary in the county, court, in which. of course, the Board would defend the posi- tion of their servant. He had never had any trouble with the Burial Board before, and he should have liked the matter in dispute to have been settled in some other way. No doubt a settlement of the matter would be arrived at in this way. He regretted having to adopt such a course, but, perhaps, both for himself and the Burial Board, it would be better that a definite deeision should be arrived at. Mr. HANDLEY (1.0 the Vicar) : I think you will see that the Burial Board could not have acted differently, having received this notice from Mr. Wright. Canon BARCLAY: lam not complaining of the Burial Board; but I think it necessary to draw their attention to the case, because Mr. Wright could send his:brother, or the gardener of the cemetery, to officiate at a funeral. Mr. LITTLER considered that when a man did certain work, whether it was in the consecrated or the unconsecrated part of the cemetery, he was entitled to the payment. Canon BARCLAY: Have you heard Mr. 'Glen's opinion? Mr. LITTLER: Yes. Canon BARCLAY: Then it is quite contrary to yours. Mr. LlrreEn still contended (that the person who per- formed the burial service ought to be paid the money. Canon BARCLAY: If that is your opinion' whyshould Father Fennelly inter any more than the Rev. Mr. Lockwood, of Halton, Mr. Preston, of Runcorn, or Mr. Ford, of Weston Point? Mr. LITTLER: I am not discussing a point of law. Canon BARCLAY said that Father Fennelly had no right to receive the fee, and if the parents of the child wished that gentleman to read the service, it was their duty to pay him (the Catholic priest) the fees, and the duty of the Burial Board to pay the fees to him (the Canon), and not to a Dis- senting minister. He had nothing to do with the notice given to the Burial Board. If he sent them a notice to burn the place down, would they do it ? He contended that the notice was illegal. Mr. NORMAN: The question is whether our secretary was justified in paying Father Fennelly or not? Canon BARCLAY was of opinion that the Board were justified morally, but legally their action was a mistake. He maintained that, as vicar of the parish, he should have had the fees. The SECRETARY then briefly stated what had taken place in regard to the claims made by the Rev. Evan Williams, and the opinion of Mr. James Handley. The VICAR said that the Congregational minister at Chester gave notice to the burial authorities there that he should claim that right. They accordingly took the opinion of the Solicitor General upon the subject, who expressed an opinion quite opposed to the minister's claim, which opinion was confit med by Mr. Osborne Morgan. The SECRETARY remarked that he should have been glad if the Rey. E. Williams had stated the case to the Board, but he placed it before Mr. Ford, the sexton. The VICAR: It seems to me that there is a much stronger case for an alien service to be performed in the church than

there is here where there is nothing but a consecrated chapel; and if there is a plea for having the service inside the walls, it is stronger there, on general grounds. Certainly the Act does not allow it. If the law is unfair on the sub- ject, let it be amended. I thought that as Mr. Salkeld briefly mentioned this matter to me at the Savings' Bank meeting, he must have supposed that I had some little smattering of ecclesiastical law, which I ought to have. The CHAIRMAN (to the Vicar) : We are exceedingly obliged to you. The VICAR: I think that it is always better where there is a mistake, or hitch, to point it out personally. Mr. Moss said he would move "That the question raised by the Rev. Canon Barclay, relative to a fee being paid to Father Fennelly in the case of Alice O'Neil, on December 12th, be referred to the next meeting of the Finance Com- mittee."
Mr. NORMAN seconded the resolution, which was passed unanimously, and the proceedings terminated.

but although the Highway Committee met on Wednesday he had heard nothing from this quarter since. He called at the office with respect to the matter, and they gave him the summons. •He was quite certain he had not been asked to remove the obstruction. He had not been told that he should be summoned if he did not.—Mr. Ashton: But the police are not bound to tell you that if you offend again they will summon you. If you commit an offence you are liable to be summoned.—Superintendent Williamson: I don't wish to press the case against Mr. Unsworth.—The defen- dant: I don't wish to enjoy a privilege that is denied to other tradesmen in the town. If the police had told me that this thing could not be allowed, I would have taken it it; but other tradesmen in the town do this thing all the year round. Even right opposite the police station it is done, and no notice is taken of it. I have asked those tradesmen if they have been spoken to by the police, and they say "No." Why should Ibe summoned ? I may now say that we did not put out the box on Saturday, because if we had done wrong we were sorry, and did not wish to offend again.— The Chairman: You have pleaded guilty to this charge, and we have no alternative but to fine you. We shall fine you , in the nominal sum of is. and 9s. Gd. costs.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before Messrs. George Pilkington and Holbrook
Gaskell:jun.

THE WAY THE RATEPAYER-S' MONEY GOES.—Martin He enegan was brought up on a warrant, charged with desert- ing his wife and family, and leaving them chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union.—Mr. Golf, relieving officer, proved the case —lt appeared that the prisoner, who is a labourer, formerly lived at Moss Bank, at which time he earned from 255. to 30s. per week. On the 31st August last he absconded, leaving his wife and family chargeable to the union. The cost of their maintenance was about £lO. Prisoner was apprehended a few days ago in New- castle-upon-Tyne.—Mr. Golf said such cases as this were be- coming very prevalent in the township, and he hoped that the Bench would deal severely with the prisoner.—He was was sent to gaol for three months, with hard labour. A STURDY BEGGAR.—WM. Jones was charged with beg- ging in Alford-street.—Sergeant Strickland saw the prisoner begging from several people on Saturday night, and took him into custody, on which he became so violent that asistarce had to be obtained in order to take him to the police station. On Jones being searched he was found to be in possession of ninepence in coppers, and a bagful' of bread. —He was sent to gaol for 14 days, with hard labour. DESERTERS —James Shaw and Sidney Redwood were proved to have deserted from the 40th Regiment of Foot, stationed at Warrington, and were each sent to Walton gaol

to await an escort. MISCELLANEOUS.-ThOS. Wilkes, a Shropshire man, was sentenced to seven days' imprisonment for begging; and Sarah Ellen Hunt, a girl, was ordered to be confined until the rising of the court for a similar offence.—Martin May, an old offender, was sentenced as a rogue and vagabond to three months' imprisonment for sleeping out.—Patrick Roach, .Tohn Cuaningham, and john Grundy, navvies, were sentenced to a month's imprisonment for being drunk and disorderly and assaulting the police, while the wife of the last-named was discharged.—George Wilson, in default of finding sureties, was committed to gaol for 14 days for causing a disturbance at Woolton, on October 31st last.— Annie Turton, an old woman of intemperate habits, was com- mitted for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for obtaining by false pretences three pairs of boots and a pair of slippers from Mr. William Williams, bookmaker, Waterloo-road.
VVEDNESDAY.—Before Me3srs. J. Bibby (Chairman), George Pilkington and John :Brock.

AN HOTEL MANAGER CONVICTED OF DRUNKENNESS.— John Barclay Reynolds, manager at West Bank Hotel, was summoned for haying been found drunk on his master's licensed premises, on the 31st ult., and he was fined 20a., and 15s. costs. A QUARREL BETWEEN RIVAL PlLOTS.—Thomas Ogden was charged by Joseph Ford, an elderly man who is well known in the police contt, with assaulting him, on the 2nd inst., and Ford was charg,ed by Ogden with a like offence.— Both were ordered to find sureties to keep the peace.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

PRESENTATION AT WINSFORD.—The pupils Of the Academy presented the principal, Mr. 3. Buckley, F.R.G.S., and hon. secretary, T.C.L., on Tuesday last with a gold ring, Albert and seal, a spectrascope, and a pocket book, on the occasion of his 50th birthdairanniversary. NEW SCHOOL BOARD, OVER.—The newly elected Board which will enter upon its duties at the next meeting, and choose its chairman and vice-chairman,is regarded by many unfavourably, but new men will be able to show what they can do for the ratepayers. BUILDING SOCIETY, WINSFORD.—The annual meeting of this society was held on the 3rd inst., at the Office in High- street. Mr. Edmund Leigh was called to the chair. Mr. Harvey read his statement, which had been audited by Messrs. Buckley and Leigh, and which showed there would be a balance of nearly £3OO when all claims were paid; a very satisfactory result. The retiring direetors. Messrs. Francis, Daggatt, Leigh, and Smallwood were re-elected. THE DROWNING FATALITY AT WINSFORD.—On Saturday an inquest was behl on the body of John Stanway, of Station-road, Winsford, who, while trying to reach his works to sleep there on the previous morning, soon after mid-night, fQII into the Weaver, and was drowned. The jury returned I a verdict of" Accidental death." LAUNCH AT WINSFORD.—On Saturday a fine steamer was launched at Knight's Grange Dockyard, Winsford. It had been built of the best English oak, under the superinten- dence of Mr. Edward Newall, foreman for the firm of Geo. Deakin, Limited. The length over all is 89 feet, breadth, 21 feet, depth in hold, 9ft. 3in., and this is the largest steamer which has been built by the firm. There were many present at the launch, among whom was the senior member of the firm, Mr. J. Buckley Deakin. The name of " Phcenix," was given by Captain Roliert Hulse, who will command her while in the salt trade. SALT TRADE ron JANUARY.—The export trade during last month was a fair average. After so mild a winter we may expect all the closed parts to be opened. Prices quoted are really nominal and very irregular. Common salt runs, Es 6d ; butter. lOs ; Calcutta, and .4 including mats, lOs ; shute stoved, us. 6d ; handed square, 169-; best fishery, 13s; second ditto. 12s; factory filled with sacks, 255; best Prussian rock, Os; picked lump rock, 9s. 6d ; ground rock, Ist quality, 8s; rough, 7s; rough riddlings, Os. 6d ; soiled agricultural, Os. Freights to all parts are higher than last year and likely to so continue. The effect of the large loss of ships last autumn is still felt. The shipments to America were 17.311; against 23,147 in January, 1881. To our colonies 0, against 2,868 • to West Indies and South America, 1,971, against 2,221; Africa, 2,295, against, 3,052; East Indies, 19,956, against 21,393 ; to Australia, 2,669, against 5,500; to Prussia, 305, against 0 ; to Russian ports' 0, against 0; Baltic ports, 1,702 against 477 ; France, 105, affainst 48; British coasts, 2,434, against 2,017; Holland, 1,166, against 1,044; Belgium, 4,038, against 2,867. The grand total from tbe Mersey reaches for January last, 61,252, against 67,106 in Jan nary previous year.

LITMAT. ACTION AGAINST A LYMM SURGEON. On Tuesday, at the Chester Assizes, before Mr. Justice Lindley, an action was brought by Mr. Cartwright, surgeon, Oswestry, to recover the value of a promissory note for £lOO, dated the 28th June, 1880, from Mr. Rawson, senior, surgeon. of Lymm.—Mr. APlntyre and Mr. Higgins ap- peared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Marshall for the defendant. —The proceedings having been briefly opened by Mr. Hig- gins, the jury was addressed by Mr. Marshall, who ex- plained that for some few years before November, 1879. the plaintiff was practising as a surgeon in the town of Lymm. About November he became desirous of leaving, and accord- ingly auvertised his practice for sale in the British Medical Journal. The defendant, also a medical practitioner of ex- perience, who had been for some years practising in the town of Bowdon, saw the advertisement and wrote to the plaintiff in regard to the matter. The advertisement was to this effect: "For sale a practice of between £4OO and £5OO a year, in a' very pleasant locality, and an increasing neigh- bourhood, Preliminary communications passed between the parties, and on the 3rd December the defendant wrote to the effect that he could not take over the business on the terms offered. The plaintiff accordingly agreed to lower the premium he required, and asked the defendant to allow a personal interview, in order that he might judge whether or not the defendant would be a suitable suc- cessor. An interview took place, and the plaintiff being satisfied with the defendant's personal qualifica- tions, the condition as to the patronage of the plaintiff's relations being extended was confirmed. The next letter received by, the defendant was in the form of a memo- randum setting forth the amount of his receipts. It was as follows : "Receipts from practice (average for the last three years, 1876-77-78), over £4OO a year, including £lO9 from clubs. Purchaser would be required to take the lease of house off my hands and pay £4OO. Reason for leaving, going to my late father's practice." A further letter was .sent to the defendant stating the amount of fees that were charged, and pointing out that they might with impunity be increased. The defendant agreed to pay £2OO down, and £lOO more on the Ist August, 1881. Accordingly he /mid the £2OO, and gave a promissory note for the £lOO, which was the subject of the action. The defendant took up the practice, and at the end of a year, when the promissory note had become due, wrote to the effect that he was disappointed with his bargain, and that his income had not amounted to more than £250. Ife thought the plaintiff had misstated the facts as to his income, and accused him of not introducini him to as many persons as he promised to do. He therefore claimed a setoff for false representation. As to the £lOO, he asked that that might stand over. The plaintiff, however, took action at once to recover it, and these proceedings were coosequeutly brought forward. The plaintiff allowed the defendant to examine his books, and it was admitted that they showed an income of the amount that the plaintiff stated in his preliminary letters.—His Lordship, interposing here, remarked that after that admission there was nothing left in the case but the question of damages for non-introduc- don. There could be no fraud in the plaintiff's statements if the kooks bore out those statements.—The defendant was then examined by Mr. Marshall. He corroborated the learned counsel's statements, but in uoss-examinatica ad- mitted that he c,ould not say he had been introduced to less than 200 persons. He was still carrying on his bueiness at Bowdon.—Ris. Lordship, again interposing, said be did not see anything in the case to go to the jury. Ha had allowed the mattes to go on in order that the plaintiff's character might 're vindicated. II a would, therefore, eve 3 'verdict fo7 the var,ourat claimed,

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

SATURDAY.--Before Mr. Alfred Thomas. BUYING WISDOM AT A DEAR RATE.—Thomas Jones, Mary Casey, and Mary Jane Ann Gallagher were charged with stealing 265., oz. of tobacco, and some matches, the money and property of Charles Dowdall. The prosecutor is a seaman on board a schooner called the Gladsto.ne, and came to Runcorn in the vessel on the previous Thursday. In the evening he went into the town, and met a young man named Peter Ormes, near Regent-street. They visited several public-houses, and ultimately entered the Blue Ball beer-house, where they found the prisoners Casey and Jones. Afterwards all agreed to go with Jones to his house, and on the way were joined by Gallagher. Dowdall arranged to remain at the house all night with Casey, and placed his clothes near where he slept. Ormes remained downstairs. On the following morning, Dowdall found that his trousers pockets had been rifled. He missed the sum of 265., a knife, two match boxes, and oz. of tobacco. Jones and Gallagher were in the same room, and he told them they had better give him his money. Casey was in bed, and he could get no answer from her. He then went downstairs, and woke Ormes. Gallagher denied all knowledge of the theft, and Jones offered to show him where the police station was. Instead of taking him there, however, he took him down to the docks. He declined to go any further, but he was afterwards shown the police station by a boy.—Sergt. _

Walley said the prisoners Casey and Gallagher were women of ill fame, and Jones lived with them, at the house in Pool- lane. On searching the house on Friday morning, he found in the chimney of the front room a match box which con- tained 35., and in the back room chimney, the knife pro- duced. Upstairs, on the ledge of the window sash, lie found five florins and five shillings. On being charged with the robbery, the prisoners made no reply. He also examined Ormes at the station, but only found 2,1-. upon him

which Dowdall said be had given to him. —On being formally charged, the prisoners denied all knowledge of the robbery.—They were each committed for trial at the Knutsford Quarter Sessions, and bail was refused. SMART CAPTURE.—Thornas Green, a man about 32 years of age, was charged with stealing a pair of trousers, the pro- perty of George Hill, iron turner, Union-street —Prosecutor said that on the night of the Ist inst. he heard a noise in the back yard of his house, caused by the falling of a clothes prop. On examining the clothes line be missed a pair of trousers. He afterwards looked over a low wall, which divides the yard from an adjoining field, and saw the prisoner running away by the side of the houses, in the direction of Halton. He rushed into the street, with the object of meeting the prisoner, but he did net come out there, having ran back. He (witness) afterwards went on the road towarAs Halton, and met Green, who had some- thing bulky under his coat, which proved to be the missing trousers. The prisoner, who, from his conduct in court, appears to be a fellow with a good deal of assurance, said, • "Who authorised you ?” which threw the prosecutor off his guard, and then ran off, and made his escape.—Prisoner now denied his guilt, and said he should not have the least difficulty in proving an ftlibi, if the police would assist him. —Superintendent Williamson said he would see that every help was given to the man, who was then remanded on this charge until Monday.—On that day he was brought up on remand, before Messrs. IV. Bankes and Alfred Thomas, and called John Black, the keeper of a lodging house in Anne- street West, Widnes, who said the prisoner's statement that he was at his house on Saturday evening was quite correct. He, however, could not help him in the matter of the rob- bery, as be was unable to fix the time to half an hour when Green was at the house.—Prisoner was then committed to the Knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial.—At Saturday's Court the prisoner was also committed 14 days, with hard labour, for having broken /S squares of glass in the window of the police cell on Friday night. MONPAY.—Before Messrs. W. Bankes (chairman) and Alfred Thomas. _ _

A DinerY CnistN-Evil:3-a-rah Allabey was ordered' to pay a fine of is. and costs for permitting the chimney of her dwelling-house to be on fire on the 27th ult. A CRUEL BOATMAN.—John Stevens was charged/ with cruelty to a horse by kicking it.—lnspector Hollingworth said that on the 24th ult. he was on Doctor's bridge- when he saw the derendant driving; a horse, which was dragging a heavily laden boat along the towing path. As Stevens fastened a leather strap round the horse, he kicked it in a savage manner in the lower part of one leg.—Superintendent Williamson, who was crossing the bridge at the time, corro- borated.—The Chairman said the defendant was a most brutal fellow, and he would be. ordered to pay a fine of 40s. and costs, and, in default of payment, be sent to gaol one month. GAMBLING.—Three lads named Aaron Ankers, Edward Ackerley, and Thomas Welsh were charged with playing at pitch and toss in Mill-street, on the 25th ult. The case was proved by Inspector Eollingworth. Witnesses were called who stated that Ackerley was not present.-Welshwas fined is., and 12s. 6d. costs, and Ankers is. and 9s. 6d. costs. The case against Ackerley was dismissed.—Superintendent Williamson said he was determined to put down the practice, which prevailed to a most alarmieg extent in Runcorn. THE SAN-AGE ASSAULT ON AN OLD WOMAN.—The oase agains Patrick Haverty for grossly assaulting an old woman named Catherine Ford was called on, but defendant did not appear, and a warrant was granted for his apprehension. ANOTHER UNMANLY FELBOW.—Thomas Hushin was fined 10s., and iris. 6d. costs for striking a young woman named Kate Carrol in the face, on the 29th ult, and in default of payment, ordered to be sentrto gaol 14 days. A BEI3RHOUSE Row.—The court was occupied a consider- able time in hearing a case in which Edward Broder, Wm. Broder, 'ohn Nockton, end. James Rewbottom, all young men, were summoned for assaulting a powerful looking man named Samuel Hawkins, whose eyes had been diS- figured. Hawkins was also charged with assaulting Nocitton and Edward Broder. The affray which is not of any general public interest, took place at the Manchester Arms beer- house, on the first inst. The house had been left in charge of a girl about 17 years of age, and the persons concerned in the case were playing at dominoes, when, it was alleged that .Hawkins charged one of the men with cheating him; A rough and tumble fight followed., in which Hawkins alleged he was very badly used, and afterwards thrown into the street. On the other hand, it was said that Hawkins com- menced the disturbance, and used a knife, and the blows he received were merely the result of the other men trying to keep him from stabbing them.—The magistrates dismissed the cases. ALLEGED OBSTRUCTION OF THE FOOTPATH BY A TRADES- MAN.—Messrs. Unsworth Brothers, hatters, hosiers, and out- fitters, High-street, were charged with causing an obstruc- tion of the footpath in that street by placing a stall upon it on the :13th ult.—Mr. Jabez Unsworth, who represented the ' firm, said he was not there to deny the facts; but such things were commonly placed outside in the town by others. —The Clerk (Mr. Ashton) : You believe you have a right to put them there P—Mr. Unsworth: No, nothing of the sort. I do not say that I have the right.—The Chairman : You feel you are not doing anything contrary to law?—Mr. Unsworth said other tradesmen in the town did the same thing, but proceedings were not instituted against them, and lie thought it unfair that his firm should have been singled out from many.' P.C. Bossons said he was on duty on the 28th ult., in High- street, between the hours of seven and ten, and during that time, in passing Messrs. Unsworth's shop, he saw a great crowd was collected there, quite blocking up the parapet. A sort of small stall had been erected right beside the window. On the sfall were a number of boxes. Near it stood one of Mr. Unsworth's askistants. He was pricing the goods, and handed them to the people standing near. He spoke to the assistant, who, in reply, said, " 'You had better speak to the guy'nor." He then went inside and pointed out to Mr. Unsworth that an obstruction was being caused. The shop at that time was crowded with people. In reply to his observations he understood Mr. Unsworth to say, "Oh, very well." He then left the shop, but he noticed that the stall remained till ten o'clock. He had since seen it in the same position—on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednes- day.—The Chairman: It was on the public footpath, was it not 2—Witness: It was, sir. The footpath was completely covered with people looking at goods in the shop.—Mr. Unsworth (to the officer): You have not had any previous causes of complaint 9—Superintendent Williamson : Per- haps, your worships, I might be allowed to say a word in die matter. Mr. Unsworth appears to be labouring under the impression that he has been made a scapegoat of by the authorities. Now, lam sure we have no feeling whatever in the matter. Mr. Unmoral hid ample notice given him to discontinue the practice complained of. I had great reluctance to putting in motion these proceedings against Mr. Unsworth. I may say that I don't wish to prevent the trading people of Runcorn from gettiag as good a business as they can, but it seems to me that it is my duty to see the public have their rights as well.—Mr. Unsworth: Am I al- lowed to speak 9—The Clerk: You can speak in mitigation of the penalty.—The Chairman pointed out that the first off ence was committed on Saturday, but it was repeated on the Mon- day, Tuesday, and Wed uesdaY following.—Mr. Unsworth said that the kind of obstruction with which he was charged took place throughout the town. He had recently con- versed with a tradesman doing business near the Police Court. He told him of the summons, and thereupon this tradesman told him that he also put boxes out last Saturday, and the police said nothing to him.—The Clerk: That has nothing in the least to do with it.—Mr. Unsworth went on to say that the parapet was 10 feet wide, while the boxes were each eight inches long. There were three boxes. His assis: tant stood by the side of them. He had a variety of goods exposed for sale on the stall, and there certainly was a large crowd collected in the vicinity; but he maintained there was nothing in all this which nas not done by people in other parts of the town. What the officer told him was that he should report the matter to the inspector. He thought per- haps the Board of Commissioners would decide the question. He saw the chairman of the Highway Committee about it,

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held on Thursday, at the Board-room, Whiston Workhouse, Mr. S. Marsh presiding. There were also present the Revs. T. Chambers and J. Barnacle, Messrs. W. Tyrer, J. Fidler, J. T. Hall, J. Leatherbarrow, W. A. Meadows, G. J. Paris, T. Dobell, Ranson, Rowe, Jackson, Fisher, Buckley, Sadler, Gerrard, Syder, Gilbody, Penketh, and Swift ; with Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk).—The minutes of the last meeting were read and, confirmed.

WORHOUSE MISTER'S REPORT. The MASTER (Mr. W. H. Bicknell) reported that there were 515 inmates in the Workhouse this week, as compared with 518 in the previous week and 521 in the corresponding week of last year. Ther. were 127 boysand girls at Kirkdale schools. The Master's journal also contained the following entry :—Referring to the refusal to admit a sick man men- tioned at the last meeting of the Board, the Master begs to state that the man was refused admission by the portress, who acted entirely upon her own responsibility, and neglected to call the attention of the porter or master to the case. The Master knew nothing of the circumstances until a fortnight had elapsed, when he was informed by one of the Guardians. The Master has given instructions for all such cases to be referred to him in future.—Rev. T. CHAM- BERS observed that had he heard at the last meeting it was the Master to whom he was referring, he should certainly have stated the case; but it was the subordinate officer he wished to shield, because he believed it was done in igno- rance. Having got the information he wanted he was per- fectly satisfied. If it came to his notice again he should bring it before the Board.

div.head: AN OLD AND DESERVING OFFICER SUPERANNIJETED.
div.p: AN OLD AND DESERVING OFFICER SUPERANNIJETED.

The CLERK read the following letter from the Local Government Board :—" Whitehall, January 31st. —I am directed by the Local Gogernment Board to advert.to their letter of the 17th of October last, and to inform you that under the provisions of the 27th and 28th Viet., cap. 42, they consent to an annual allowance of £5O being granted by the Guardians of the Prescot Union to William Watkin, late assistant overseer for the township of Whiston, who had resigned the office in consequence of his having by reason of his old age and permanent infirmity of body, become incapable of discharging efficiently the duties of such office. EDWARD SUTTON, assistant secretary."—ln answer to a question, Mr LEATITERBARROW said Mr Watkins was 83 years of age.—The Board having continued Mr. Watkin's pay from the time he was superannuated to the end of September half-year, the Clerk was authorised to communicate with the Local Government Board with a view to getting the money sanctioned, as the Guardians would probably be surcharged with it.

FINANCIAL-TIE ARREARS OF POOR-RATE. From a statement submitted by the Clerk it appeared that since the last meeting £621 had been paid in respect of the poor-rate, of which Hale had paid £3O, P.rr £240, Prescot £lOl, Rainhill £l2O, and Tarbock £l3O. The arrears amounted to £14,106, of which Bold owed £248, Cronton £531, Ditton £837, Eccleston £2,018, Hale £3O, Halewood £633, Huyton-with-Roby £728, Knowsley £lO9, Parr £240, Rainford £172, Sutton £1,620, Whiston £3OO, Widnes £5,783, Windle £460, Little Woolton £lOO, and Much Wool- ton £3OO. Prescot,Speke, Rainhill, and Tarbock had paid up. There was a balance in, the bank of about £900.-It was resolved that the Clerk write to the overseers of those townships in arrear, pressing for immediate payment.-The CLERK read a communication from the Local Government Board stating that they had paid over to the Board's treasurer the sum of £.324 2s. 10d. being one-half of the salaries of the medical and other officers of the Union. THE COUNTY RATE PRECEPT.-CONSIDERABLE INCREASE. The CLERK stated that he had received the county rate precept for the present year, which showed that the amount of money required by the county was considerably more than had ever been demanded before. The amount was £6,593 ss. 86., as compared. with £5,411 2s. 2d. last year, an increase of £1,182 3s. 66.-In answer to Mr. Meadows, the CLERK said the increase was in the amounts charged for general purposes and the constabulary (Prescot Division), for the former of which £ss4. 7s. 9d. was charged as against £569 us. 106. last year, and for the latter £3,417 10s. 9d., as against £2,278 7s. 2d.-The CHAIRMAN, in answer to a question, said the staff of police was being increased.-The CLERK scarcely thought the increase of £l,OOO would be permanent.-Mr. FIDLER,: it has been increasing every year.-The CLERK: But not at that rate.-Mr. DOBELL re- marked that the constabulary charge was an extraordinary one, and the CLERK replied that it was.-The following are the townships comprising the Union, and the amount required from each : Bold, £156 is. 91; Cronton' £4O Bs. 2d. ; Ditton, £lOO 145.26. ; Eccleston, £529 3s. 10d. ;Hale, £4B 9s. 106.; Halewood. £224 6s. 86.; Huyton-with-Roby, £451 15s. 9d.; Knowsley, £164 2s. 7d.; Parr, £333 4s. 7d.; Present, £132 4s. 7d.; Rainford, £240 Os. 101; Rainhill, £l7B 12s. 9d.; Speke, £ll3 Os. id.; Sutton, £1192 10s. 7d.; Tarbock, £62 12s. 96.; Whiston, £244 15s. 7d.; Widnes, £llO5 12s. 01; Windle, £792 78. 106.; Woollen (Little), £lB7 19s. 5d.; Woolton (Much), £275 is. 11d.; total, £6593 ss. Bd.
THE QUESTION OF OUT-DOO.R. RELIEF TO DESERTED MARRIED WOMEN.

The Rev. T. CHAMBERS, in pursuance of notice, moved " that rule 4 of the regulations for relief adopted by the Guardians on the 20th August, 1875, be altered to 'married women with or without children deserted by their husbinds, save those three years deserted and in special cases approved of by the full Board of Guardians." He (Mr. Chambers) thought the alteration of this rule would be beneficial to the union and the ratepayers, as it vrould enable the relief com- mittees to give a little out-door relief to young women with families who were respectable and endeavouring to gain a livelihood, and enable them to detect and prevent collusion between wives and their husbands, who had deserted them. Several women with young children in the Workhouse, if granted a little out-door relief, be enabled to support them- selves and their families.—Mr. DOBELL seconded, and the motion was agreed to. RECOMMENDATION THAT AN ADDITIONAL SCHOOL ATTEN-

DANCE OFFICER BE APPOINTED. The CLERK stated that the School Attendance Committee had decided to appoint an additional school attendance officer at a salary of £BO per annum for a period of twelve , months, subject to the approval of the Guardians and the Local Government Board.-:--Mr. PARIS moved that the , recommendation be adopted. He thought that Mr. Welch was unable to devote, through want of time, that attention to the affairs of each township that was necessary.—ln answer to the Chairman the CLERK stated that the duties of the new officer would 1:e defined by the Attendance Cora- mittee.—Rev. J. BARNACLE thought a school attendance officer ought to consider it part of his duty not only to visit schools and inquire from the masters and mistresses the number of absentees for the last two or three weeks, but to see his way by some means or other to visit the parishes, so that he might pick up those who were not known to the masters and mistresses. Thus a good, great, and very efficient work would be done; but if the new officer was simply to get all his information from the teachers, who simply knew a portion—a fourth—of the absentees, then by far the greater number of children not attending school would remain unknown.—Rev. T. CHAM- BERS seconded Mr. Paris's motion. Since the meeting of the School Attendance Committee he had heard that the course they adopted had been highly approved by the town- ships which memoralized the committee.—Mr. HALL was was not sitisfied that the duties were properly performed hY the present officer, who had to devote a considerable time to his duties as registrar of marriages. With a view to the matter being properly investigated be suggested that it be referred to a special committee. Mr. TYRER did not agree with this suggestion, as the School Attendance Com- mittee had already considered the question. If the guard:ans did not think another officer was necessary. then the only thing they could do was to refer it back.—Mr. MEADOWS supported Mr. Hall's suggestion. The appointment of a new officer meant £BO per year to commence with, and the officer would no doubt expect to get as much as Mr. Welch got— LllO per year. He suggested that Mr. Seddon, the collector of repayments of relief, who travelled over the whole of the district and whose time was not fully occupied, should be asked to assist Mr. Welch,. and the guardians could offer him a little more money to make it worth his while. He thought the matter should be referred back.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS Chairman of the School Attendance Committee obseeted to the suggestion. Letters were read to the committee from gentlemen—chairmen of the various committees in the dis- trict—urging the appointment of a second officer, and he , maintained that the appointment should be made. It would be discourteous to the gentemen in question if that Board declined to appoint an additional officer as recommended.— The CLERK, in answer to Mr. Tvrer, said they could not , compel Mr. Seddon to undertake the duties.—Afer some further discussion Mr. MEADOWS moved, as am amendment, that the mattrz be referred back to the committee with a view to Mr. Seddon being appointed.—Mr. Itim, seconded, but the motion was carried by ten votes to e;ght.

MISCEIZIANEOTIS.—Edward Houghton was fined, 2s. 6d. and costs for being asleep in his cart, on Warrington-road, Bainhill,. on 31st nit.; and William Darwin, who failed to appear, was fined ss. and costs for a 1:ko offence.—TimothY I Carol, Nicholas Lawrenson, and Edward Melia (two charges)' were each fined 55., imeluding costs, for failing to send chil- dren to school.—William Collins, who was £2 1.25. in arrear with oentributions towards supporting his parents, under an order obtained by union authorities, was ordctrod to pay the amount at the rate of 2s. per week; Charles Chubb was I ordered to pay immediately £2 10s, ed. due towards support- ing his wife; andu similar case against Edward Lewis was , remanded.—Sevoral licenses went transferred.—liour lads named John Saggerson, Joseph Woodward., James Hunter, :and George Ceitchley, were brought up on remand' charged with stealing /21b. of fish, value 45., property of John Welsby, fish dealer, Prescot, on the previous Thursday night. Woodward, who had been several times previously con- victed, was committed for trial; Saggeoson was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment, and Hunter and Critchley went each fined 10s. and costs, in default 14 days.—Francis Casey, a lazy-looking fellow, charged with stealing an oven, value 25., from an unoccupied house at Whiston, property of Jobn Edwardson, was sent to vrison for two months with hard labour.—E)hraim Heyes was charged with breaking and entering er the house of Mr, Gardner, Bale View, Huyton ,Quarry 4 on Sunday evening, In the absence of Mr. Gardner and his .fimily At el:lure:4 and stv,iiri; Ss., ss.;,,d was re- manded.
